Heading: An XL problem for British passengers as airline packs up - Indian Express
Content:
Having neutralised the anti-India faction within the ruling Communist Party of Nepal-Maoists (CPN-M) by giving them plum posts, Prime Minister Pushpa Kamal Dahal 'Prachanda' began hectic exercises on Saturday in an attempt to formulate a common 'country approach' on his India visit.

He called on Nepali Congress leader G P Koirala at his residence soliciting the former Prime Minister's 'advise and guidance'. According to a Koirala aide, the former Prime Minister advised Prachanda not to go for any treaty or agreement as it was 'not within the realm of mandate' of the present Government. Koirala however, advised Prachanda to convince India and the international community that he is sincere about the peace process being taken to its logical end.

On Friday night , he along with four key ministers had dinner at the Army officers club where Army chief R Katawal, joined by senior generals, pledged full support to the Government, but there are visible discomfiture between the two on the issue of integrating Maoist combatants in the Armed Forces, something the present Government has set to implement within the coming six months. Apparently, this was for the first time that Defence Minister Ram Bahadur Thapa Badal met senior officers.

Prachanda also had a meeting with Indian ambassador Rakesh Sood. "The issues that would figure during the Prime Minister's visit in Delhi were discussed," Sood told media persons outside the Prime Minister's office.

Prachanda told the ambassador that review of the 1950 treaty on peace and friendship, and the crisis caused by the breach on the Kosi embankment would be discussed during the visit.

Prachanda will visit India on a five-day official trip beginning Sunday.

Heading: FIIs to lower their NCDEX holdings to 5% - Indian Express
Content:
Britain's already struggling travel industry suffered a series of setbacks on Friday when a large tour operator collapsed, British Airways offered thousands of managers a buyout and Richard Branson said he would fight "tooth and nail" to prevent a combination of British Airways with American Airlines.

More than 89,000 people were stranded abroad, mainly in Orlando and the Caribbean, when the XL Leisure Group, a tour operator, ran out of money and had to ground its airplanes. Another 2,00,000 people had bookings with XL, which fell victim to higher fuel prices and slower economic growth.

A spokeswoman did not know how many planes were grounded but said it was the entire fleet.

The Civil Aviation Authority said about 10,000 of the stranded passengers would have to find and pay for their flights back home because they booked flights directly with the company and are thus not eligible for any compensation.

The rest, who booked package holidays or flights through another tour operator, will be flown home at no extra cost because they are covered by the Air Travel Organisers' Licensing compensation plan.

XL joined about 24 other airlines and tour operators that went out of business this year, according to the International Air Transport Association. Zoom Airlines, a trans-Atlantic carrier based in Ottawa and at Gatwick airport in London, filed for bankruptcy protection last month. Eos Airlines, a business-class-only carrier, stopped flying in April.

Heading: Steepest fall for forex kitty since Dec ’05 - Indian Express
Content:
Foreign institutional investors (FIIs) will bring down each of their holdings in NCDEX, the country's leading agri bourse, to 5 per cent or below by June 2009.

This follows the finance ministry guideline that an FII cannot hold more than 5 per cent in a commodity exchange.

NCDEX chairman R Ramaseshan said Goldman Sachs and Intercontinental Exchange have to bring down each of their holdings to 5 per cent or below from 7 per cent and 8 per cent, respectively, in the bourse.

"We have informed both the investors and they will have to decide over the exit price," Ramaseshan said. Although NCDEX is not yet decided over an IPO, in case of the FIIs offloading the shares, the company may come up with an IPO before June next year.

Heading: India pips China in contract research and manufacturing - Indian Express
Content:
India's foreign exchange reserves have fallen by $ 6.49 billion this week — the steepest fall in nearly three years — due to massive intervention by the Reserve Bank of India (RBI) to stem the slide in the rupee.

With this, India's forex kitty has dipped by over $ 26.8 billion in the last three months. "The RBI and the government were fighting the problem of plenty due to massive forex inflow till October 2007. Now it's time to start worrying about the massive outflow," said a dealer with a private sector bank.

Experts said dollar sales will help the RBI and the government in fighting inflation. This is because when the RBI sells dollar, an equivalent amount in rupees is sucked out of the system. A major reason for the sharp rise in money supply — that led to higher inflation — in the system last year and early this year was the huge inflow of forex reserves.

Six months after the reserves crossed the $300 billion mark in March this year, the reserves have now fallen to $288.8 billion on Friday, as per the RBI figures. Still the reserves — which touched an all-time peak of $315.6 billion on June 6, 2008, — are nearly $58 billion higher when compared to the same period of last year. China and Japan are ahead of India.

The fall in reserves started accelerating ever since crude oil prices ballooned. Oil firms have been buying dollars in a big way following the steep rise in crude oil prices in the last two months. Besides, foreign institutional investors (FIIs) have been sellers in the Indian stock market, pulling out nearly $8 billion this year.

Heading: Fed holds emergency talks to solve Lehman crisis - Indian Express
Content:
A Large pool of skilled manpower and initial investments made in pharma, has helped India gain a march over China in the $2-billion contract research and manufacturing services (CRAMS) space.

India has over three times as many US FDA-approved plants as China in terms of drug master files (DMFs). Additionally, the country has filed 1,155 DMFs between 2000 and June 2007, against 329 filings by China. And in the formulations manufacturing space, India has a head-start of over three to five years over China, says a latest survey by KPMG in association with CII.

At present, India has about 75 US FDA-approved plants. This is the highest number of the FDA-approved plants outside the US and in terms of DMFs, Indian market share has grown to almost 46 per cent in 2007 from a mere 14 per cent in 2000.

The introduction of product patents in 2005 gives India a significant advantage in contract manufacturing outsourcing. The Indian CRAMS market was estimated to be at $869 million in 2007 and it is projected to grow at a compound annual growth rate of 41.7 per cent to touch $2.46 billion by 2010, said the survey.

Besides, Indian companies also have a significant expertise in regulatory compliance and supply chain management system. Eastern Europe is gradually losing out on its cost-efficiencies to India. The cost of manufacturing in India is a fraction of the cost of manufacturing in the US or Europe. India is one of the lowest cost manufacturer and one of the lowest manpower rates in the world, the study pointed out.

Indian companies through their high quality and low-cost production models, have bagged more impressive deals in this space, the report says. These deals validate India's potential to achieve a larger share of the global manufacturing outsourcing market.

(FE)

Heading: It’s small, that’s all - Indian Express
Content:
As Lehman Brothers teetered on Friday evening, US Federal Reserve officials summoned the heads of major Wall Street firms to a meeting. Resuming discussion on Saturday, the Fed is reported to have insisted they rescue the stricken investment bank and develop plans to stabilise financial markets.

Fed president Timothy F Geithner called the meeting so bank officials could review their financial exposures to Lehman and work out contingency plans over the possibility that the government would need to orchestrate an orderly liquidation of the firm on Monday, according to people briefed on the meeting.

A Fed spokesman confirmed the meeting but declined to provide details on discussions. The meeting was reminiscent of the circumstances that preceded the near-collapse 10 years ago of Long Term Capital Management. At that time, the Fed summoned the heads of big Wall Street banks to stop the failure of the hedge fund firm which had already lost $4.5 billion. The bankers ended up committing $3.65 billion to save LTCM.

But the fallout from a failure of Lehman Brothers could be even more severe, given the firm's much larger size and its entanglements with trading partners around the globe. Policy makers fear its losses could ripple through the financial industry at a time when banks and securities firms are trying to overcome $500 billion in write-downs.

Bank of America and two British firms, Barclays and HSBC, have expressed interest in bidding for Lehman Brothers. But, they have indicated that their bids are contingent upon receiving support from the government, just as it did with the rescues of Bear Stearns, and the government-sponsored agencies, Fannie Mae and Freddie Mac.

But treasury secretary Henry Paulson made it clear that the government has no plans to put taxpayer money on the line.

(With Reuters inputs)

Heading: This side of the tunnel - Indian Express
Content:
You are forgiven for thinking it is a make-up box. Yes, it is small, and yes, it is a laptop. You are looking at the little master of netbook land — the Asus EeePC.

Though Asus says the name Eee is derived from "the three Es," of its advertising slogan, "Easy to learn, Easy to work, Easy to play", I don't understand how it can be used as a main workstation and I don't think the manufacturers want you to either. This is a netbook, ideal for surfing the Net with Wi-Fi connectivity, jotting down your thoughts at the most unlikeliest of places, storing music as a backup for your ipod and well, that's it.

First let's take a look at what it is good at. It is small and hence can go anywhere, does most — and I mean most, not all — functions you'd expect from a computer and has enough power to execute them. Its primary use would be as a netbook, which allows you to link to the Net anywhere, provided you have the 'right connections'. The inbuilt 1.3 mp webcam also make life a lot easier for those of us who can't live without their daily session on Yahoo chat or Camfrog.

It is something an aspiring author could kill for; just open and type the latest twist in the tale wherever you are. And the 80-GB storage space means you can tuck in most of your pictures, songs and DiVX movies and link it to your iPod, phone or digicam.

But the good news pretty much ends there for by then you would find a little detail missing. This small wonder has no CD/DVD drive. You have to either download everything from the Net, do a shuttle service with an external drive or bluetooth stuff from your bigger, smarter, laptop. Or you can pay extra and get a DVD drive that plugs in to the tiny laptop.

Despite the Dolby sound, the speakers leave a lot to be desired. We all know laptops are notorious for poor sounds; be sure to carry along a good pair of earphones for this one.

That's not all, don't even look this way if you have big fingers, for every time you press a key four others will join the party. Moreover, you have to do a balancing act of sorts to keep the fingers from coming in contact with the touch pad and moving your cursor to unexpected destinations. May be, you will get used to it.

But, maybe that is the price of technology. As things get smaller, they also tend to become more complex. Why would you want a netbook, when you can pay as much — around Rs 33,000 — and get yourselves a laptop that does all this and much more, but is a bit more bulky. Well, I think the jury is out on this one.

Heading: A battle to stay afloat - Indian Express
Content:
When CERN switched on the Large Hadron Collider on September 10, scientists in India followed the developments closely. Many of them have been associated with the project since the mid-'90s. But this is just one of the many pioneering scientific projects that India is a part of. The Sunday Express takes a look at a few of them

Facility for Anti Proton and Ion Research (FAIR)
Like the Large Hadron Collider (LHC), this is an accelerator-based research facility, based in Germany. Often referred to as an 'all-in-one' facility, FAIR will help scientists carry out experiments in atomic, plasma, nuclear, radioactive and high-energy physics. The facility will enable beam intensities of at least 1,000 times more than are available anywhere else, which means there will be more collisions and more 'events' to study. The 1.8 billion-Euro project got underway in September last year and is set to be commissioned by 2012. The first beams are likely to be introduced in 2013. Germany will bear 75 per cent of the cost, while partner countries will contribute the rest.
Indian connection:
India was among the first countries to associate itself with the FAIR project. It will make an 'in-kind' contribution of about 3 per cent of the total cost, worth about Rs 500 crore. It will build and supply superconducting magnets for the main accelerator as well as construct mini linear accelerators. Besides the Variable Energy Cyclotron Centre, the Saha Institute of Nuclear Physics, the Tata Institute of Fundamental Research and IIT-Bombay, at least 30 universities have expressed interest in joining research activities at FAIR. The Indian scientists will participate in experiments related to atomic physics, high-energy physics, nuclear physics and hadron physics.

International Thermonuclear Experimental Reactor (ITER)
The ITER (above) is the largest global effort to tame nuclear fusion energy. To be constructed at Cadarache in southern France, ITER aims to demonstrate the technical and scientific feasibility of harnessing nuclear fusion, which is what provides power to the sun and the stars, for peaceful purposes. The facility will attempt to produce fusion energy from deuterium-tritium plasma. As per the current schedule, the first reactions should be possible by 2016.
Indian connection:
India is one of the seven partners in the project, along with the European Union, the United States, China, Japan, Korea and Russia. It is the first international project of such magnitude in which India will participate as a full partner.
India's contribution to ITER will be in the form of equipment manufactured by Indian industries, worth nearly $500 million. It is a project an energy-starved India is banking on for getting hands-on experience in the design, fabrication and operation of latest fusion technologies in the hope that some day, a nuclear power plant based on fusion reaction will be a reality.

NEUTRINO OBSERVATORY (INO)
This is an example of India taking the lead in one of the most sought-after research areas in nuclear physics. INO is proposed as an underground laboratory situated near Singara township near Masinagudi in Nilgiris district of Tamil Nadu. Neutrinos are sub-atomic particles, one of the most readily available in nature, whose behaviour can reveal fundamental information about the origin of the universe and the production of energy in the stars. Apart from being of fundamental interest to particle physics, research on neutrinos has widespread implications on nuclear physics, geophysics, astrophysics and cosmology. At present, it is a purely Indian project, but many countries are expected to participate later.
The project has received most of the necessary clearances and is currently under review. Funds for the project are likely to be made available during the Eleventh Plan.
Amitabh Sinha

TIME MACHINE
A peek into the world's largest, highest-energy particle accelerator
Dark matter, extra dimensions, supersymmetric particles, ephemeral mini-black holes and a subatomic curiosity called the Higgs boson, elevated to the status of 'God particle'. When CERN's Large Hadron Collider (LHC) was fired up to global applause and astonishment on September 10, these sci-fi staples leaped from the pages of fantasy into the collective consciousness of a people eager for a flashback to the beginning of time.
"Twenty-seven kilometres, a tunnel underground, designed with a mind to send protons around," went the rap composed by CERN scientists at the Franco-Swiss border, near Geneva. It was hardly tunnel vision that made the world's largest, highest-energy particle accelerator a realityit succeeds the Large Electron-Positron Collider, which was shut down in 2000, and uses some of its parts. Such is the precision of the LHC that lunar cycles were kept in mind while it was being designed, since high tide could throw off the circumference of the accelerator by 1 mm.
With 9,300 magnets cooled to -271 degrees Celsius by 60 tonnes of helium, the LHC is a leviathan. Six experiments fit cosily into the LHC's larger scheme of things (so large it aims to simulate the universe as it was after the Big Bang)ATLAS (A Toroidal LHC Apparatus), CMS (Compact Muon Solenoid), LHCb (LHC-beauty), ALICE (A Large Ion Collider Experiment), TOTEM (Total Cross Section, Elastic Scattering and Diffraction Disassociation) and LHCf (LHC-forward).
At full capacity, each of the 3,000 bunches of up to 100 billion protons that will course through a vacuum will generate energy enough to melt 500 kg of copper or power a 400-tonne train. The proton collisions (up to 600 million per second) will spew a large number of subatomic particlesone of which could be the Higgs boson, believed to imbue matter with massat a speed comparable to that of light. Giant detectors will track the immense streams of data, filtering and processing it through a computing gridincluding some Department of Atomic Energy (DAE) labs in Indiafor analysis.
The results from the $10-billion experiment will be analysed over the next 15 years, the estimated lifetime of the LHC.
V Shoba and Apurva

TEAM INDIA
Two hundred of the nation's scientists pitched in for one of the biggest scientific experiments in the world
There was no way that the land of Vedantic unity-in-diversity would have missed being part of an epoch-making experiment that might just throw up a 'theory of everything' to sum up the physical world in all its unity. About 200 members of the Indian particle physicist community have hobnobbed with 1,800 scientists from other countries over two experimentsALICE and CMS.

Nine Indian institutes, led by the Variable Energy Cyclotron Centre (VECC) and the Saha Institute of Nuclear Physics (SINP) in Kolkata, are actively involved in ALICE. The Photon Multiplicity Detector (PMD), one of the 14 detectors used in the experiment aimed at studying the 'quark-gluon plasma' that expanded to form protons and neutrons after the Big Bang, was constructed in India. It will determine the correlation between photons that result from the collision of lead nuclei in ALICE.
"The PMD is a 5m-by-5m lead wall that acts as a photon counter. It has two lakh cells, which are like tiny gas detectors in a honeycomb structure," says Dr S. Chattopadhyay of VECC, who is part of the core group involved in the project, along with Dr Y.P. Viyogi, who is now with the Institute of Physics (IOP) in Bhubaneswar, and Dr G.S.N. Murthy, who retired last month. They were assisted by a group of 30-odd experimentalists, electronics experts, software engineers and research scholars from the institute, besides scientists from Rajasthan University, Panjab University, IIT-Bombay, IOP, and Jammu University. The project cost is estimated at about Rs 10 crore.
Rajasthan University's Sudhir Raniwala was among the three scientists who had defended the need for the PMD in front of the LHC committee in Geneva in the late 1990sthe project actually took off only in 2003. Raniwala has been involved in the detector's research and design since 1991, when he took part in another experiment at CERN aimed at studying the correlation between photons and charged particles.
For VECC, too, this is not a first. In the late 1980s, a similar detector was built with the collaboration of VECC scientists. The detector was used in the Super Proton Synchrotron accelerator experiment in 1994 at CERN. In 2003, VECC again provided a PMD for the Relativistic Heavy Ion Collider experiment at the Brookhaven National Laboratory in the US.
SINP was the first to produce Application Specific Integrated Circuits (ASIC) on a large scale in India. Its indigenously designed Multiple Analog Signal Processor (MANAS) chip is the sole readout chip for ALICE. The MANAS processor, a 7mm-by-7mm silicon chip comprising a microcircuitry of 10,000 transistors, amplifies, processes, tracks and stores signals from the detector before they are read out by a multiplexer. The R&D began way back in 1999, but the green signal from CERN came only in 2005, and by January 2007, a total of 1,10,000 chips of these front-end chipsfabricated at Chadigarh's Semiconductor Complex Limitedwere delivered. A team of five researchers from SINP and Aligarh Muslim University worked on the project.
While IIT-Bombay catered to most of the PMD's software requirements, the Tata Institute of Fundamental Research (TIFR), Mumbai, helped create the Outer Hadron Calorimeter (OHC), an integral part of the CMS. Says Tariq Aziz, head of the Department of High Energy Physics at TIFR, "There is a lot of hard work ahead. We will analyse the data once we start receiving it." The DAE will help CERN develop software for data analysis.

While the scientific side of India's contribution was led by Kolkata and Mumbai, institutes from other parts of the country, spearheaded by the Raja Ramanna Centre for Advanced Technology (RRCAT) at Indore, were involved in constructing essential parts of the accelerator. RRCAT designed the jacks to align the magnets in the LHC tunnel. About 1,800 superconducting magnets were manufactured by Kirloskar in Bangalore and Crompton Greaves in Bhopal. Machine control software and parts of the protection systems for the LHC also came from India.
The Panjab University's Department of Physics was involved in the fabrication of the OHC. Five of the faculty membersJ.M. Kohli, Suman Bala Beri, J.B. Singh, Manjit Kaur and Vipin Bhatnagarmade 860 'scintillation counters' over three years and helped install them. Says Professor Singh, "The mechanical part of the detector was built in Ludhiana. It took four years of hard work before satisfactory results were achieved."
Twelve of the 48 modules that constitute the PMD were designed and fabricated at the IOP by PhD students, professors and technicians in collaboration with VECC. It took seven days to make one module. Putting together the physical circuit boards in the modules was a laborious process, as it involved soldering tiny circuits with gold-plated tungsten wires. "We used to tell the students to take a break every two hours to avoid straining their eyes," says Durga Prasad Mahapatra of IOP. The initial days were frustrating as the hardware and components could not make the grade, forcing the team to modify the design time and again. Somewhere down the line, the shape of the PMD changed from hexagon to rectangle.
All the hard work has paid off. Over the course of the next few years, as the landmark experiment at CERN throws up hints to unlock the secrets of the cosmic cauldron, Indian scientists will keep a hopeful eye trained on the universe of miniscule particles and Brobdingnagian accelerators.
Mouparna Bandyopadhyay, Suchetana Haldar, Apurva, Riya Kartha, Khushboo Sandhu and Debabrata Mohanty

Heading: Two days with the iPhone - Indian Express
Content:
As the Kosi spread havoc in Bihar, several kilometres to its east, people in Majuli fought the fury of another river, the Brahmaputra
When John Peter Wade, a British traveller toured Assam between 1784 and 1800, he had put the area of Majuli at roughly "160 miles by 60". That's 24,863 sq km. Exactly 100 later, The Gazetteer of Bengal and Northeast India (1901) said the island's area stood at around 485 square miles or 1,256 sq km. The latest available government figures put the total area of Majuli at 552.65 sq kilometers.

Majuli is the largest freshwater island in South Asia, formed as the Brahmaputra branches out into two between the districts of Dibrugah and Lakhimpur, before joining again downstream.
Three weeks ago, the Prime Minister was in Jorhat—from where Majuli is just across the Brahmaputra—but he could not make it to the island because there was no dry land in the flooded island where his helicopter could land. He also had to cancel his plan of undertaking an aerial survey of the island because of bad weather.

"Majuli is not an ordinary island. It has a special significance in the history of human civilisation, art and culture," says Pitambar Deva Goswami, eminent Vaishnavite scholar and preacher who also heads the 40-year-old Auni-ati satra on the island. "It is the epicentre of Assamese art and culture, with its Satriya dance and music recognised as classical Indian art forms by the Sangeet Natak Akademi. The Mishing tribal community of the island is also one of the most vibrant ethnic groups of the subcontinent. And being cut off from the rest of the world by the Brahmaputra, Majuli is also, by default, an organic area where no farmer has ever used any chemical fertilizer," Goswami said.

Majuli in fact is a phenomenon by itself, with the Brahmaputra, which created it about 400 years ago, playing havoc with it. Every protection measure initiated by the authorities to prevent flood and erosion has had to give in to the might of the river.

"The soil is soft and technically too young to hold any major structure. Moreover, silt and sedimentation in the river is so high that it is difficult to keep track of the water's currents and channels," said Bharat Chandra Narah, Assam's former minister for water resources.

Over the years, unabated erosion and the annual floods have rendered several thousand families homeless in the past two or three decades. While some families have quit the island in search of land elsewhere in the state, the majority stayed back. In fact hundreds of families can be seen living in small huts on the roadside or on embankments in Majuli for years together, waiting for the water levels to subside.

The floods are receding, and the people are beginning to get back to normal life. "But most of the road network in the island has been badly damaged. Almost every house has been damaged," said PC Deka, sub-divisional officer of the Majuli sub-division.

Relief is slowly trickling in. "We are getting calls from people and organisations wanting to send relief materials. We have asked them to route it through the district administration," added LS Changsan, deputy commissioner, Jorhat. He said Majuli urgently needs a huge quantity of medicines and nutrients, especially for its 40,000 children who have been the worst sufferers.

Heading: Garden of verses - Indian Express
Content:
It's a great phone, but with many flaws, so if you want to own one wait for a better price and 3G
The iPhone is finally here, and it is not making waves except in Page 3 circles. I know you want the phone, I want it too, but is it worth the money you have to dish out— as a friend used to say, "now we need to take housing loans to buy gadgets". Anyway, I got a chance to live with the Jesus phone for two days, and this is what I felt.
Though I have never seen a better phone for business use, it has a whole lot of shortcomings. But still, if I were to buy a phone, it would be an iPhone, but only if the price was right.

The biggest complaint would be that the battery dies out too quickly. Though I was not using Wi-Fi or 3G, or any of the connectivity features, I had to recharge the phone and pray it would last. Since the phone was on loan, I did not have the car recharge kit. I could always recharge it using the USB port on a laptop, but the other end of the phone requires a proprietory connector—why can't all companies stick to USBs so that it can be recharged anywhere? The phone has a string of features like Bluetooth, Automatic Screen Brightness, Edge, 3G and Wi-Fi; to make sure you get good battery life, turn these off, but then that would make it just another phone.

I did not try out Edge, as I think no one should buy this phone to use it on Edge, it will have to be used as a 3G phone. Luckily both my house and office, and most of the places I work out of—friends' homes, cafes etc—have wireless. Connecting on Wi-Fi was not bad, though pulling email every time I went into a Wi-Fi zone was rather tiresome. I'd rather stick to a Blackberry for now.

The interface is brilliantly done. However, getting the search in contacts took some getting used to. But the way the phone asked me each time if I would like to take the call on the speakerphone, the regular iPhone or my bluetooth headset was something I liked. Connecting to the bluetooth headset was also a breeze.

I loved the fact that Apple has given a standard headphone jack on the phone. I also loved the ease with which conference calls can be made. In a usual business day I end up doing about two to three conferences with my team and my customers, and it's a painful experience with most phones. With the iPhone, all you have to do is press the Add button, call the person, and then press Join. I managed a three-party conference call, even going into private mode with one.

I also managed to crash the phone quite a few times, very unlike other Apple products. I then realised that the phone had over a 100 apps installed in it. Once I removed some of these Apps, the phone was easy to work with. I felt the typing was a bit slow, but then I am used to a regular keypad.

People have complained that it does not have a flash and can't do picture messaging, but these were not big issues with me. Usually, I do not send MMSes and don't really know a lot of people who do. The missing flash, though, can be a bit of a problem if you use your phone camera too much.

Another little problem is that you need a pin which comes with the phone to take the SIM card out. Though no one needs to swap SIMs regularly, if you lose the pin, you are in trouble.

The capability of the iPhone to sync with my Mac or Windows PC is great. The way contacts are stored is also awesome, but sadly I could not search the contacts by first name, maybe I was doing something wrong. The switch to turn the phone from ring mode to vibrate is reminiscent of the Palm. The volume keys felt sturdy, and added to the solid feel Apple has built into the product.

So, do I want one? Yes. Why don't I have one right now? One the cost is too high, and 3G is still not here. But there is no other phone that offers the same experience, and no one, yes no one, beats the touch interface.

For now, I am going to buy the new iPod Touch, as it can do email on Wi-Fi, along with music, video and even the apps, only the phone is missing.
Gagandeep S. Sapra is the Chairman and CEO of System3 group of companies,

Heading: The live art of storytelling - Indian Express
Content:
Edna St. Vincent Millay's poetry and her home are all set to be restored
The staircase looks innocent enough, three narrow steps up to a landing, turn left, 11 more steps up to the second floor of this farmhouse called Steepletop. "Are these the stairs, where...?" asks the visitor. "There's only one set of stairs in this house," replies Peter Bergman, acting as guide.

Sometime in the dawn of an October morning almost six decades ago, poet Edna St. Vincent Millay tumbled down these stairs. Her neck was broken, and she had died as fiercely and adamantly as she had lived. Her death at 58 extinguished an incandescent chapter in American literature. In 1920 when she came here, Millay was one of the most famous women in the US, not just for her work, but also as a bohemian who predated the sexual revolution of the 1970s.

"She was a rock star," said Bergman, executive director of the Edna St. Vincent Millay Society. Addicted to morphine and alcohol, and never far from the next cigarette, Millay had gone into physical, emotional and creative decline years before her death. She was beginning to write brilliantly once more after weaning herself off the dope and the grief of the death of her husband, Eugen Boissevain, the year before she died.

The house is imbued with Edna from top to bottom. In the drawing room, there's her Steinway piano. The kitchen still contains the modern breakfast bar and counters. In her bedroom there's her collection of handbags, her wool socks. In the bathroom, her monogrammed towels still hang. On the table in her library is a yellowed copy of The New York Times from April 24, 1950.

Millay had a deep knowledge of the natural world. She had a large fruit and vegetable garden. She named her farm after a beautiful pink flowered native spirea called steeplebush.

Up on a hill, is Edna's cabin. A plain cedar structure, it measures 10 ft by 17 ft and contains a wood-burning stove, two lamps, two small desks and chairs, and sheaves of notepaper. Edna's alarm clock sits on one of the desks. Her normal routine was to have breakfast in bed, work in bed, get up, do some gardening, take lunch and then retire to the cabin where she would write such works as Fatal Interview, her collection of sonnets inspired by her affair with the young poet George Dillon.

Mine the Harvest, a collection published posthumously, was penned in this cabin, as was The Murder of Lidice. She later wrote that it was bad poetry and had caused her a breakdown. Poet J.D. McClatchy wrote, "In their day, her poems startled readers with their edgy candour."

Bergman is trying to restore the property and her reputation. He is confident that her star will rise again. Not least because of a recent incident. A man came here with his girlfriend. "She felt she couldn't die without first seeing where Millay wrote," he said, "There were these kids, 23-24, soldiers who had just been assigned to Afghanistan. This is what they wanted to see."
_Adrian Higgins, LATWP

Heading: Is it safe to drink distilled water? - Indian Express
Content:
In Brooklyn, New York, three photographers were given a Polaroid camera each, an audience of 300 women and men dressed as grandmothers, and two hours to shoot 150 photographs and create a mosaic narrative. The project was conducted by LVHRD, which promotes creative interaction.

Jonathan Harris' Polaroid Project (see picture) tells a story of identities dissolving and genders blurring. On the project website, Harris explains: "Both genders twist towards the centre along curved paths, discarding clothes, wigs, shoes, and other accessories along the way, as the photos start to shatter, becoming less about objects and more about flesh. Approaching the centre, the pictures are increasingly difficult to discern, as body parts blend together and their owners' identities dissolve." Harris, a visual artist and storyteller, designs projects to explain the human world.

Elizabeth Weinberg asked participants what their grandparents' best advice to them was and wrote them down underneath their pictures: eat the fish eye; use a condom; read the classics.

Joseph Holmes created a whole new sign language dictionary. He writes: "The story here, with these words, with these hand-signals, I don't remember what they mean anymore. I wanted to make a critique of storytelling."

Heading: Arizonian adventures - Indian Express
Content:
It is safe and it does not leach out minerals, two experts on water quality and nutrition at Cornell agree. But they questioned drinking distilled water when water can be made safe with far less energy than distillation takes.
Joseph H. Hotchkiss, professor of food science, said that accepting the idea that distilled water could draw minerals out of the body would mean assuming that it was not actually absorbed into the body.

"The inside of your body is a lot like a tube," Hotchkiss explained, with membranes inside to isolate what you eat from the body. The membrane controls what crosses it, and if water did not cross that membrane, it would pass directly through the body, causing diarrhoea. Instead, distilled water is absorbed like other water, and its excretion is controlled by the kidneys.

Distilled water lacks minerals and has a flat taste, Hotchkiss said, but he pointed out that except for iron and calcium in women of childbearing age, minerals are not in short supply in the United States diet, and water is not a significant source of minerals anyway.

A water-quality expert, Ann T. Lemley, a professor at the College of Human Ecology, agreed that distilled water was safe. Most dissolved substances get removed when water is distilled, Lemley said, including salts and most potential contaminants.

"The high temperature of distillation kills microbiological content," Lemley said, "one for-sure advantage of distilled water." It might be valuable for an immune-compromised person, she said, but advanced filtration would also work.
_NYT

Heading: Despite Raj Thackeray - Indian Express
Content:
A linguist documents rock art dating back 300,000 years and finds that the same 15 patterns are repeated in rock art all over the world
In his mid-60s, Ekkehart Malotki, a retired linguistics professor, willingly dangled from a rope tied to a car that was backed to the edge of a cliff. A half-dozen times, he descended with his rope, photographed the cliff face and climbed back up.

He was documenting a rock art panel a quarter-mile long in northern Arizona. These adventures are commonplace for Malotki, a German-born American who is now 69.
Malotki fell in love with America's desert Southwest as a 20-something graduate student of languages at the University of California, San Diego. There, he debunked the long-standing notion that the Hopi tribe of northern Arizona did not talk about time. He believes time is a fundamental, universal concept that is likely to appear in the words of any human culture, and with respect to the Hopi, he was right. As a linguist at Northern Arizona University in Flagstaff, Malotki spent decades chronicling the nuanced Hopi tongue.

Malotki began roaming the desert in pursuit of Kokopelli, the southwestern deity depicted as a man playing a flute, which had been incorrectly linked with a Hopi kachina, or spirit. He found much evidence to dispel the association. And everywhere he went, he found art: pot shards, carved petroglyphs and painted pictographs.

Malotki has published three books about rock art, including The Rock Art of Arizona: Art for Life's Sake. He has taken thousands of photographs, and he keeps his secret GPS coordinates in files that line his office walls. Malotki's latest focus is on designs called phosphenes, which are as fundamental to art as time is to language. He said the same 15 abstract geometric constants appear globally in art created as early as 300,000 years ago. They are grids, zigzags and patterns of dots. They are the first objects drawn by children; we doodle them when we talk on the phone.

"Phosphenes have been defined as a kind of test pattern of the visual system," said Robert Bednarik, a rock art expert in Australia. He said he had determined three decades ago that all prefigurative art consisted entirely of phosphene motifs. "This hypothesis has never been falsified, and it stands nearly 30 years later," he said.

Many archaeologists have neglected these ancient symbols in recent decades, Malotki said, because of a view that "they didn't allow insight into the minds of the creators". He disagrees. Malotki has brought rock art to the attention of Ellen Dissanayake, an independent evolutionary psychologist affiliated with the University of Washington. She has argued that art, especially music, is part of our biology, as expressed through the mode and filter of culture. Malotki, Dissanayake and Henry Wallace of the Center for Desert Archaeology, a conservation group, have embarked on a book project to show that the earliest rock art was linked with human survival.
Bednarik called Malotki's photographs "sublime" and he said they were important to the preservation and protection of rock art.
_ANNE MINARD, NYT

Heading: True Brit: Ritchie returns - Indian Express
Content:
As the MNS leader targets the Bachchans and his uncle Bal Thackeray hits out at 'Dilliwalla' Shah Rukh Khan, The Sunday Express profiles a bunch of aspiring actors, scriptwriters and directors who have travelled from Muzaffarpur, Patna and Kanpur to make the city of dreams their home

PRAVEEN DODEGA, Aspiring director
'I wanted to pursue my dreams and hopes. I came to Mumbai with the sole aim of making films'
Praveen Dodega worked at a print designing firm in Delhi for eight years before finally deciding that he had had enough. So he packed his bags and leftfor the city of dreams. "I wanted to pursue my dream of making films. And I came to Mumbai to do that," says the 30-year-old.
In Mumbai, he worked with Wilson Louis, whose film, Ho Sakta Hai, did no wonders at the box office but did the rounds of several festivals. That was Dodega's first foray into the world of cinemaan off-beat one.
With no formal training in filmmaking, Dodega worked on a series of TV commercials for Akai Television and also made short films. His first was a sensitively made short film, Aaj Ka Sach, about the difficulties of ageing.

Dodega then went on to make a short film for a film competition about the struggles of a man who is both HIV positive and gay. His third venture was a murder mystery called The Perfect Murder. Next, he set up Prodigy Creations and Raj Motion Pictures, the banner under which he hopes to launch his first feature film. "The film is still in the planning stage. We have about 40 per cent of the funds with us and we're looking for more interested investors to cobble up the rest of the amount."
Dodega has had to work hard but he's not complaining. "There's a wonderful energy and exuberance in Mumbai. People have been extremely helpful and supportive."

He counts Ram Gopal Varma and Ashutosh Gowariker among his inspirations but has never approached them for work. "I love their work. But I want to do something on my own."
Nikhil Roshan

FARID KHAN, Scriptwriter
'In day-to-day life, humein double dikkat hai. Ek toh hum Muslim hain aur doosra hum Bihar ke hain'

Farid Khan is an achiever in his own right. This Patna-born writer who has a Masters in Urdu is translating the Upanishads for Dr Chandraprakash Dwivedi's television series, Upanishad Ganga.
The scholar got this opportunity after a fair bit of struggle. Khan, who came to Mumbai in 2002 to write and direct Hindi films, is yet to find a footing in the industry. "When I came to Mumbai, I thought the film industry would be a concrete set-up. But when I came here, I realised that there is no organised space. I knew I wasn't going to get anything easily," says the 36-year-old.
An alumnus of Patna University, Khan was associated with the Lucknow-based Bharatendu Natya Akademi (BNA). It was at BNA that he met Dwivedi. "We got talking and something about me must have impressed him. He promised to work with me if I came to Mumbai," he says.
So when Khan decided to come to Mumbai, he took to heart the words of fellow actor and good friend Vineet Kumar, who told him, "If you come to Mumbai, you have to treat it like your sasural. Come what may, you cannot go back."

That motto saw him through the toughest of situations. For a long time, Khan lived in his friend Pradeep Chaudhary's house before moving into a chawl in Goregaon. "In day-to-day life, humein double dikkat hai. Ek toh hum Muslim hain aur hum Bihar ke hain. Renting a flat is a huge problem. But one has to make the best of the situation. My present landlord is a Maharashtrian Hindu and he is very kind."
Despite the odds, Khan has never thought of going back home. He considers the late playwright Vijay Tendulkar his idol for his ability to straddle both commercial cinema and realistic theatre, but feels he is miles away from his destination. "I haven't got a chance to even write a dialogue for a film. But it's ok. Meri raftaar dheemi zaroor hai magar meri chaal theek hai (My speed might be slow but I am walking right)," he says.
While the big screen remains elusive, the small screen has given Khan a raison d'etre in Mumbai. He has written dialogues for soaps like Reth, Mili and Kittu Sab Janti Hai. He's hoping Dwivedi's serial will get him noticed and that his first film will come his way soon.
 Harneet Singh

PARITOSH SHRIVASTAV, Actor
'There's a huge Marathi and Gujarati lobby operating in TV and theatre. Those who come from UP and Bihar have to stick it out on their own'

It all started with the applause. An impressionable four-year-old attended a cultural function in his school and got hooked to the thundering ovation the other students got. He decided that one day he'll be the one who receives that applause. That was in Muzaffarpur in Bihar.
Mumbai, 25 years later: Shrivastav is still the same four-year-old, waiting to take centrestage. His dream to be a "fine actor" took him from Muzaffarpur to Mumbai via Gorakhpur. " I looked around for a teacher or an institute in Bihar where I could learn acting but I didn't find any so I went to Gorakhpur," he says.
His stint in Gorakhpur was fruitful. He almost became a Bhojpuri star after auditioning for Ajay Sinha's Sasura Bada Paise Waala. He was short-listed for the smash hit but didn't make the final cut. Shrivastav was disappointed but a couplet by Harivansh Rai Bachchan kept him going. "Harivansh Rai ji's lines, Mann ka ho toh achcha...mann ka na ho toh aur bhi achcha, acted like a sanjivani booti for me. I decided to fight it out," he says.

Shrivastav joined Manvendra Tripathi's theatre workshop and honed his acting skills. Under Tripathi's tutelage, he did classic plays like Munshi Premchand's Bade Bhaisaab and Kalidas' Meghdootam (in Bhojpuri). He even formed his own theatre group, Sanskritik Sangam. "My theatre experience boosted my confidence and everybody told me that I must go to Mumbai," he says.
And so Shrivastav came to Mumbai in August 2007 and insists he is here for the long haul. In Mumbai, he has gone through the drill, having dropped off his photos at Aamir Khan Productions, Dharma Productions and Balaji Telefilms. But he hasn't got a call from any of them yet. "I meet people and they tell me to stay in touch and if something comes up they will let me know. They haven't. If nothing else, I've learnt to stay in touch now," he says. While he waits for that big call, he is sustaining himself in the city by working in Bhojpuri serials for Mahua channel.
So does he feel like an outsider here? "There's a huge Marathi and Gujarati lobby in the television and theatre industries. Those who come from UP and Bihar have to stick it out."
Has he ever thought of heading back home? "This thought has crossed my mind a couple of times but my inner voice tells me to stay put," says Shrivastav who wants to do character roles. He's still waiting for the applause.
 Harneet Singh

ARFIE LAMBA, Actor
'There is space for everyone here. I agree with the tagline of a cellular provider: Mera number Mumbai ka toh main Mumbai ka'

The day began like any other for Arfie Lamba. After putting in a hard day's work, this chemical engineer decided to meet a friend. Luck met him on the way when an advertising headhunter spotted him on the road and signed him as the cover face for the (now defunct) in-flight magazine of Air Sahara.
Lamba quit his job in Delhi and came to Mumbai. "It just happened. I just knew that I had to come to Mumbai and try my luck. I wanted to be a hero," he says. Lamba's decision was a shocker for his family back home in Moga, Punjab. Till date, some members of his extended family do not know that Lamba is in Mumbai. "My mom is still upset. She thinks I should be getting married now but my dad supports me. He told me to chase my dream," says the 27-year-old.
In Mumbai since 2005, Lamba has been actively involved in theatre and has trained with the likes of Dinesh Thakur and Mahabano Modi Kotwal. His stint with modelling continues. He has modelled for the promos of 9X channel and shows like Bathroom Singer on Sahara Filmy channel. He has also worked on his networking skills and is a regular at Prithvi theatre. "I didn't know a soul when I came to Mumbai. I had thought I would get a break a few months. Life had been good to me but the wait here really hurts."

Lamba signed a "big film" with a Bangalore-based producer but it was called off when the car they were travelling in met with an accident. "We were on our way to Shirdi and this mishap happened. The producer suffered a brain haemorrhage, the director broke his leg and I broke my wrist," he says. But Lamba is optimistic about his career. He has meetings lined up with some powerful biggies and also has a play coming up.
Lamba's affair with Bollywood is as enduring as the one he has with Mumbai. "It was a dream to see the sunrise in Colaba and when I did that I sang the Shah Rukh Khan number, Jaanam Dekh Lo. I treated Mumbai like a lover," he remembers. And the lover, he says, will never let him down. "I believe that Mumbai gives you everything but for that, you have to give it everything," he philosophises. And other than a stray comment on his Punjabi twang, he has never faced any unpleasant moments in the city. "There is space for everyone here. I agree with the tagline of a cellular provider: Mera number Mumbai ka toh main Mumbai ka," he grins.
Harneet Singh

OM, Actor
'Actors are taught that even if your co-performer gets it wrong, you must continue doing the right thing, and sooner or later he will fall in line. This could well apply to the situation in Mumbai'

He is a familiar face on Mumbai's local theatre scene. Om has been part of Naseeruddin Shah's troupe Motley since 2005. Om, 28, grew up in Kanpur, nursing the dream of becoming a cricketer until he realised acting was a more challenging option, "In acting, there are no 11 players as in cricket. You are essentially playing solo. There are no extras sitting on the sidelines."
"It was while watching Amitabh Bachchan in Yaarana that I really got interested in acting," he says. And though his father, who was a homeopathic doctor, initially opposed Om's idea, he eventually came around.
In 1997, Om moved to Delhi to join the National School of Drama (NSD), where Shah, who later became his mentor, noticed him. In July 2000, Om formed his own theatre group called Rang and also joined Shah's repertory. "The biggest question an aspiring actor faces is: 'how do I survive'? And if you're not established, it's rare to find the kind of roles you're looking for".
But Om refuses to view his experience as a struggle. "The word 'struggle' has a negative connotation. Acting is something I love."
Om is now all set to make his foray into cinema. He has written a script and has a couple of films in the pipeline even as he continues to be a part of Motley and takes theatre classes.
In the city of migrants, Om's experience so far has been pleasant. He lives by the lesson he learnt in his acting classes: "In acting, we're taught that even if your co-performer gets it wrong while performing, continue doing the right thing, and sooner or later the other performer will fall in line." Is Raj Thackeray listening?
 Nikhil Roshan

Heading: Globe spotting - Indian Express
Content:
Madonna's husband is back in business with a British gangster movie, his cinematic forte
Like many English pubs, the Punch Bowl carries quite a history. The Mayfair drinking establishment first started serving ale in the middle of the 18th century, when King George II ruled. Like some pockets of London, though, the two-story tavern turned into a grimy relic of a forgotten era—the janitor did the pub's cooking and the beer was as uninspiring as the ambience.

And then filmmaker Guy Ritchie bought the place. The pub's scary meat pies have since been pushed aside by organic smoked salmon, and authentic, hand-pulled British pints have replaced the modern, soulless lagers.

"I love pubs, I love pubs," Ritchie said during a recent visit to his bar as the refurbishment of the Punch Bowl was just beginning. "Pubs just happen to be one of those institutions that are just quintessentially English, and four pubs a day shut down in the U.K."

The Punch Bowl isn't Ritchie's only restoration project. The 39-year-old writer and director is also trying to breathe life into his own filmmaking career. After a commercial and critical slump that included Revolver and the remake Swept Away (which starred his wife, Madonna), Ritchie, with his new movie, RocknRolla, is returning to the genre that established his cinematic identity: the British gangster movie.

In 1998, Ritchie and producing partner Matthew Vaughn made Lock, Stock and Two Smoking Barrels, a low-budget London crime caper that overflowed with kinetic visuals, colourful dialogue and distinctive heavies. The drama grossed more than $100 million worldwide, and two years later Ritchie and Vaughn collaborated on Snatch, which helped to further Ritchie's subspecies of stylishly violent British crime stories; similar efforts included Vaughn's Layer Cake and Paul McGuigan's Gangster No. 1.

But while Ritchie's honour-among-thieves movies always had exhibited a complex mix of attitude, nihilism and convoluted plotting, the combination proved caustic to 2005's Revolver, which was drubbed by critics and ignored by moviegoers. Even Gerard Butler, who stars in RocknRolla, admits he didn't see it.

"I think it's impossible for a movie like that to do well. It's an inaccessible concept," Ritchie said in a postmortem of his movie about revenge, self-doubt and philosophy, "because it's about the idea that there is essentially no such thing as an external enemy, that ultimately you are the enemy."

He began developing a remake of The Dirty Dozen with Matrix producer Joel Silver, while also sending his RocknRolla script to Silver and producing partner Susan Downey, who said of RocknRolla, "It's a return to form and an advancement of form."
Downey and Silver will produce Ritchie's first American studio film, next year's Sherlock Holmes, which stars Downey's husband, Robert Downey Jr.

Like Ritchie's best work, RocknRolla is filled with memorably duplicitous characters: a deceitful accountant (Thandie Newton), an equal-opportunity thug (Butler), a strung-out but savvy rock star (Toby Kebbell), a double-dealing crime boss Lenny Cole (Tom Wilkinson) and his not altogether loyal aide-de-camp, Archie (Mark Strong).

The setting is low-rent thuggery (although the film is largely free of Ritchie's sometimes explicit violence), but the impetus is immigration and London's rapidly evolving cultural and financial mix. Billionaire Russians are behind a suspicious land deal, and Lenny believes he can line his own pockets along the way.

Lenny also thinks he can still run the town, but the Russians have more pull. "He's desperately trying to retain his position," said Ritchie, who has also been working on a documentary about what he calls "the esoteric aspects of religion".
_John Horn, LATWP

Heading: Off track - Indian Express
Content:
TORONTO INTERNATIONAL FILM FESTIVAL
Okay, so the Toronto International Film Festival wasn't exactly an Oscar preview party, what with free drinks being rationed and notable misses like Baz Luhrmann's Australia, Oliver Stone's W and the Sean Penn starrer, Milk. But the red carpet wasn't wanting for star shimmer. Brad Pitt's comedy Burn After Reading, directed by the Coen Brothers, upped the ante, especially among young obsessive female audiences, even as Jennifer Aniston kept a safe distance—from him. Anne Hathaway was "adorkably" turned out for Rachel Getting Married and a waif-thin Keira Knightley hardly looked The Duchess. The real show-stealer was The Wrestler, Darren (Requiem for a Dream) Aronofsky's film about an ageing professional wrestler with Mickey Rourke.

MTV VIDEO MUSIC AWARDS
It was a rockin' night to remember at the 25th MTV VMA awards and who should win three Moonmen, including video of the year for Piece of Me, but Britney Spears? The chaste Jonas Brothers (believe it or not, their father is a pastor) rubbed shoulders with the music fraternity and host Russell Brand's ribald humour spawned hate communities on social networking websites. The British comic with the outrageous hairdo called George Bush a "retard and cowboy fella", made politically incorrect remarks on Palin's pregnancy and took a dig at teen celebs wearing "purity rings", that drew the ire of American Idol winner Jordin Sparks and angry fans. "A little sex once in a while never hurt anybody," was all he offered by way of apology.

NEW YORK FASHION WEEK
Diane Von Furstenberg's Spring 2009 "Rock Goddess" collection (Woodstock's 40th anniversary is round the corner), with flowing dresses, tunics and retro froufrou, created a splash—Jennifer Lopez, Eva Longoria and Uma Thurman added to the bling value by walking the ramp. Tracy Reese's creations were big on flower power and Donna Karan made waves with her cutesy streetwear. Tie-die, lace, the colours purple and navy blue, and feminine chic (as also laptops for handbags) were the new runway staples. All this fashion frenzy made Victoria Beckham—in a short spiky hairdo—decide it was about time she launched a line of her own, and so she displayed ten "classy" dresses at private viewings at well, where else but the Waldorf Astoria.

Heading: Old faithful: the evolution - Indian Express
Content:
Fifty out of 80 porters in Pune's 'coolie village' opted to be gangmen. But now, months later, they are back in their village, saying they can't handle the pressures of their new job.
Every February, when the Railway Minister rises to make his Budget speech in Parliament, houses across Dhore Bhambure erupt in loud cheers before hushing up and turning on the television volume to a blast. Here in "coolie village", where people in 80 out of 300 families worked as porters in the Pune railway station till very recently, the Railway Budget is an important annual occasion, with people hanging on to the minister's every word.

About 45 kilometres from Pune, Dhore Bhambure sits on the banks of river Bhima, a tributary of the Krishna. With its rows of bajra and groundnut fields, the well-stocked local market, the gram panchayat office, the Marathi-medium school, and with most of the men working for the railways—of the 255 coolies in Pune station, over 80 are from here—Dhore Bhambure seems as placid and content as the Bhima that flows by.

There are a few ripples though: the village school is only up to Class VII, after which children have to go to the Rajgurunagar school, 2 km from the village. The nearest hospital is in Rajgurunagar too and the state transport bus passes the village only thrice a day. The frequent power-cuts are a problem too, say villagers.

But these are mere quibbles. These days the villagers are worried about something more basic: their jobs. It began with the last Railway Budget, they say. In his Budget speech, Railway Minister Lalu Prasad Yadav said that licensed porters would be appointed as gangmen, a job that would make them employees of the Indian Railways and also give them salaries and other benefits, which includes pension after retirement. According to rules, a licensed porter should be medically fit and not be more than 50 years old to be eligible as gangmen. It was a populist move that resulted in a substantial increase in the railways' salary bill.

On the day of the Budget, Dhore Bhambure let out the loudest cheer—all the porters would now have secure jobs and fixed salaries. Or so they thought. Now, over six months after the announcement, most of the porters who opted to become gangmen are back home. The job of a gangman is too demanding, they say, and now they want their porter licences back.

Shantaram Thigale, a porter-turned-gangmen, said the lure of a secure future in the Railways was too hard to turn down and by May 15, 50 out of 80 porters in the village became gangmen without understanding the nature of work that they were to do. "There were rumours that if we lose this opportunity, we would lose our jobs as porters too. Most of us are illiterate and did not understand that it was voluntary," he said.

"As porters, we were used to working at our own will. Also, we would get time to rest in between train arrivals. But as gangmen, we don't get a minute's rest. We have to clean the tracks, put gravels, change rails, patrol and so on. We walk over 16 kilometres every day for patrolling and repair works. The equipments that we carry weigh 35-40 kg and working in the sun is exhausting. At times, we patrol the tracks all alone and this is unsafe," said Santosh Tukaram Dhore, 30, who worked as a porter for five years before becoming a gangman.

Soon, the newly-appointed gangmen began complaining about their pay slips too. As porters, they said, they would earn as much as Rs 300-400 a day but the gross salary of Rs 7,488 they got as gangmen was deceptive. After the deductions, they got around Rs 5,000 in hand.

More complaints: the railway ministry had taken away their badges and now they want it back. Also, they have to travel a lot more than they did earlier and that meant eating out while at work and other expenses.

Some of them were transferred to railway lines far away from their village and had to live away from their families. "Our expenses have grown and our salaries have shrunk. If only I knew this before opting to be a gangman," said Dyaneshwar Bhambure, 45, who was transferred to Jejuri line, about 80 kilometres from Dhore Bhambure.

Heading: A dash of exotica for diversity - Indian Express
Content:
The Corolla's new avatar has many new features, but is still simple, safe and sturdy. Gayatri Verma takes the Altis for a ride
Like its legendary predecessors the new Corolla Altis is a testament to the amazingly simple but shatteringly effective approach Toyota is famous for—subtle and unhurried but with ample substance packed into it. But while the Corolla has been synonymous with dependability, it has never been an exciting car. And true to form, the Altis, while a very classy car, is no fire breather either.

Riding on the success of the Camry, the Corolla Altis does try and mimic its style and comes with completely new skeletal dimensions with subtly wrought changes that make for a more roomy interior and also enhance the aero efficiency of the overall automobile. Build quality is typically Toyota efficient and the attention to detail is terrific.

The seating is extremely comfortable and spacious in the front. But in the Altis, the back seat is the place to be. With plenty of leg space and a floor that is virtually flat, the back seat passengers, even those tucked in the middle, will have less to complain about. They also have a three-point seat belt thrown in for extra safety.
The boot is spacious and thanks to the use of a Torsion Beam in the rear suspension, wheel arch intrusions into the boot are kept to a minimum.

The new version has an electric adjustable drivers seat, the controls of which are easy to figure out and swiftly get you into a comfortable driving position. But for those expecting something different in the interior, the 2008 Altis fails to deliver. Honda raised the bar for interior styling with the Civic, and instead of attempting to compete, Toyota has gone ultra conservative with the interior styling, going for the traditional and ubiquitous fake wood and fake chrome. The overall impression is one of economy than style.

The switches and controls are not at all extraordinary when you consider how strong the competition is. In terms of tactile quality, one would probably find the Honda Civic to be a more pleasurable deal. But for those of a practical frame of mind, the new Altis is relatively issue-free.

The controls are all well laid out, the audio equipment is easy to adapt to and operate; everything on the console is very neatly put together. The steering wheel is similar (like many other features) to that of the Camry, and the dials are clearly visible through them with large self-illuminating digits surrounding a conventional-sized radial speedometer and rev-counter.

However, Toyota has not delivered the new Dual VVT-i engines employed in the Japanese and American markets, and so the new Altis has an ageing engine line-up. The 1.6 litre 3ZZ-FE and the 1.8 litre 1ZZ-FE units have power output of 109 hp and 132 hp respectively, both achieving this peak at 6,000 RPM. At idle the engine is all but silent.

During the test drive the engine was found to be a bit sluggish. The pick-up, too, could have been better, but it still remains the solid and reliably powerful engine of the older Corollas. The Civic might have more power in its 140 hp 1.8 litre, but I think you would be hard pressed to notice that extra 8 hp, and given Toyota's expertise in the area, the refinement in the Altis is impressive.

The car deals with bumps and potholes adequately, though it can be a bit uncomfortable for those riding in the back seats. Though you do feel them, minor bumps don't really affect the riding pleasure and the car settles down quickly afterwards.

The car, with its fuel saving power steering, handles very well even in mildly inexperienced hands, accelerating, braking (the brakes are new) and taking corners very smoothly. The car comes with the latest generation ABS coupled with EBD (electronic brake force distribution system) while the GOA body structure is intelligently designed for best impact dissipation.

To help put things in perspective for those dithering between the sleek and powerful Honda Civic and meticulous Corolla Altis, it really comes down to the temperament of the buyer and driver. The Civic is built for those who love to drive and revel in the knowledge of having a powerful engine under the hood. The Corolla seems tailored to deliver the comforts that those who like to be driven expect with an eye towards making it family and children friendly.

The Corolla has never positioned itself as a car out to capture the imagination of the youth and is at the end of the day just an entry-level car in markets like the US. But despite the less exciting engine, the acceleration and performance will still be enough to make it an enjoyable car to drive.

There are many who may call the Altis boring, but there is great comfort in owning a car that always starts when the key is turned, has brakes that do as they are told and comes packed with features that ensure you return home safe.

Heading: You Can Survive a Nuclear Blast - Indian Express
Content:
New Zealand is home to 2,065 native plants found nowhere else on Earth. They range from magnificent towering kauri trees to tiny flowers that form tightly packed mounds called vegetable sheep.

When Europeans began arriving in New Zealand, they brought with them alien plants—crops, garden plants and stowaway weeds. Today, 22,000 non-native plants grow in New Zealand. Most of them can survive only with the loving care of gardeners and farmers. But 2,069 have become naturalised. There are more naturalised invasive plant species in New Zealand than native species.

Dov Sax, an ecologist at Brown University, and Steven D. Gaines, a marine biologist at the University of California, Santa Barbara, point out that the invasion has not led to a mass extinction of native plants. The number of documented extinctions of native New Zealand plant species is a grand total of three.

While some invasions are indeed devastating, they often do not set off extinctions. They can even spur the evolution of new diversity. "I hate the 'exotics are evil' bit, because it's so unscientific," Sax said. Sax and his colleagues are at odds with many other experts on invasive species. Their critics argue that the speed with which species are being moved around the planet, combined with other kinds of stress on the environment, is having a major impact.

Some invasive species have driven native species extinct. But Sax argues that they are far more likely to be predators than competitors. In their new paper, Sax and Gaines analyse all of the documented extinctions of vertebrates that have been linked to invasive species. Four-fifths of those extinctions were because of introduced predators like foxes, cats and rats. The Nile perch was introduced into Lake Victoria in 1954 for food. It then began wiping out native fish by eating them.

Ecosystems have often been seen as having a certain number of niches that species can occupy. Once an ecosystem's niches are full, new species can take them over only if old species become extinct. But as real ecosystems take on exotic species, they do not show any sign of being saturated, Sax said.

Fish also show this pattern, said James Brown of the University of New Mexico. In Hawaii, 40 new species of freshwater fish have become established, and the five native species are still present. Brown acknowledges that invasive species can push native species out of much of their original habitat. But they argue that native species are not becoming extinct, because they compete better than the invasive species in certain refuges.

These scientists also point out that exotics can actually spur the evolution of new diversity. A North American plant called saltmarsh cordgrass was introduced into England in the 19th century, where it interbred with the native small cordgrass. Their hybrid offspring could not reproduce with either original species, producing a new species called common cordgrass.

Long before humans moved plants around, many plants hybridised into new species by this process. "Something like a third of the plant species you see around you formed that way," Sax said.

Biological invasions also set off bursts of natural selection. House sparrows, for example, have moved to North America from Europe and have spread across the whole continent. "The natives themselves are also likely to adapt," Sax added. Some of the fastest rates of evolution ever documented have taken place in native species adapting to exotics. Some populations of soapberry bugs in Florida, for example, have shifted from feeding on a native plant, the balloon vine, to the goldenrain tree, introduced from Asia by landscapers in the 1950s. In five decades, the smaller goldenrain seeds have driven the evolution of smaller mouthparts in the bugs, along with a host of other changes.
_CARL ZIMMER, NYT

Heading: Time runs out - Indian Express
Content:
On www.ted.com, disaster-medicine expert Irwin Redlener talks about the implications of a nuclear detonation in a post-Cold War era and how to survive it. While an all-out nuclear war is not survivable, it is much less likely than before. Nuclear terrorism, however, is a real threat, as the global nuclear weapons stockpile is not uniformly secure and fissionable material is relatively available, particularly in Russia. From 1993 to 2006, the IAEA documented 175 cases of nuclear theft, 18 of which involved highly enriched uranium or plutonium. Nuclear know-how—instructions on how to assemble a weapon, floor plans for a "terror farm"—is just as accessible to anyone with a basic understanding of physics.

In the arms race era (1949-1991), response planning was largely delusional as a detonation would have triggered simultaneous counter-action, creating a globally destructive nuclear holocaust. But survival in case of a nuclear detonation now is not a moot point. Efforts at mitigation, involving planning and the engagement of citizens, can help minimise the number of casualties. Incredibly, if you are two miles away from the site of detonation, you have a 50-per-cent chance of survival, which goes up to 80-90 per cent if you are within a radius of up to eight miles.

How can you save yourself from the heat, radiation and blast effects of a nuclear bomb going off? Redlener offers a survival plan:
a) Don't stare at the light flash and keep your mouth open so your eardrums don't burst
b) If very close, stick to the standard advice: duck and cover
c) You have 10-20 minutes to get away from the initial fallout from the mushroom cloud, or find shelter in a basement or a tall building, above the ninth floor
d) Move crosswind for 1.2 miles, away from damaged buildings
e) Try to keep your skin, mouth and nose covered
f) Decontaminate at the earliest and seek medical attention

Heading: In Orissa’s ‘liberated’ zone, two villages take on the Maoists - Indian Express
Content:

Yet, lapses by the intelligence machinery lead to repeated terrorist attacks throughout the country. A discreet examination of the functioning of these agencies is essential. A thorough revamp might boost the morale of the personnel.

The all-party meeting mooted by the railway minister is apt as the NDA could come out with concrete propositions to combat terror. L.K. Advani's role in framing new norms for the intelligence bureau and for local police forces will be helpful. Singh need not only be "keen" but also "king".

Mumbai

Our ministers have the habit of putting words in the mouths of their benefactors when their chair is threatened because of their own inefficiency.
