A group of sadhus, led by Mahant Yugal Kishore Sharan Shastri, has demanded legal action against senior Vishwa Hindu Parishad leader and former BJP MP Ram Vilas Vedanti for allegedly claiming that he had received a death threat from SIMI and Al-Qaeda.

Shastri, the Mahant of Saryu Kunj temple which is adjacent to the disputed Ram temple in Ayodhya, chaired a meeting of more than 500 Sahdus and Mahants on Saturday in the temple premises. "A memorandum signed by 100 Sadhus, has been dispatched to the Chief Minister's office demanding immediate arrest of Vedanti for conspiring to create communal violence in Ayodhya and adjoining areas," Shastri told The Indian Express.

On August 30, Vedanti had lodged a complaint with the Ayodhya Police alleging that he had been receiving death threats from the Al-Qaeda and SIMI. The district administration immediately provided a security cover and deployed additional men to his X-category security.

Following the complaint the police swung into action and Vedanti's mobile phone was brought under electronic surveillance to track down the callers. Soon after, the police arrested Ramesh Tiwari, Bajrang Dal's city president in Katra and Pawan Pandey, a local convener of Hindu Yuva Vahini from Katra in Gonda district.

"Vedanti has conspired with two of the local leaders of Bajrang Dal and Hindu Yuva Vahini to pose as Al- Qaiyeda and SIMI activists. In fact Vedanti had a plan to disrupt the communal harmony and to create a riot type of situation that would help the BJP to prepare their grounds for the coming Lok Sabha elections," said Shastri. Vedanti would contest the elections as a BJP candidate from Gonda.

According to the police, during interrogation Pandey said "my Guruji was not getting Z-category security as enjoyed by VHP leaders like Ashok Singhal and Praveen Togadia, so we took the step after Guruji gave us the consent".

"After we arrested the duo Vedanti told us that he knew them and requested us not to take any legal action against them. So we released them," Superintendent of Police Gyaneshwar Tiwari said.

Heading: JE vaccine supply to UP loses potency - Indian Express
Content:
Having failed to construct flush toilets in their houses, 30 elected members of various village Panchayats in Bilaspur district have been dismissed from their posts under a law that makes it compulsory for peoples' representatives to adopt safe and hygienic practices at their homes.

The Chhattisgarh Panchayat Act stipulates that all elected representatives of Panchayat bodies have to construct flush toilets in their houses within one year of their election, failing which they could be removed from their posts under Section 36 of the Act. Once a panch or a sarpanch is expelled under this provision, the state Government recommends the state Election Commission to conduct a by-election to fill up the vacant posts. This provision was incorporated in the Act to discourage the habit of defecation in the open and to create awareness regarding sanitation, as the elected Panchayat members have to play a vital role in ensuring the success of Total Sanitation Programme by motivating the masses to use toilets.

As Bilaspur district administration had received complaints against panchs that they have not constructed flush toilets in contravention to the provisions of the Panchayat Act, they were referred to the court of Additional Collector for hearing. Subsequently, show-cause notices were issued to all concerned and Chief Executive Officers (CEO) of Janpad Panchayats of their respective areas were asked to conduct an inspection of the residences of these elected representatives. During the course of hearing, some of the Panchayat members said that they had already constructed toilets in their houses and had even produced photographs as proof.

After the hearings, Bilaspur additional collector's court ordered removal of 30 elected members of Devri, Silli, Tkakurikapa, Bagbudva, Goidri and Boindra panchayats However, no action was taken against 19 other members, as it was found that they had constructed toilets within one year after their election. "It's a quasi-judicial procedure. Each complaint is heard and disposed off separately," said Bilaspur Additional Collector Dhananjay Dewangan.

State Panchayat and Social Welfare Director Dr P P Shiroti said, "The sprit of this particular provision is not to remove anyone from the post but to create awareness about sanitation." He said this provision for disqualification of members had yielded desired results. "Earlier, only 17 per cent of the 1.5 lakh elected representatives of Panchayat bodies had toilets in their homes. Now, a majority of them have constructed toilets in their houses," he added.

Heading: U’khand: more pitch for Gar Sain as capital - Indian Express
Content:
After an inspection, experts have found that a large number of vaccine vial monitors (VVM, which is the potency indicator) on Japanese Encephalitis vaccine stored at the Government Medical Store Depot (GMSD), Karnal in Haryana, have reached stage 2 of exposure to heat. The implication is that the vaccine's efficacy has slightly reduced.

The inspection, carried out by international NGO Path on Saturday, followed disclosure by health officials in Uttar Pradesh that a large portion of a consignment of the vaccine dispatched to the state from the GMSD had become ineffective (reached stage 3 or 4) due to exposure to heat. The NGO is providing technical support to the Government in implementation of the JE programme.

Though stage 2-exposed vaccine can be used for vaccination as its efficacy is reduced slightly, it is a cause for concern since such an exposure at initial stages could lead to stage 3 exposure during transportation. Once the vaccine reaches stage 3 exposure to heat, it becomes ineffective.

Dr Jagdish Chandra, CMO in-charge of the GMSD, told The Indian Express, "It is true that when we inspected the storage on Saturday some of the VVMs had reached stage 2. There seemed to be some problem with the initial supply itself because we have been maintaining the required temperature from 2 degree Celsius to 8 degree. However, it should not be much problem as stage 2 vaccine can be used for vaccination."

Chandra, who has recently taken over the charge, accepted that the vaccine supply to UP had already reached stage 2 at Karnal before the dispatch. "The vaccine dispatched to UP was at stage 2. But again I would say that if proper temperature is maintained during transportation then it would not have deteriorated further," he said.

"After the report from UP, one of our officers visited Karnal and found some of the samples in stage 2. Though these can be used for vaccination, there is something wrong somewhere because if the VVM reaches stage 2 of exposure at initial storage then it means that even a slight exposure during transportation can easily make the vaccine ineffective," said Dr Pritu Dhalaria, the JE Programme Manager for Path in India.

The issue came to light when around 4.5 lakh doses of JE vaccine reached UP from GMSD on Thursday. When the VVMs were checked, state health department officials found that majority of them had either turned mauve (stage 3) or purple (stage 4), both of which cannot be used.

Following this, the officials wrote a letter to the Central Government asking them to change the supply. While UP has already underdone its regular JE vaccination programme, this vaccine was to be used for its routine immunisation programme.

For further investigation into the matter, a team from the Union Health Ministry is expected to arrive in Lucknow on Monday.

JE VACCINATION PROGRAMME

•Imported from China, JE vaccine is initially stored at GMSD

• From there it is supplied to 24 dsitricts in 10 states — UP, Bihar, Haryana, Kerala, Assam, Karnataka, West Bengal, Maharashtra, Tamil Nadu and Andhra Pradesh

• The programme in majority of the states has been completed

• It is going on in Tamil Nadu and West Bengal, whereas in Kerala it is supposed to begin on September 17

• UP, Bihar and Tamil Nadu are to introduce it under routine immunisation

WHAT IS VVM

• Used for the first time on JE vaccine

• It is a tiny sticker on vaccine vial that changes its colour from white to purple in four stages when exposed to heat

• It is the most effective way of finding whether vaccine's potency has been reduced due to break in the cold-chain

Heading: Silt twice that of Nile, Kosi difficult to clear - Indian Express
Content:
While the ruling BJP and the opposition Congress prefer to downplay on the demands for a permanent capital for Uttarakhand, individuals and smaller parties like the Uttarakhand Kranti Dal (UKD) are raking up the issue time and again insisting Gair Sain be made the permanent capital.

The movement has gained momentum ever since the Justice Virendra Dixit Commission submitted its report on the issue to CM B C Khanduri on August 17.

An All India Congress Committee (AICC) member Dhirendra Pratap organised a day-long all meet at Ram Nagar on Monday demanding Gair Sain be made the state capital.

A partner in the ruling alliance, the UKD has also been demanding Gair Sain be made the state capital and threatened a state-wide agitation if their demands were not met.

UKD workers had staged a token dharna in support of their demand outside Gandhi Park in Dehradun.

Heading: Mail refers to ‘Mujahids’,scholars say it’s an insult - Indian Express
Content:
With the Kosi accumulating over 1 lakh cubic metres of silt in its river basin — twice that of the Nile and five times that of the Sutlej — every year, large-scale desiltation of the river is virtually impossible.

Even if it is attempted, owners of vast stretches of land on either side of the riverbank would not allow silt to be disposed of in their fertile fields.

Kosi Project engineers said a 20-metre-wide and five- to eight-feet-long river channel from the breach point to the Birpur barrage and subsequently till the 125 km stretch at Kopadia (Saharsa) was the best available option to lessen Kosi's unpredictability.

Kosi Project Eastern Bank Superintending Engineer Satish Kumar told The Indian Express: "Desiltation has been a big problem, with the project having no dredgers (silt removers) for the past 22 years. We hire it at times from private companies. But there has never been sustained digging of a pilot channel to allow faster water flow."

Kumar said the riverbed accumulated six to eight feet silt in its six-nine km width and the 125 km stretch till Kopadia, where it meets six small rivers.

"At most places from Birpur to Kopadia, the river-bed has become higher than the agricultural land on either side of the embankment. Much to our dismay and helplessness, the river bed is even at the same level as the banks at some places." Partial desiltation can be done but that too requires a large workforce and involves heavy expenditure, he added.

Mithilesh Kumar, a retired superintending engineer with Kosi Project, said that once water flow gets normal by December-January, a head regulator (a bridge like structure) should be placed at the Kushaha breach. "The regulator would allow discharge of water to the Nepal side (the new river course), helping engineers carry out desilting effectively from the barrage to the breach point," said the engineer who worked at Birpur.

Researchers at the Nepal Water Conservation Foundation say the Himalayan country gets 80 per cent of its water during monsoon rains, of which 50 per cent falls in just 15 hours, leaving river gorges to act as sloping channels.

Kosi plunges nine km over 200 km during its course from Mount Everest to Birpur in Bihar. It brings over 25,000 cubic metres of water per second, a good enough force to sweep tonnes of silt.

Heading: Two faces of SIMI - Indian Express
Content:
Two 19th century personalities find mention in the e-mail sent by Indian Mujahideen as "visionary legends" in whose memory the serial blasts which marred the Capital on Saturday evening have been carried out. Even as the group terms the two — Sayeed Ahmed Shaheed and Shah Ismail Shaheed — as "Mujahids", Islamic scholars differ to say they were "scholars" who fought the British rule and are celebrated as "freedom fighters".

"We have carried out this attack in the memory of two most eminent Mujahids of India — Sayeed Ahmed Shaheed and Shah Ismail Shaheed — who raised the glorious banner of jihad against the disbelievers in this very city of Delhi," reads the e-mail transcript. But Mushirul Hasan, an Islamic historian and faculty with Jamia Milia Islamia University, does not agree. "This is an insult to the memory of two leading scholars of the 19th century. Shah Ismail was a freedom fighter who fought against the British rule."

Hasan says the "jihad" fought by the two was the war against the British Government. "They were men with perspective. Their jihad was a response to the British governance. Ismail was called Shaheed because he was a martyr in the cause of freedom struggle." One of the great works of Shah Ismail is the 'Mansab-i-Imamat', says Hasan, who terms Ismail as a critic of the "despotic rule of Sultans of Delhi".

S Z H Jafri, the Head of History Department in Delhi University and an Islamic scholar, said the mentioning of the names of these two personalities were "totally unjustified".

"Historically, the war fought by Sayeed Ahmed and Shah Ismail was a jihad against the Sikhs of Punjab. They fought in the north-western provinces and established a government in Peshawar. History records their deaths in the Battle of Balakot in 1831," Jafri says. "There are hundreds of books written on Shah Ismail. Their reference in the e-mail is misleading," he adds.

Reference sites on the Internet record Sayeed Ahmed as a 19th Century "warrior" from Rae Bareilly and founder of a revolutionary Islamic movement 'The Way of the Prophet Muhammed' who was killed by the Sikh army in Balakot in 1831. Shah Ismail is termed as a scholar of Islam and a distinguished warrior in the jihad proclaimed by Sayeed Ahmed against the Sikhs in Punjab.

Heading: Rajasthan Police in Delhi to help probe - Indian Express
Content:
Seven years after the September 9 World Trade Center attacks spelt the first ban for Students Islamic Movement of India (SIMI), two profiles about the organisation continue to clash — one that of a ghost which "has ceased to exist" and the other of a "group of youths and students easily influenced by hard-core Muslim terrorist organisations operating from within the country and abroad". Both profiles came to fore in July 2008 before the Unlawful Activities (Prevention) Tribunal, comprising Delhi High Court judge, Justice Gita Mittal, set up to decide on the question of a fourth consecutive ban on the SIMI. Probe agencies say Indian Mujahideen, reported to be behind the blasts in Delhi, is a front for SIMI.

The author of the first description about SIMI, Shahid Badar, the organisation's president during the first ban in September 2001, stated on oath before the Tribunal that "SIMI has ceased to exist after the first ban". "SIMI does not endure any illegal or violent activities and has issued strong press statements condemning illegal and violent activities," the organisation says in its affidavit.

But the Home Ministry's take on the SIMI has achieved the fourth ban for the latter in the Supreme Court, followed with an extension till October. The ministry, in its affidavit, describes SIMI as an association which is not only "financially sound" but capable of orchestrating frequent trans-border movements of its cadres to partner with international terror outfits like Lashkar-e-Toiba, the architect of the 2005 pre-Diwali blasts in Delhi, Hizb-ul-Mujahideen and the Liberation Tigers of Tamil Eelam.

The bans have not been "effective", admits the ministry, "It (SIMI) has supporters in the Gulf countries. It has contacts in Pakistan, Afghanistan, Saudi Arabia, Bangladesh and Nepal. Pakistan-based Hizb-ul-Mujahideen and Lashkar-e-Toiba have successfully penetrated into SIMI cadres."

The ministry quotes information by intelligence agencies of "pan-Islamic linkages of ex-SIMI activists with the LTTE cadres in carrying out militant activities in the country" during the years of ban.

"Its members being students and youths, SIMI is easily influenced by hardcore Muslim terror organisations operating within the country and abroad," describes the ministry. To counter this Badar's version is that SIMI no longer exists. "It is for this reason that there is no office-bearer or member who could represent the organisation (in the litigation) and I have appeared in the present proceedings on the basis of having been the past president," he says.

Heading: Kalam for strict anti-terror laws - Indian Express
Content:
A Rajasthan police team was dispatched to Delhi on Sunday, a day after serial blasts rocked the capital and security for senior state police officers was beefed up following the Indian Mujahideen threat to target a Rajasthan Additional Director General of Police (ADG).

The state police said the team would help investigations in Delhi and try to find out whether there are similarities between Saturday's terror strike and the May 13 serial blasts in Jaipur, which claimed 68 lives.

The police will also question SIMI president Shahbaz Hussain, who was arrested in August, about the Delhi blasts because investigations had revealed that he had sent the terror email following the May 13 strikes.

Rajasthan Director General of Police K S Bains said security for ADG (Crime)A K Jain, who heads the Special investigation team (SIT) probing the Jaipur terror strike, was beefed up after the Delhi blasts.

"The email sent by the supposed perpetrators of the blasts referred to Jain, who has been responsible for the terror probe since May 13," Bains said.

He added that a team of the state police led by DIG Saurabh Srivastava would arrive in Delhi to begin investigations on Sunday. According to Srivastava, the Rajasthan police team's role in Delhi is two-fold. "First, we will try and determine if there are any connections or similarities between the Delhi and Jaipur strikes. We will also make available the intelligence records on the Jaipur terror probe to the Delhi police," Srivastava said.

Heading: LeT says no role in Delhi blasts - Indian Express
Content:
Former president A P J Abdul Kalam on Sunday night backed the demand for stringent laws in the fight against terrorism, and favoured setting up of a unified intelligence agency. "We need to enact laws which will provide stringent punishment and deliver faster justice through quick disposal of cases," he said.

Attack barbaric: IUML

The IUML has strongly condemned the "barbaric" blasts in Delhi, saying no civilised people will accept the "dastardly act". In a resolution adopted at the Party's National Executive meeting here, it asked the Centre to take stringent action against the persons responsible for this "cowardly" act.

Heading: Haywood lesson: ATS to keep off mail chase - Indian Express
Content: The Lashker-e-Toiba (LeT) on Sunday claimed that it was not even "remotely involved" in the serial blasts that rocked Delhi terming such acts as "un-Islamic". "We have no link with the serial blasts in Delhi. We are not even remotely involved in such acts as we consider these un-Islamic," LET spokesman Abdullah Gaznavi said. "We are active in Kashmir. To link Kashmiris with blasts that took place in India is aimed at maligning the ongoing movement," Gaznavi said. "It is unfair to link the outfit with these blasts. We do not believe in triggering explosions at public places to kill innocent people," he said, adding "Islam is a religion of peace and does not allow targeting of innocent people through such acts."

Heading: MNS lets up, Sena targets Bachchans - Indian Express
Content:
After drawing a blank on the earlier two terror e-mails sent from the city and its suburbs, the Maharashtra Anti Terrorism Squad (ATS) today washed its hands of the Delhi terror e-mail sent from a building in Chembur. Stating that the "Ken Haywood episode" had been a "learning experience", the ATS said it was focusing on locating suspects rather than splitting hairs over cyber forensics.

"We have realised that the source of these e-mails is leading us nowhere at all. That is why we are not concerning ourselves with the Delhi e-mail being traced to a Chembur building last night. Our officers have taken down the statement of the person whose WiFi internet connection was used to send this e-mail, but we are not going to investigate this further. The Mumbai Police Cyber Crime Investigation Cell will conduct a separate technical probe," said Parambir Singh, ACP, ATS.

Saturday's e-mail from the Indian Mujahideen claiming responsibility for the Delhi serial blasts was traced to the residence of M K Kamath at 201/202 on the second floor of a two-storey building named Eric House in Chembur. According to police, Kamath owns Kamran Power Controls Pvt. Ltd which manufactures and exports electrical panels and control panel boards.

The July 26 mail, sent minutes before the Ahmedabad blasts, had been traced to the unsecured WiFi connection of US national Kenneth Haywood in Mumbai, but its senders are yet to be traced. The senders of another mail traced to Khalsa College in Matunga on August 23 are also at large.

"The whole Ken Haywood episode has been a learning experience for us, and we will not handle the matter the same way. Our time and resources will now be spent on hunting for suspects such as Abdus Subhan Qureshi alias Tauqir, and a graphic designer named Qayamuddin. We have certain leads in the matter and the names of several other suspects which we cannot reveal. Though we have know about him for some time now, Tauqir has somehow manage to evade him. But the constant attacks on the ATS in the e-mails suggest that his pride has been pricked as we are closing in on him," said Singh who added that the threats issued through the latest e-mail were being taken seriously by the ATS.

When contacted, Joint Commissioner of Police, Crime, Rakesh Maria said, "The Cyber Crime Investigation Cell is yet to be handed over the probe into the Delhi e-mail. Our investigations are on with regards to the Khalsa College e-mail."

Meanwhile, Sarika Kamath, wife of M K Kamath, today said they had become "victims of technology" and had been questioned through the night by the ATS.

"Hacking has become a terror for common citizens like us. We are innocent and hard-working people who have become victims of technology. We did not feel the need to secure or password-protect our internet connection. But now it has clearly become a necessity for all citizens to do so," she said.

Heading: India has sovereign right to conduct test: Pranab - Indian Express
Content:
The Shiv Sena has picked up where the Maharashtra Navanirman Sena (MNS) left off in its criticism of actor Amitabh Bachchan and wife Jaya over her alleged anti-Marathi remarks.

Days after MNS leader Raj Thackeray accepted Amitabh Bachchan's apology, the Shiv Sena revived the controversy by saying that it was necessary to look into Jaya Bachchan's remarks "from a political perspective", considering the Bachchans' association with the Samajwadi Party.

The Shiv Sena claimed credit for having raised such issues in the first place. Writing his weekly column in party mouthpiece Saamna, Shiv Sena spokesperson Sanjay Raut said the MNS was raising issues the Sena had taken up four decades ago.

The assertion by Raut, who is the executive editor of Saamna, comes at a time when the MNS is eating into the Shiv Sena's vote base on the issue of Marathi.

"Raj Thackeray's party reiterated what the Shiv Sena has been saying for the past 40 years. Jaya Bachchan just helped them. Jaya Bachchan had no reason to get involved in politics, but she did. Hence she will have to bear the consequences," the column said.

Raut highlighted the family's political connections, pointing out that Amitabh had campaigned for the Samajwadi Party while his wife Jaya represented the party in the Rajya Sabha. "Hence the statements had to be looked at from a political perspective," Raut wrote.

Raut acknowledged that the Bachchans are great actors but added, "They can never be greater than Maharashtra."

The column drew parallels with southern actor Rajnikant, who had supported Tamil Nadu in a water dispute with Karnataka, and said that the Hindi film industry had not stood by Maharashtra in times of crisis. Raut also followed Raj Thackeray in taking on Mumbai Joint Commissioner of Police K L Prasad for his remarks on "Mumbai not belonging to anyone's father."

"Civil servants need to exercise more restraint than politicians. If an officer had made such remarks in any other state, he would not have been allowed to stay in the post or in the state for a day. This was allowed as Maharashtra is tolerant and silent."

Heading: Capt away, Badal gives Rs 250 cr to Patiala - Indian Express
Content:
India can conduct nuclear tests in the future, if necessary, but it has to be ready to face consequences, External Affairs Minister Pranab Mukherjee has said.

"If the country considers it is necessary to conduct nuclear tests, it can do so. Nothing stops us in this (123) agreement," he told a television news channel.

Mukherjee said, "Every country has its own rules for nuclear tests and therefore, we (India) also have sovereign right to go for the nuclear tests, if required."

However, he added that if the country conducts a test, it has to face consequences as witnessed in 1974 and 1998, hinting at possibility of sanctions as were imposed after the Pokhran I and II atomic tests.

On the BJP's opposition to his statement that India is committed to non-proliferation goals and maintaining its unilateral moratorium on testing, Mukherjee said the saffron party should not forget that it was the BJP, which, after the 1998 Pokhran explosions, declared unilaterally that India would not conduct any more nuclear tests.

Heading: Need to strengthen police force: Patil - Indian Express
Content:
Making the best of the absence of his bete noire Capt Amarinder Singh, Chief Minister Parkash Singh Badal announced a liberal package of Rs 250 crore for the makeover of Patiala.

"There will be no shortage of funds for Patiala, which will get Rs 117 crore in near future for improving power infrastructure," he said. Sources said Badal has earmarked Rs 50 crore for improvement of civic amenities in the town.

Sources said Badal's decision to visit Patiala came soon after former CM Capt Amarinder Singh left for London in the aftermath of being unseated from the Vidhan Sabha.

The CM also held a closed-door meeting with top political leaders of Patiala and discussed city's development plans. "A committee, headed by Lt Gen Dhaliwal (retd), will directly report the development works in progress at Patiala to me," he told The Indian Express.

Badal also visited 10 wards and held a Sangat Darshan programme. However, the attendance was thin as many people with grievances were turned away by the CM's security staff and the local cops.

"My one-room house in Patran gave way in the recent hailstorm and the CM is not willing to meet us," said Reema Rani from Patran, who was not allowed to meet Badal. In another corner of ward number 5, some jathedars, who failed to meet the CM, went back perturbed. "Is this the way to treat his soldiers who have been fighting for him," said Gurcharan Singh and Hakam Singh, both jathedars.

Heading: Initial probe indicates little role of locals in Delhi blasts - Indian Express
Content: The serial blasts in Delhi had similarities with the explosions that occurred in other cities in recent times, sais Home Minister Shivraj Patil, who was in Guwahati to assess the flood situation on Sunday. He also indicated that there has been an over-dependence on the IB and RAW. "We should not be dependent only on the IB and RAW. The state police forces should also be modernised and strengthened," he said.

Heading: Mumbai’s Ganesh frenzy scales new heights - Indian Express
Content:
As investigations behind Saturday's serial bomb blasts in Delhi gained some momentum on Sunday with the detention of a few suspects, initial indications pointed to a lack of any major local involvement in the attacks.

Investigators probing the incident believe that the attack was carried out mostly by people from the outside with involvement of locals, most probably, being limited to arranging for accommodation and logistical support for the terrorists, sources said.

They said the police had detained about seven-eight people so far, including a few from neighbouring Haryana and Uttar Pradesh. But there are indications that the terror module behind Saturday's blasts had its base in western India with links in the cities of Mumbai, Indore or Ahmedabad. The fact that the email sent by Indian Mujahideen was traced to Mumbai and also references in the mail to a few scarcely reported raids in some areas of Mumbai has also given credence to this theory.

Another crucial lead the investigators are said to be working on is the stark similarity in the nature of explosives used in the blasts in Delhi and Ahmedabad. With both Ahmedabad and Delhi blasts being believed to be carried out by the same module, this has given rise to suspicion that the explosives expert of this module is not among those who have been arrested by the Gujarat Police in connection with the Ahmedabad blasts, the source said.

The explosives used in Delhi were exactly similar to the ones used in Ahmedabad blasts about two months back. The manner in which they were packed, the C-shaped boxes they were kept in, even the carpentry of the box, all point to the same group behind their assembling.

The investigators are banking heavily on the footage from the four CCTV cameras at Greater Kailash market. The sources said video footage in three of these were clear and would be crucial in identifying the people who placed the bombs. The fourth camera was said to be malfunctioning.

Heading: J-K poll security: more dog squads sanctioned - Indian Express
Content:
That Mumbai loves its annual 10-day Ganesh festival is no secret. But the sheer magnitude of the financial capital's love and devotion for the elephant-headed god scaled new heights this year, as a host of other competing events and pilgrim centres were left lagging behind.

The giant Ganesh idol in the heart of Mumbai has been worshipped by an average of three lakh devotees every day for the last nine days. Mumbaiites stood in queues for eight to 12 hours for an audience with the idol named Lalbaugcha Raja, the king of Lalbaug.

While there were 8,805 Sarvajanik Ganesh Mandals in 2005, this year it went up to 11,200, says N Dahibaonkar, chairman of the co-ordination committee of all mandals. "There will be 15 lakh people at Girgaum Chowpatty on Sunday evening for the immersion," he adds. And even before the grand finale on Sunday, 1,34,207 idols have already been immersed.

The embellishments are more vivid than the numbers: the Lalbaugcha Raja has tied up with a portal for daily updates, traffic updates and step-by-step directions from your home to the idol's feet; just the diamond-studded tilak on the forehead of the Goud Saraswat Brahmin Mandal's Ganesha idol is worth Rs 14 lakh; all big mandals have queue systems within halls or adjacent grounds, modelled after the Vaikuntam Queue Complex at Tirupati or the Siddhivinayak Temple; the décor ranges from terrorism to the changing horizon of the city's mill lands; darshan timings are announced at many mandals, 24 hours on all day.

Heading: Post-Amarnath blows, Valley police gears up to handle unarmed mobs - Indian Express
Content:
In the wake of increased militant threats and with Assembly polls round the corner , the J-K Crime Branch of Police will soon have more dog squads to help search militants and explosives, as also with crime investigations in the region. Forty dog squads have been sanctioned by the state Government, official sources said.

The state Crime Branch of Police, which had been facing a severe crunch of dog squads, is expected to be relieved after getting the new squads. The Crime Branch, at present, has only five dog squads in Jammu, sources said.

Heading: Asian tennis body finalises new tour schedule - Indian Express
Content:
The Jammu and Kashmir Government is finally waking up to the changing course of Kashmir's separatist movement. The state police have procured an urgent consignment of riot gear, tear smoke shells, rubber pellets and riot control guns as part of their preparation to control unarmed protests.

Sources reveal that the police have always been short of standard riot control gear. "Then there is the problem of mindset as well. The continuous fight with militants has completely changed the attitude of the police. They have become more of like the army," a senior police officer said.

"Because the emphasis was on fighting insurgency, where nothing but firearms were used, over the years, the J-K Police have forgotten the basics of normal law enforcement. It's unfortunate, but true," he added.

The police department admits that the current protests in the Valley have caught the top brass off guard. "Our men are used to carrying sophisticated weapons and the situations have been such that they had to open fire whenever they were attacked. We urgently need a transformation from a military mindset to a police mindset in our men," a senior officer said. He said the casualties increase because the policemen fire without making a difference between a militant group and a stone-pelting mob.

In fact, the doctors in Kashmir's premier SHMHS hospital, too, point out this strange phenomenon. "More than 90 per cent wounded people, who were brought to the emergency (during the current protests), had received bullet injures above the waist," Dr Saleem Iqbal of SMHS told The Indian Express. "This is alarming," he added.

The first step towards changing the approach was to look for a standard riot gear. Initially, the police used old tear smoke shells, which were dumped in their stores ever since militancy erupted in the Valley in 1990. "We would normally get 3,000 shells every year as our quota. We never demanded more because we didn't need them. These annual consignments were lying in our stores," an officer said. "Apart from Srinagar, where the police occasionally used tear smoke shells to stop protests, there was hardly any such need anywhere else. And once these protests started, we were short of fresh material. Initially, we used whatever we had, including the expired stock."

Sources said the police needed riot control guns which fire tear smoke shells, the new hand hurled stunt grenades, guns to fire rubber pellets and more importantly lathis and shields. When the state police approached the Border Security Force's factory in Takenpur (the only factory producing tear smoke shells, rubber pellets and other riot-control arms), it was shut for two months. The demand was met when the Union Home Ministry intervened and arranged the material from the Delhi Government. Sources say additional consignments were borrowed from Rajasthan as well.

"The rubber bullets can also prove fatal if hit above waist. We have issued clear direction to use the rubber bullets in extreme circumstances," a senior officer said.

Heading: Ghosal’s tour de France begins with victory - Indian Express
Content:
After plans for a new Asian tennis tour were mooted by Anil Khanna in 2007, the president of the Asian Tennis Federation announced the final outline of the venture on Sunday.

The tour will feature 12 tournaments in different Asian countries, the minimum prize money being $50,000. There will be an Asian Championship in New Delhi this year to kickstart events.

The tour will end with a Masters tournament, featuring the top eight Asian players and prize money of $30,000.

'No rebellion'

Khanna also said the tour was not intended to be rebellious. Having long insisted the current ranking system of the Association of Tennis Professionals (ATP) did not allow players from Asia to make it to the top ranking level, he said this was an attempt to ensure equal opportunities.

"Players who are 100-plus or 150-plus, many among them being Asians, are not making money. This is an opportunity for them to compete in easily accessible places and earn handsome money, which they can use to travel and earn points," he said.

Asia will be divided into five zones: East, South East, South Asia, Central and West Asia and there would be regional representation in our Tour events. The winner of the Asian Championships will be given wild cards for the ATP Qatar Open.

Players would be given free hospitality and a subsidy of $ 500 for their travel expenses, if they appear in a Tour event. Asian rankings would be issued every week, taking into account players' ATP rankings and their ranking on the Asian Tour.

Heading: Young Vettel records stunning win - Indian Express
Content:
Now that he is free from his university juggling of studies and squash at Leeds, Sourav Ghosal can focus solely on the sport. The 22-year-old India No. 1 crossed the English Channel half-expecting to explore France a country he's never visited before, but ended up lasting the duration of the inaugural Ornano International Open tournament, to clinch the biggest PSA Tour title of his career.

"I just ended up playing all the time in France and didn't get to see anything!" Ghosal chuckled, after pocketing his fourth crown, having entered the tournament at Bordeaux facing a draw so stiff, that he hadn't really bothered checking the list at the outset.

But an upset win over French top-seed Renan Lavigne in the quarter-finals got him going, and after fending off three match-balls against Egyptian Amr Swelim in the semi-finals, Ghosal was up against third seed and world No. 30 Davide Bianchetti, a former World Open quarter-finalist, beating the Italian in four games.

String of upsets

"Beating a world No 27 (Lavigne) is my career best on PSA," Ghosal, ranked 45, confirmed of his top-scalp, though Ghosal was more pleased with the entire string of wins (three in a row) over higher-ranked players in the $15,000 event. This triumph will push Ghosal into the top-40 of the world next month, and his steady rise, after the completion of his degree and an easing of academic schedule, means the graph is headed upwards.

"There's just been a lot more time now to sit and think about the game, work on details," Ghosal says, and besides the wealth of advice he's picked from hitting with top-10 players like James Willstrop and Lee Beachill, he's also carried forward his association with Leeds University physical trainer Robb Wordsworth.

In his lead-up to the World Open in October, the physical conditioning will count as he runs into world No 22 Shahir Razeik — the two stand 1-1 head-to-head. What will also matter is his consistency and his ability to hit the straight length and cut the angles — some of the follies that made his national title win last month a rather laboured effort.

Renewing the French bond

"It's good to be No.1, but beating Sidharth (Suchde) wasn't easy in the final. I was missing my shots, and the last two tourneys in India, I didn't play my best squash" Ghosal recalls.

Rising steadily on the PSA rankings since having overtaken Ritwik Bhattacharya as the country's top player, expectations have risen even amongst the domestic audience. So, besides the onus of retaining his No 1 reputation, Ghosal also gets straddled with the responsibility of winning with flair, in style.

Heading to Paris for the 5-Star event from September 22-27, where Ghosal plays the qualifying draw, the Kolkatan is looking to renew the French connection once again. If he stays the course — the whole length, he wouldn't mind missing out on a trip to Eiffel Tower on his French sojourn, though this time he's carefully read the draw.

Heading: Fab fourth for Russian women at Fed Cup - Indian Express
Content:
Germany's Sebastian Vettel stunned Formula One as the sport's youngest race winner on Sunday with an exuberant victory for tiny Toro Rosso at their home Italian Grand Prix.

The 21-year-old, already the youngest to start a Grand Prix on pole position, gave his Ferrari-powered team their first win with a remarkably assured drive through spray and slippery conditions.

It was an astonishing result for the smallest of teams, formerly tail-enders Minardi, in a paddock dominated by mighty manufacturers.

Emerging from Ferrari's immense shadow at the temple of Italian motor racing, Toro Rosso became the only other Italy-based team to win a Grand Prix since Juan Manuel Fangio triumphed for Maserati in 1957.

"It's amazing, I can't believe it. I'm lost for words," declared Vettel, who was almost crying with joy before taking the chequered flag 12.5 seconds clear of McLaren's Heikki Kovalainen.

"It is the best day of my life. These pictures and emotions I will never forget."

McLaren's Lewis Hamilton, who started 15th after losing a gamble with the weather in qualifying, retained his championship lead by a single point after overtaking a string of cars to finish seventh.

Ferrari's Brazilian Felipe Massa, Hamilton's closest rival, failed to make the most of starting nine places ahead of the Briton and finished sixth in a wet race that began behind the safety car.

With four races remaining, Hamilton has 78 points to Massa's 77 and Robert Kubica's 64 for BMW-Sauber.

At 21 years and 74 days old, Vettel became Germany's first race winner since seven-time world champion Michael Schumacher retired in 2006. The Ferrari ace, who won at Monza in 2006, was present to witness the triumph of a youngster dubbed 'Baby Schumi.'

"What he did today was absolutely first class — to make no mistakes in these conditions and dominate the race from the start, and that in a car that is not the fastest," said Schumacher.

Kubica, himself only 23, took third place at the circuit where he took his first podium in 2006.

Renault's double world champion Fernando Alonso, who held the previous record for the youngest race winner after chalking up his first victory in Hungary in 2003 at 22 years and 26 days, finished fourth.

The title contenders could only rue an afternoon of missed opportunities.

"With me being right at the back they both missed an opportunity of taking lots of points off me. I showed that I was quickest in the wet and had great pace. I think a win was possible today," said Hamilton.

Heading: ‘Confident’ Saina strikes gold - Indian Express
Content:
Russia lifted the Fed Cup for the fourth time in five seasons on Sunday after Svetlana Kuznetsova beat Spanish number one Anabel Medina Garrigues and their doubles pair completed a whitewash.

The world number seven's 5-7, 6-3, 6-4 victory in two hours and 39 minutes gave Russia an unassailable 3-0 lead that was achieved despite the absence of the country's top three players and underlined Russia's dominance of the women's game.

The victory for Kuznetsova, who had not won a tournament all year, was no easy matter, however. Medina Garrigues fought bravely with the noisy backing of the near full 4,000-seater stadium, before finally running out of steam in the last set.

"Today it was important for me," said the 23-year-old from St Petersburg. "I felt very nervous, I had so many ups and downs but still, bringing the win for my team, it's amazing".

As on Saturday, Medina Garrigues, ranked 29, in the world was slow out of the blocks, meekly conceding her first two service games in the face of her opponents powerful groundstrokes.

Kuznetsova said after the match she was leaving the Sanchez-Casal Academy in Barcelona, where she has trained for over a decade, to return to Russia. "I miss my country and I think I need to do a few things differently to change my game. I love Spain but I think it's time to change, this is what my soul is asking me to do," she said.

In the final rubber, Elena Vesnina and Ekaterina Makarova beat Carla Suarez and Nuria Llagostera 6-2, 6-1 in just over an hour.

Heading: Don’t mix sports with politics, says Misbah - Indian Express
Content:
Saina Nehwal doesn't believe in half measures. The 18-year old shuttler might have missed out on a medal at the Beijing Olympics last month, but that didn't put her charge on hold. On Sunday, she added another feather to her cap by winning the Chinese Taipei Grand Prix Gold Open, defeating Malaysian Li Ya Lydia Cheah 21-8, 21-19 in the final.

Her second international title after the four-star Philippines Open in 2006, it makes her India's most successful woman shuttler at the international level. The fact that the win has come two years after her maiden title triumph makes it even more special. "It definitely feels good to win a title," Saina told The Indian Express over the phone from Taipei after the match.

"But honestly speaking, I never think about numbers. I just try to give my best in every tournament and every game that I play and go all out for a win. Coming after 2006, this is definitely a precious win. I had worked hard for this tournament and I was confident going into the final. I have been in good form, I played well today and I think I deserved to win," the Hyderabadi teenager added.

Best shot every time

She wasn't being arrogant. Her final opponent was ranked 58 places below her in the world rankings — Saina is 14th, Cheah 72nd. The second-seeded Indian was quick on court, her opponent relatively slower. Cheah's strongest weapons were her half smashes, which Saina had no trouble countering. She had an easy semi-final outing against Indonesian Pia Bernadet, who had upset Saina's nemesis Maria Yulianti earlier.

"There are times when everything falls in place; sometimes, it just isn't your day. That was what happened in Beijing. But for me the most important thing is to give my best shot every time," Saina said.

Saina came with a plan and attacked her opponent from the word go. She blew away the Malaysian in the first game and survived a couple of anxious moments in the second before clinching the issue in less than an hour.

With 7000 ranking points from the win, she is set to climb two places to 12th in the world rankings, inching closer to her aim finishing inside the top 10 by the yearend. "It's not easy, because the other girls in the top league are all far ahead in terms of points, but if I continue to win tournaments, I am sure I can do it," she said confidently.

And confidence is what put Saina in a different league. Reaching quarter-finals and semi-finals consistently but failing to win could've demoralised others, but it didn't affect her. "I never saw it that way — that I am the first Indian woman (to be so successful in badminton). It's all about believing in yourself. Of course, there are girls in India who are talented but seem to have some kind of a metal block, thinking that the Chinese or the Indonesians are strong and dominant. But my thinking is that if we work as hard as they do, there is no reason why we can't be as good as them. I have never thought of pressure against any opponent."

She has become an icon at home after her show in Beijing, nevertheless the pain of losing out of an Olympic medal still pinches Saina.

"Olympics are the biggest stage, and come only once in four years. So that disappointment will always be there. But it has also made me stronger and I have put it behind me. I'm looking forward to winning more and more tournaments and go for the gold in 2012," she said.

Saina next plays in the Japan Open starting September 16 before the China Masters from September 23-28.

Heading: Karthik keeps his eyes on the ball - Indian Express
Content:
Misbah-ul Haq has developed a great taste for Indian bowlers, scoring the bulk of his runs against the neighbours. And the Pakistan vice-captain has the perfect reason for this. "That's because I end up playing a lot of matches against India," he says.

Incidentally, Pakistan's next Test series, slated for January, is also against India. He calls the India-Pakistan series even greater than the Ashes but the lack of other international assignments has hampered the continuity in Pakistan cricket.

"Yes, we will be a little rusty for the India series because we would hardly play Test cricket or get to face top quality teams in ODIs. It is frustrating that we will play just a Test this year and even our one-day appearances have mostly been against Bangladesh and Zimbabwe. The players definitely need more exposure," he added.

"I think sports should never be mixed with political issues, it should be kept aside because at the end of the day, it's cricket that suffers. According to me, every team should play everywhere irrespective of the situation, otherwise the game's promotion will suffer. Of course, the postponements of the Australia series and the Champions Trophy have affected the game in Pakistan.

"The series against Australia was very important for us, not only from a players' perspective but also for the public," says Misbah. "But as a professional cricketer, these problems should not bother us. We need to prepare ourselves for every eventuality," he says.

Misbah, however, refused to make explain why he declined the Pakistan captaincy offer. More so, since the present skipper, Shoaib Malik, has recently come under fire from his team mates on his captaincy.

In Karachi, Malik echoed similar views. "I hope we will get to play a couple of series before the Indian tour because when you don't play cricket for sometime, then it is very difficult to stage a comeback against a strong opposition," Malik said today.

Heading: ICL effect: Six Bangladesh cricketers quit - Indian Express
Content:
Dinesh Karthik is aware that the tough climb has started again; quite familiar with the comeback route, the wicketkeeper and opening bat speaks about the importance of an India A outing in the backdrop of a disappointing Sri Lanka series. Excerpts:

You made a great comeback to international cricket after being dropped in 2006.

• Yes, things actually turned out to be good then. I was scoring runs and the best part was my consistency. I had a good South Africa tour as an opener, followed by England.

So what went wrong after that?

• I don't know, I can't point out any specific area. I had just one bad series but before that I have scored runs and kept wickets well too. Sometimes things don't go as you want to but that doesn't means that one should sit and think about it all the time.

Is it because of lack of runs that you can't concentrate on your keeping or is it the other way round?

• I don't think there is any relation between wicketkeeping and batting. When I keep wickets I only concentrate on my collection and when I bat, the focus is entirely on playing a long innings and scoring runs.

Your 'keeping came under the scanner in the Sri Lanka Test series.

• I agree and I also know that people might have different opinions over that but you can't stop them. I realise that I failed to keep well against Kumble on a couple of occasions but such things happen.

Earlier it was Parthiv who was competing with you, now you will be trying to replace him.

• Competition will always be there, and it is good for every player. Without it, there won't be any excitement. Everyone in the team works hard for their place; Parthiv has also worked his way in by scoring heavily in domestic cricket. Now it's my turn.

Whenever you have been dropped you have come out stronger?

• (Laughs) Is it? I just try to enjoy my game. That's it.

With the India A tri series starting, what are your expectations?

•I'm hoping to score runs and come out with a consistent show. We all know performances against good teams help and it counts for a lot.

Heading: Ganguly’s absence interesting: Ponting - Indian Express
Content:
A day after The Indian Express reported the Indian Cricket League (ICL) was planning to launch a full-fleged Bangladesh team, six Bangla players, including former skipper Habibul Bashar, resigned from the national team on Sunday.

Bashar, Shariar Nafees, Aftab Ahmed, Mosharraf Hossain, Farhad Reza and Dhiman Ghosh informed the Bangladesh board they wouldn't be available for the national team due to "personal reasons". However, it is apperent they are set to join the Zee-bankrolled league's ranks. Bashar, who is Bangladesh's most succesful skipper and leading Test scorer, admitted he had an offer to join the ICL but said he was yet to sign any contract.

In the wake of the resignations, the board huddled for an emergency meeting on Sunday. "We have summoned all six players to appear before the board on Tuesday to explain the reasons for retirement," said Gazi Ashraf Hossain, chairman of the board's cricket operations committee.

More resignations

Meanwhile, local media reported eight more players could quit the national team in order to join the ICL team, which will be called the Dhaka Warriors. Other former or current national team players who were also expected to the join the ICL include Mohammad Rafique, Alok Kapali, Nazim Uddin, Manjurul Islam, Tapash Baishya and Mohammad Sharif.

The loss of so many top players would devastate the Bangladesh national team, which already struggles to compete against the top sides in international play. Recently, they were vanquished by Australia 3-0 in an ODI series Down Under.

They host New Zealand in a Test and one-day series next month. Incidentally, New Zealand have also lost many of their top stars, including their pace spearhead Shane Bond, to the ICL.

The latest move gives a boost to the ICL's plans of staging a cricket world cup of their own this year.

Heading: India tour on, but no ‘double standards’ - Indian Express
Content:
Sourav Ganguly's omission from the Irani Trophy, which many believe is a sign of things to come, has baffled Australia captain Ricky Ponting, who believes it would be "interesting" to face an Indian team sans the belligerent left-hander.

"But Sourav hasn't been named in the initial squad and that is going to be interesting for me during the tour," said the Australian, who is recovering from a wrist surgery.

Heading: Season’s greetings from Pak - Indian Express
Content:
Australia's tour of India is likely to go ahead as per schedule despite initial concerns over the fate of the four-Test series after Saturday's serial blasts in New Delhi.

According to The Australian, Cricket Australia and the Australian Cricketers Association have asked for urgent reports from their security advisers, which are expected to be presented on Monday, but the situation is not considered anywhere near as bad as Pakistan.

CA has engaged regular security consultant Reg Dickason and will consult the Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade in Canberra, the Australian High Commission in New Delhi and the Board of Control for Cricket in India. The 15-man squad is expected to leave on Sunday.

Meanwhile, ACA chief Paul Marsh insisted security assessments would be made impartially and not swayed by the lucrative nature of an Indian tour compared with Pakistan.

The Australians were criticised for postponing this year's tour of Pakistan on security grounds, and expressing subsequent concerns over the staging of the Champions Trophy.

The four-Test tour is scheduled to begin with a practice match against a Rajasthan Cricket Association's Centre of Excellence XI on September 27.

"I expect there will be heat if we decide to tour," Marsh was quoted as saying by the Sydney Morning Herald. "As much as it's sometimes reported that we cancel series at the drop of a hat, that is simply not the case. We receive specific, expert advice from people who have served us well in the past, and we will consult them again. I would not say there is panic among the players I have spoken to, but a degree of concern.

"If the team stays in India, there might be some who criticise us for double standards. But people need to understand our starting point is that we always want to tour. We go to extreme lengths to obtain the best advice on the situation of each country we visit. In Pakistan's case this year, people we rely on told us not to tour. If they say not to tour again, we'll listen. Bombs going off anywhere are a concern."

Australia are scheduled to play the first Test against India on October 9 in Bangalore, which hit by eight synchronised bomb blasts in July. The third Test of the series is due to be played at the Ferozeshah Kotla on October 29.

Heading: Despite blasts, it’s business as usual for cricketers - Indian Express
Content:
The gleam in their eyes outshone the glaze on the brand new SG Test balls. And understandably so, as it was for the first time the bowlers from the visiting Pakistani team, the Sui Northern Gas Pipeline Limited, were using the SG Test balls meant exclusively for Indian cricket.

"I bowled with it for the first time. It loses shine a bit quickly but achha reverse hoga isse," says medium pacer Adil Raza. "I am excited and hopefully I can use it to my benefit," says left-arm spinner Imran Khalid.

Pakistan vice-captain and senior member of this team, Misbah-ul Haq, who has successfully dealt with the ball in the past, says: "The Grains ball that we earlier used in our domestic cricket is somewhat similar to this. But we now use the Kookaburra at all levels. The SG balls will definitely provide a different charm to the game," he adds.

No doubt they will be an important aspect in this Mohammad Nissar Trophy match, but the Qaid-e-Azam champions will have another problem to counter — the Ferozeshah Kotla wicket.

It has been laid out specially to benefit the stroke-makers in the Delhi team. The binding on the wicket means spinners will have little role to play and the onus will be on the fast bowlers to make use of the 9.30 am start to swing the ball and reverse swing it in the last session.

Both sides are expected to go in with three specialist pacers with Ishant Sharma, Ashish Nehra and Pradeep Sangwan looking more compact and well equipped than their little-known counterparts from Pakistan.

The hosts look overwhelming favourites with the star power in their ranks but the picture could become hazy on Monday morning as skipper Virender Sehwag is still recovering from a swollen left ankle. He is most likely to sit out and joining him on the sidelines with a minor thigh niggle could be deputy Gautam Gambhir.

Though Sehwag batted for 20 minutes at the nets, he looked uncomfortable and reserved the final call on his availability till the morning of the match. If he walks out to the middle for the toss, it will be a surprise considering the high stakes in a hectic season ahead.

Delhi's batting will revolve around Aakash Chopra, Virat Kohli, Mithun Manhas and Rajat Bhatia while Pakistan will rely on Misbah, Mohammad Hafeez and the Akmal brothers — Adnan and Umar.

Teams

Delhi: Virender Sehwag (capt), Gautam Gambhir, Aakash Chopra, Mayank Tehlan, Mithun Manhas, Virat Kohli, Rajat Bhatia, Puneet Bisht (wk), Ishant Sharma, Pradeep Sangwan, Ashish Nehra, Chetanya Nanda, Amit Bhandari, Narender Singh, Gaurav Chhabra. Reserve player: Rahul Diwan

Sui Northern Gas Pipeline Limited: Mohammad Hafeez (capt), Adil Raza, Adnan Akmal, Asad Ali, Azhar Shafiq, Imran Ali, Imran Khalid, Khurram Shehzad, Misbah-ul-Haq, Saleem Mughal, Samiullah Khan, Tauqeer Hussain, Umar Akmal and Yasir Arafat. Umpires: UL Dubey and Sudhir Asnani. Match referee: Arun Sharma.

Heading: What’s changed? - Indian Express
Content:
The series of bomb blasts in Delhi haven't quite triggered an atmosphere of paranoia at Hyderabad, where the 'A' teams of Australia and New Zealand are getting ready for the tri-series starting tomorrow.

Justin Sternes, the Austalia A manager-cum-assistant coach, told The Indian Express that the blast will have no effect on the A tour. "We haven't got any calls from Cricket Australia so far and there is no sign of panic. The tour will be on," he said.

Speaking to the A team players, it is clear they are keen to take the field, since incessant rains have seen Australia A's last game being washed out.

Though the prime concern seems to be the weather, there is no denying the fact that the visitors have been receiving endless calls from friends and family back home after Aussie news channels beamed pictures of the Delhi blasts.

The players have been advised not to speak on safety issues, but it is evident that the mood in the visitors' camp is quite relaxed. As one meets an Aussie player at the breakfast table, the first thing he asks is about the rain forecast.

When one drops that uncomfortable question about the bomb blasts and the threat perception in the team, the player mimics a state of panic and in an exaggerated tone asks, "What kind of blast, where did it take place?"

Soon, he gives up the act and breaks into a naughty grin and adds that no one is pressing the panic button at the moment.

Career at stake

Australia A coach Simon Helmot puts things in perspective. "For the players here, playing matches is more important than any other thing. Their career is at stake and this series means a lot to them. I won't give any comment regarding the bomb blasts, but everyone is thinking about the matches," says Helmot.

The players got to know about the blasts Saturday evening when they were attending a dinner hosted by the Hyderabad Cricket Association.

Initially, there were a few worried faces but after the locals gave them details, normalcy was restored.

In the hotel lobby, a group of New Zealanders stood in a bunch, from which peals of laughter could clearly be heard. During a discussion on the number of calls received the previous night, someone's phone buzzes.

Before picking up the phone, he makes an announcement, "Another panic call from home."

But the conversation strangely consists of a few harsh words before he hangs up. "Somebody was asking me if I use pre-paid or post-paid," he says, and there are smiles all around.

Heading: A footballing heresy - Indian Express
Content:
In a pattern that is becoming too familiar, terrorists identified the heart of India's capital on Saturday evening as sites of ordinary transactions among residents. The geography of ordinary commerce, as our columnist today calls it, busy marketplaces that the city's people gather at for a leisurely evening out, to find in the hubs desired objects of trade, an activity that harks back to the founding principles of cities. If the outrageous sadness of the occasion did not make the exercise so perverse, to look at the areas targeted, from Mumbai, Malegaon, Hyderabad, Jaipur, Bangalore, Ahmedabad to Delhi now, would be to map each city's peculiar ways of sociability. The terrorist carries a clear reading of what makes our cities hum. The state's inability to break the cycle of attacks, to be even seen to have done enough in an attempt to break it, carries danger for this sociability.

Because by doing so it is failing in meeting a key requirement in its contract with the people: to provide and enforce a law and order framework to free them from being on perpetual alert in everyday movements and transactions. More than four years into its term, the UPA government's record on this account is looking even more shocking. Each terrorist strike must invite a repetition of charges against the government and its home ministry. That they have simply not done enough to bring closure to any of the terrorist incidents of the past four years, to follow leads thoroughly, to crack the organisations behind the incidents and, consequently, their ability to surprise at another time, another place. As the blasts in Delhi's Connaught Place, Greater Kailash and Karol Bagh markets on Saturday evening show, both the time and place remain of the terrorists' choosing.

There is an innate resilience in modern societies for people to rally around their governments in the face of terrorist aggression. To carry on with everyday life with as much normality as can be mustered. To do so in the face of fear that the appurtenances of ordinary use — in Delhi's case, the municipal trash bins — can be turned against them as instruments of terrorism. On Sunday, the day after, many of the city's trash bins were seen emptied out and turned upside down. Yet, life throbbed on Delhi's streets. But it would be a failing of India's government and its politics if once again a sane response to terrorism was to be offered by the people alone.

Heading: The fear within - Indian Express
Content:
Adverts appeared in the press this week for staff to work on England's bid to host the 2018 World Cup. The aftermath of a startling victory against Croatia may feel like perfect timing for this patriotic campaign. But the logic is the opposite: Wednesday's triumph in Zagreb showed why the World Cup must never come back to this country. Apart from the boost to national status and reduced travel costs for supporters, the benefit of a World Cup on home turf is that, as statistics clearly show, it is easier to progress — for reasons of familiarity with pitches, quantity of fans in the stadium, and lack of jet lag for players.

But Fabio Capello, the coach brought in from Italy, has started to argue provocatively that the idea of home advantage does not apply to England. Even before adding his 4-1 in Zagreb to Sven-Goran Eriksson's 5-1 in Munich — meaning that the team's two outstanding performances of the past 10 years have occurred in away games — Capello was suggesting that our boys are better when playing in the arenas of their boys.

He advanced this footballing heresy after observing the way in which England's players freeze at their new expensive Wembley home. In this jingoistic arena, the slightest mistake or hint of failure brings howling derision from the crowd, communicating to the team a lurid preview of next morning's headlines. This terrifying judgment comes from an unrealistic assessment of England's abilities. The memory of being the world's best team in '66 — and the folk belief that they might have been again in 1970 if someone hadn't poisoned the goalkeeper — encourages supporters and reporters to dust the trophy-room shelf every four years. If Wednesday's fixture had ended in defeat, the back pages would have been calling for Capello to be fired; instead discussion turned to the formation he should play in the World Cup final.

Excerpted from a comment by Mark Lawson in 'The Guardian'

Heading: Captain of his fate - Indian Express
Content:
I vaguely remember having read a remarkable poem by Nizzim Ezekiel in school, where he poignantly described divergent streams that flow in each soul. There has never been, nor can there ever be, a perfect being or thing. I can say with a certain pride that I have always felt compassion towards all living creatures. Although never actively involved with any animal rights group, I have always been a passive supporter of the cause. But the strength of my conviction in alleviating the suffering of animals was shaken by one seemingly mundane incident.

I have for ever been mortified by slithering creatures, including lizards. One day, while in office, I was repeatedly distracted by a lizard coming too close for comfort, destroying my concentration. As I cursed it, it fell from the wall under which I was sitting, missing me by the narrowest of margins. Aghast at the narrow escape, I leapt from my chair, and ran outside for dear life. After regaining my composure, I returned a few minutes later. 

What I saw moved me. The hapless lizard had got entangled in a piece of adhesive tape lying on the floor. It was fixed to its right hind leg, severely hampering its movement. Every time it tried to climb the wall to reach its favourite perch on the window frame, it fell down, after going up only a few inches. Its ordeal moved me, and for a moment I thought I should use a stick to remove the tape and assuage its misery. But sadly, despite my best intentions, I could not garner sufficient courage to overcome my dread, and allowed my compassion to be buried under my fear.

Feeling ashamed, I wound up for the day, locked the room and departed, leaving the suffering lizard to its fate. The incident, however, refuses to let go of my conscience. If only there was a door which could be closed, to leave out unpleasant memories.

Heading: New Nepal - Indian Express
Content:
In an unprecedented major political development that is likely to have its implications for the forthcoming Lok Sabha elections in the state, the Punjab assembly on Wednesday, amidst great pandemonium created by the protesting Congress legislators, unseated the former chief minister, Captain Amarinder Singh, and disqualified him for the remaining tenure of the 13th Vidhan Sabha. The decision came, after a nine-member House committee indicted Capt Singh and three others, including two of his former ministerial colleagues for apparent irregularities in the grant of permits for the transfer of 32 acres from the Amritsar Improvement Trust to a private developer, supposedly causing a loss of Rs 60 crore to the public exchequer. The House also accepted the committee's recommendation that a criminal case be registered against the accused and investigations entrusted to the Punjab Vigilance Bureau with the direction to submit its report on the alleged scam within two months.

Capt Singh, who has been named in 13 criminal cases of corruption since the SAD-BJP took office, called it "the darkest day in the history of democracy in Punjab". He has claimed that the decision to exempt land for private development by his government was based on policy laid down by Badal himself during his previous tenure as chief minister and that the Badal government in the last one and a half years exempted 1,260 acres from the Punjab Urban Development Authority in the same manner. The Congress for its part has stood by Singh, who was recently given the responsibility to lead the party campaign in the forthcoming elections after months of sulking in the wilderness.

The SAD, meanwhile, has drawn attention to the fact that the matter was raised first by a Congress legislator, Bir Devinder Singh, in the former Vidhan Sabha and Amarinder Singh himself had agreed to constitute a committee to probe the matter. Moreover, when the issue was revived in the present assembly in January, 2008, the Congress legislative party's leader, Rajinder Kaur Bhattal, consented to the constitution of the privilege committee.

Incidentally, Bir Devinder was not given a ticket by the Congress in the 2007 elections, and has now been divested of his post as the chief spokesman of the party after he suggested recently that corruption did indeed take place.

There is a sense of déjà vu when one comes across the chorus of "political vendetta" from Congressmen. One can very well say that it all was started by Amarinder Singh himself, who left no stone unturned to convict members of the Badal family, way back in 2002. In what has now become a familiar feature of the Punjab tradition of politics, individual politicians are constantly subjected to a no-holds-barred media war; public statements verging on personal slander emanate primarily due to personal animosity, whether it is Badal versus Singh or Singh versus Bhattal. So Singh is probably right when he says that the charges against him have been initiated to settle a personal grudge. He probably would not comment on Bhattal seeking the directive from the Centre on the move — after all, she may be nursing her own grudge against Singh for pursuing a long-standing corruption case against her during his regime. 

Having said that, some points are pertinent. First, unlike the previous Congress government, the SAD-BJP government used a hasty legislative route rather than waiting for the law to take its course. Second, can an executive order passed by an earlier government, which needed no legislative sanction and yet allegedly brought the House into disrepute, be taken up by a newly constituted House reviving the issue? The answer is probably yes, but then again, like the decision of expulsion and registration of FIR against Singh without custodial interrogation, it should have been done only in the rarest of rare cases. Otherwise it would set a dangerous precedent and would go against the doctrine of separation of powers. Third, the volatility of Punjab politics has always been attributed to the interplay of several determinants like caste, clan, region, religion and language. Now one has to factor in "family" as well.

Whether Amarinder Singh gains à la Indira Gandhi during the Janata regime, or is checkmated by his own party colleagues, or whether the Akalis have managed to subdue Amarinder Singh on the eve of the Lok Sabha elections are important questions. However, one thing is clear; the real losers are the people of the agrarian state, who have been desperately looking for practical politics at a time when the current incarnation of the technological solution that went by the name of the "green revolution" has long outlived its utility. Indeed, the day Singh was expelled, the assembly was due to discuss the flood situation in the state and predictably failed to do so. Who bothers?

The writer teaches at Punjab University, Chandigarh express@expressindia.com

Heading: Now it’s Delhi - Indian Express
Content:
Pushpa Kumar Dahal's visit to Delhi this week will not, of course, be the first time he has been in India. He has been here before, for stays both long and short, over- and underground. This time, though, he arrives not as Prachanda, the shadowy leader of an insurgency but as Prime Minister Dahal, the duly elected leader of a new and hopeful republic. His visit will not consist of his slipping in and out but will be surrounded by all the attention and ceremony that an official visit engenders. He arrives with a large staff, a packed schedule, and, apparently, a desire to rework the Indo-Nepalese relationship to bring it into the 21st century.

New Delhi has justifiably been wary of the Maoists north of the border. Their ideological comrades in India have turned large portions of Indian territory into no-go areas for the state, and parts of the Communist Party of Nepal (Maoist) would be more than happy to tilt Nepal's foreign policy towards that of China, at India's expense. Yet that must not stand in the way of engaging in the best of faith with Dahal, who has several new ideas on how to reinvigorate a bilateral relationship that has become mired in resentment. Whether the 1954 Kosi treaty affected the likelihood of the recent floods is just one example of the areas where old paradigms should be reviewed; there is no better time to do so than when Nepal is self-consciously reinventing itself.

Nothing as complex and multifaceted as the Indo-Nepali relationship can be reworked overnight, or even over a five-day visit. Even if it technically could, it would require a domestic consensus in Nepal that needs to be built. But that does not mean that in their talks with their new northern colleague, India's leaders should not have one eye on a more equitable, efficient and sustainable set of agreements. Not only is it good for foreign policy, but, as these columns have consistently argued, India's margins need all the help they can get — and a genuinely friendly, stable Nepal could be very helpful indeed.

Heading: Arjun ails, HRD trails - Indian Express
Content:
Terrorists have once again taken a warped agenda and incarnated it into senseless violence. None of the platitudes that we usually take recourse to can hide the profound sense of vertigo the continued spate of terrorist attacks is producing. A geography of ordinary commerce, M. Block Market, Connaught Place, Karol Bagh, like numerous familiar spaces in other cities, is being converted into a geography of dread. The state's ability to abide by the fundamental tenet of its contract with citizens, providing basic security, is appearing increasingly hollow. The taunts directed at its functioning make a mockery of its legitimacy. Our sense of ideology is being increasingly unsettled. What do these groups want? These groups allude to jihad. But what sort of a jihad is this, characterised by rank cowardice and bereft of even the diabolical martyrdom that usually characterises such visions?

There is the appeal to a fight for justice. But what sort of conviction is this in the justice of one's cause that it can be articulated only anonymously, and can speak only the language of bloody revenge? Then there is the narrative of victimisation: portrayals of a community at the receiving end in assorted episodes from Babari Masjid to Gujarat. But this narrative of victimisation seems to become simply a pretext. It has its own self-fulfilling logic, so that everything that happens is simply more grist for the victimhood mill. Every political party, every state organ, every media intervention is portrayed as one vast conspiracy to reduce Muslims to victimhood, as if there are no spaces left to address legitimate grievances.

There is something of a subterfuge by which these groups contrive to create an impression that they are nothing but voices of the oppressed. If this is a battle on behalf of Muslims, what sort of a battle is this? For if nothing else, these acts make life more, not less difficult for Indian Muslims. It is as if the terrorist is besotted more with the cult of violence than genuine care for Muslims whom he uses as a pretext. "Irrational terror," Camus once wrote, "transforms men into matter." This is exactly what terrorists propose to do, convert citizens, including their fellow co-religionists, into fodder for their own designs. This is not an ideology as much as a "dare" — daring the state, daring ordinary citizens, daring democracy. Its object is its own impunity.

There is also the sheer elusiveness of the group in question. It seems more of a state of mind than an organisation. Indeed, each touted success in apprehending a master mind, as apparently the Gujarat government did, seems not to affect the prospect of the next attack. There are also few convincing profiles of the perpetrators. They subvert prior expectations, and resist easy psychological profiling or sociological analysis. In that sense this is a genuinely political project, an act of culpable choice. While we can console ourselves that terrorism will remain numerically marginal, in a subtle psychological sense it will exercise a far-reaching influence.

The silver lining is that so far the backlash this dare intends to provoke has not occurred. It is clear that these groups do not appear to have an interest in justice; they have an interest in polarisation. In so far as this polarisation does not become visible, at least something of a resistance to terrorism is being offered. When fresh scenes of violence invade our television screens again, this may seem to be scant consolation. But it bears repeating that avoiding a politics of reprisal is a necessary ingredient both of combating terrorism and ensuring we are not reduced to the same moral plane. But it would be the height of complacency to assume that somewhere under our characteristic modes of coping, resilience, fatalism, escapism and even denial, there is not a seething revolt brewing. How it will be articulated will be one of the defining questions of our politics. But a lot of it will be directed against the state.

In a way the terrorists' e-mails have hit an exposed nerve: their taunting the state is something, if we did not know the source, we would be tempted to share.
