There are still numerous brave and inventive individuals trying to secure us. And the public understands that this is a difficult challenge to tackle. What citizens cannot understand is how the most visible expression of our will and the most potent instrument of our security, the state, appears in such disarray. The unseemly spectacle of parties squabbling with each other, the Centre and the states grandstanding, the national security advisor and the home minister at odds on the legal instruments necessary to combat terrorism, the complete absence of any sense of urgency in combating this menace, politicians openly feeding excessive narratives of victimisation that give terrorism aid and succour, and the inability of any national leader to assuage the people that they sincerely understand their anxieties, will add up to a deep sense of disquiet. No state has more experience of handling terrorism than India, yet there seems to have been no institutional learning, reorganisation or innovation in dealing with it.

So many obvious things to be done, creating cross-party structures to evolve a shared understanding of the problem, better coordination between the Centre and the states, legal reform, more imaginative forms of engagement with different communities to enlist their proactive help in defusing this phenomenon. The disquieting challenge is going to be this. While there may be widespread revulsion against terrorism, what will be the form of politics that will overcome the sense of victimisation that is now creeping in on all communities? How will we break the vicious circle the Indian Mujahedeen have identified: that any action taken by the state, investigation or punishment will be taken as further evidence of victimisation? Can the state overcome the accusations from all sides that it is partisan in the prosecution of its core duties? It may turn out that our biggest vulnerability is not communalism; it is a state structure now floundering for credibility, legitimacy and effectiveness.

Repeated terrorism is effacing the individuality of the victims, now converting them into a mere statistic. Or if their individuality emerges, it is in the grotesque use made of their pictures by certain television channels, as if victims' bodies were fodder for their presentations. In the long run the enduring structures of our society may withstand these assaults to snap them. But for the foreseeable future those who claim the freedom to kill seem to have great resourcefulness. Our faith, on the other hand, is hanging by a thread.

The writer is president, Centre for Policy Research, Delhi express@expressindia.com

Heading: Patil’s woes pile - Indian Express
Content: Arjun Singh's ill health and consequent absence from Shastri Bhawan for over a month now is sure not boding well for the HRD Ministry's several proposals lined up for Cabinet approval. First, the long-awaited Right to Education Bill was taken to the Cabinet in Arjun Singh's absence but the Planning Commission and Finance Ministry raised some objections on it and promptly referred it to a Group of Ministers. Now it is the proposal for subsidising higher education loans for the non-creamy layer during the moratorium period which seems to be headed for a similar fate. While it was on the Cabinet agenda last Thursday, after the Finance Ministry's questions on its viability, it has also been referred to the Committee of Secretaries.

Heading: From land of rising sun - Indian Express
Content: The Jammu and Kashmir crisis, Orissa violence and terrorist attacks apart, Union Home Minister Shivraj Patil is being cornered in the Cabinet over smaller issues as well now. It became clear to Patil when his proposal to revive Indira Gandhi's old scheme of recognising freedom fighters through sammanpatras came under opposition from Sharad Pawar and Congress minister Vyalar Ravi, with the Prime Minister a mute spectator. Ironically, it was Raghuvansh Prasad, a minister with socialist credentials since the Janata Party experiment and who had, in fact, discontinued Indira's scheme for a brief period in 1978, who came to Patil's rescue. It was only after he lauded the proposal that the Cabinet agreed to not stall Patil's proposal.

Heading: Modi Bangalor-ed, party floored - Indian Express
Content: While BJP president Rajnath Singh remains preoccupied with the rough and tumble of domestic politics, his political advisor, Sudhanshu Trivedi, has a busy overseas schedule. Trivedi, also an ace astrologer, is currently in the US after an eventful visit to Japan. In his e-mail, he explained: "Even as the world awaits a new order to take over, a new generation of young people is building themselves into a relationship... for working closely with the developed world." Quite a tall order this, but a group of luminaries who have undertaken the job besides Trivedi are AICC spokesman Manish Tewari, BJP youth wing general secretary Vani Tripathi, Delhi BJP MLA Vijay Jolly and India Centre Foundation of Indo-Japan Global Initiative Vaibhav Upadhyay. Japan being a "country of tremendous value to emerging great economies like India", Trivedi said, the group stopped over in Japan on its way to Manila to attend the Magasayay Foundation's Golden jubilee celebrations to interact with "the mighty and the famous political elite of the Japan upper brass". The young leaders had an eventful time during their two-day stay and met important people, including former prime minister Shizo Abe, several ministers and political leaders.

Heading: A mellowed star - Indian Express
Content: With the entire BJP brass descending on Bangalore, the country's IT capital last week wore a saffron look. During a felicitation function organised by party workers, NDA's PM candidate L K Advani got emotional when he said that the Parivar's journey in the state had begun way back in 1967, when the Udupi district first elected a BJP (then Bharatiya Jan Sangh) representative. While the cut-outs of Advani, party president Rajnath Singh and other leaders adorned every nook and corner of the city, it's Narendra Modi who was the party karyakarta's clear favourite. The Gujarat Chief Minister, too, devised newer ways to spring a surprise — he came to the national executive attired in a safari suit, looking like a CEO. Asked on the sartorial makeover, Modi cited Bangalore's pleasant climate. The exchanges and vibes between many senior leaders inside the executive venue, however, generated much heat.

Heading: IB, ego, superego - Indian Express
Content: BJP delegates were pleasantly surprised when Yeddyurappa chose to serve lunch to all of them personally on Day One of the BJP Executive. What has not changed one bit, however, is the CM's stout belief in astrology, vastu and numerology, a trait that he shares with his party president. So when the state unit was finalising the National Executive itinerary, the organisers' first stop was the CM's favourite astrologers to decide on the shubh muhurtam.

Heading: Rah-rah Rajiv - Indian Express
Content: Had it not been for the weak "advisory" sort of letter that the Intelligence Bureau (IB) sent to the Delhi Police a week ahead of Saturday's blasts, it would have been running for cover by now on account of unsolved cases and cold trails. And for that too, the IB has to thank Gujarat DGP P C Pandey, a batchmate of the IB Director, who brought Delhi on the radar. But what has many Delhi cops annoyed is that the IB just acted as a post-box, providing no actionable intelligence, no additional information on the likely modules present in the Capital or any assessment from where cops on the ground could organise their pre-emptive efforts. With decisions being taken by what is now an "infamous clique" of a few officers within the IB, the agency is under severe criticism from state police departments for concentrating on winning the blame game rather than seriously working out cases and passing on leads. However, just like previous occasions, there is a "letter" to act as a shield and it may carry the final word.

Heading: UPA vs NDA to Norwegians - Indian Express
Content: Union Minister Mani Shankar Aiyar, who had earlier gone public with his reservations against the Indo-US nuclear deal, revised his stance at the Cabinet meeting last Thursday. While he congratulated Prime Minister Manmohan Singh and his team for securing the NSG waiver, the irrepressible minister asserted that it was the late Rajiv Gandhi's espousal of a time-bound nuclear disarmament plan — enunciated at the UN General Assembly in 1988 —  that got the UPA Government the clearance. In the past 20 years, nothing has been done to follow up on the former prime minister's plan, rued Aiyar. For once, his remarks pleased Congressmen no end. A day after the NSG granted the waiver, Congress president Sonia Gandhi and a group of Cabinet ministers had called on the Prime Minister to congratulate him. Sonia and Singh had a closed-door meeting, emerging from which she goaded the PM to say what he had told her inside. The PM obliged, recalling how Rajiv's nuclear disarmament plan was the basis on which India had successfully argued its case at Vienna.

Heading: Handling China - Indian Express
Content: With a 13-member Norwegian Labour Party delegation visiting the AICC headquarters last Thursday, the foreign affairs cell of the Congress was seen desperately looking for people to match the strength of the visitors. Half of the eight representatives that the ruling party finally managed to gather had nothing to do with foreign affairs. Among the Congress delegates were Foreign Affairs Cell chairperson Dr Karan Singh, secretary Ravni Thakur, senior party leader Devendra Dwivedi, former minister of state for external affairs Salman Khursheed, Ex-Servicemen Cell secretary Praveen Davar, who once looked after foreign affairs in the Youth Congress, Vishwajit Singh who looks after the party's computer department, AICC Secretary (rtd) Major Ved Prakash and former AICC secretary Dalbir Singh. Even this strength was soon depleted as Karan Singh and Khursheed left the meeting midway. But that was not before Karan Singh had explained to the curious Norwegian delegation the "difference" between the UPA and NDA. "You see we (UPA) are secular and they (NDA) are not so secular," he said.

Heading: Common friends - Indian Express
Content: Tibetans may not be able to harass the Chinese in New Delhi, but they gave a headache to the Indians handling the Chinese in New Delhi early this week. When the foreign minister-level talks were to be held at the Taj Mahal Hotel on Mansingh Road, policemen barricaded access for fear of Tibetan protestors. So high was the security that even the head of the China desk in the MEA, Vijay Gokhale, had a tough time entering the hotel. The moment he had made his way to the lobby, he blasted the security and protocol personnel. The goof-up was apparent, as External Affairs Minister Pranab Mukherjee had reached the meeting venue much before Gokhale or his boss, Foreign Secretary Shiv Shanker Menon, had arrived.

Heading: Fighter frenzy - Indian Express
Content: While Chinese Foreign Minister Yang Jiechi was being questioned by the Indian press over what happened in Vienna and was upset at not being able to meet Sonia Gandhi, he was not completely "friendless" in New Delhi. At his lecture at Hyatt Regency on Indo-China relations, among those anxiously waiting to meet him were Pakistan Ambassador Shahid Malik and the RSP's Abani Roy. MEA mandarins, who were trailing the Chinese Foreign minister, were hardly amused at their presence.

Heading: Services for self - Indian Express
Content: With the $10 billion race to provide 126 fighter aircraft to India gaining pace, global manufacturers get jittery even over minor comments made about their equipment by IAF officers. At a recent international seminar, a top officer innocuously made a statement that Russian-made jets are the most expensive to maintain, pointing out that maintenance costs in the first five years add up to 25 per cent of the original cost price. The officer also rated British jets as the cheapest in terms of upkeep. This led to a frenzy among the six competitors for the contract, who immediately activated their "networks" to unravel the "hidden message" behind the statement.

Heading: Bihar’s river of opportunity - Indian Express
Content: The three armed forces may not see eye to eye on a lot of issues, like the allotment of senior officer posts or composition of the tri-services institutes, but their camaraderie came to light during the controversy over the "dilution of standards" in the pay panel. The manner in which the services acted in tandem amused South Block babus. As bureaucrats describe, the initial heat over higher scales for armed forces was borne by the Army Chief, who discussed it during a senior officers' conference and even brought it up to the President. After that, the Air Chief swung into action and shot off a letter to the Chiefs of Staff Committee — which got "leaked" to the media — protesting against an "unfair deal". The mantle was then taken up by the Navy Chief, who raised the issue with Antony and even talked to the PM on the subject. The only party silent in the whole affair was the low-profile Coast Guard. The new scales have taken care of a long-standing grouse of the Coast Guard by putting its officers at par with those of the Indian Navy.

Heading: Fare battle, or fair war? - Indian Express
Content: Like the surging waters of the Kosi, there is no stopping RJD chief Lalu Prasad Yadav in beating Bihar Chief Minister Nitish Kumar to take credit among the state's flood-ravaged masses. Last Friday, Kumar was scheduled to meet PM Manmohan Singh and demand an economic package for the flood damages. Lalu immediately utilised his clout and got a high-level meeting of the National Disaster Management Group (NDMG) held at 7, Race Course Road, as well as media coverage of all that he was getting the Centre to do for Bihar — just ahead of the Nitish-PM meeting. Realising that they had been outsmarted, Nitish's media managers tried to gain some ground by hurriedly distributing press notes to the waiting mediamen before Lalu emerged out of 7, RCR.

Heading: NHAI down the same road - Indian Express
Content: Rising airfares may have brought back a fair number of passengers to the Indian Railways, but those managing its Passenger Reservation Enquiry website seem to have not noticed. So, if you are lucky, you may actually find airline ads flashing on the website offering cheap fares, even cheaper than trains at times, even as you try to fish out the train-fare details. Realising the potential damage this could inflict to its coffers, Railway Ministry officials are now trying to choose between the two evils — losing ad revenue or losing passenger revenue.

Heading: First Hindu school opens in UK - Indian Express
Content: Minister T R Baalu's drive to get NHAI Chairman N Gokulram replaced has suffered a small jolt. The three candidates in the fray whose names are being considered are reportedly not suitable enough to head the country's highway development agency. While Baalu is putting his weight behind Tamil Nadu-cadre official Brijeshwar Singh, others are not quite convinced. UP-cadre official Prabhat Chaturvedi, who had earlier done a stint with NHAI, and Kiran Dhingra, who is in the Shipping Ministry, are also being considered. The matter will now be resolved after another high-level discussion among officials from the PMO and the Road Transport Ministry.

Heading: Army kept in dark on Pak-US war on terror: Musharraf aide - Indian Express
Content:
Britain's first state-funded Hindu school is all set to welcome its first batch of 30 pupils from Monday, promising to merge the best of British education with Hindu religious and cultural values.

Similar schools for other faiths have been functioning in Britain, but this is the first time that a Hindu school funded by the British Government has been set up.

After three years of Government approval and at a cost of 10 million pounds, the school, named Krishna Avanti Primary School, opens its doors in the London borough of Harrow, which has the highest Hindu concentration in any borough in the UK.

Naina Parmar, head of the school, described the development to PTI as "a huge step forward for Britains one million Hindus".

She said: "We aim to create an effective, calm and happy learning environment where the vision and mission statements are 'lived' by combining the wisdom of Vedic teachings and exemplary professional practice."

Beginning with its first batch of 30 pupils, it hopes to gradually increase its intake every year for pupils aged from 5 to 11. By 2014, it aims to provide places for 236 pupils, including a nursery.

Teaching will include lessons in meditation, yoga and Indian instruments such as sitar and tabla. The schools official faith advisor is ISKCON UK, which provides advice on integrating aspects of Hindu faith in the Government approved school curriculum.

A new, state-of-the-art school building with a meditation garden, an amphitheatre for outside teaching and numerous green innovations — such as a grass roof — is being constructed in Harrow, which will be ready by September 2009.

"The school will combine the best of education in Harrow with Hindu teachings. I want our school to be a haven of peace. Hinduism is a very inclusive faith which naturally promotes a calm, caring and cooperative learning environment," Parmar said.

"I am determined that we will be concerned not just with achieving excellent results, but also developing the whole child, including through integration with the wider community," Parmar said.

Councillor Anjana Patel, Harrow Council's portfolio holder for schools and children's services, said: "Harrow is truly delighted to be playing host to the UK's first Hindu school. We are one of the UK's most diverse boroughs.

Jon Benjamin, Chief Executive, Board of Deputies of British Jews, added: "We are pleased to welcome the UK's first state Hindu school to the family of voluntary-aided faith schools.

Heading: I nearly defected to Soviet side: Le Carre - Indian Express
Content:
A key aide of former President Pervez Musharraf has said the army was in the dark about the country's cooperation with the US in the war on terror and top military commanders had opposed the handing over of Pakistani terror suspects to America.

Lt Gen (retd) Shahid Aziz, who served as Chief of General Staff from October 2001 to December 2003, said the army's powerful General Headquarters did not know "most of the controversial things Musharraf did, including the handing over of Pakistani nationals to the Americans".

Aziz told The News daily that the Pakistan army "as an institution was in the complete dark about what was going on between Washington and Islamabad in the war on terror".

The General Headquarters and top army commanders had "strongly opposed the handing over of Pakistanis to the US but Musharraf did so on his own", he said.

Aziz said the Pakistan army used to apprehend targeted foreigners and locals and hand them over to the Inter-Services Intelligence agency for interrogation but "they were handed over to the Americans without the knowledge of the army".

The army, he said, had "made it clear that no Pakistani would be delivered to US authorities while the problematic Arabs would be deported to their respective countries".

Aziz said: "We did not know for a long time that the Pakistani nationals were being handed over to the Americans by the ISI."

This caused a lot of resentment in the top echelons of the army, he said.

Heading: No survivors in Russia crash - Indian Express
Content:
Spy-writer John le Carre toyed with the idea of defecting to the Soviet Union while working as a British secret agent in the Cold War, he has disclosed.

Le Carre said his work for Britain's secret service, when he spent hours examining and analysing the Soviet threat, left him wondering what it would be like to slip over to the other side.

"I wasn"t tempted ideologically," he told Britain's Sunday Times newspaper when asked whether he ever thought about defecting.

"God, no, no, no. Never for ideological reasons." "But when you spy intensively and you get closer and closer to the border... it seems such a small step to jump... and, you know, find out the rest."

Le Carre, author of more than 20 novels including A Perfect Spy and Tinker, Tailor, Soldier, Spy, worked for MI6 in the early 1960s after stints with the British Foreign Office in Germany.

His career ended prematurely when his cover was blown by another former British agent, Kim Philby, who defected to Moscow in 1963 and revealed the identities of scores of British agents, many of whom were subsequently killed.

Le Carre, whose real name is David Cornwell, said he was contacted by a Russian intermediary in the mid-1980s who offered him a meeting with Philby shortly before the defector died, but he turned it down.

"I just couldn't do it. I said no," Le Carre said.

There was always an instinct towards corruption in him. And remember, he was responsible for sending countless British agents to their deaths, to be killed — 40 or more in Albania.

The 76-year-old author's latest novel, A Most Wanted Man, is a return to his classic spy-thriller genre after a foray into other topics, such as the role of pharmaceutical companies in Africa as explored in The Constant Gardener.

A Most Wanted Man looks at the travails of a Russian-Chechen Muslim living in Germany who is believed to be a fundamentalist.

In it Le Carre, who has been outspoken in his opposition to the war in Iraq, is again forthright in his views on US foreign policy under President George W Bush.

Heading: With White House push, US arms sales jump to $32 b - Indian Express
Content:
An Aeroflot passenger jet crashed near the Ural mountains in Russia on Sunday, killing all 88 passengers and crew including 21 foreign nationals.

The Boeing 737-500 plane was on an internal flight from Moscow. It ploughed into wasteland while trying to land in the city of Perm.

Small pieces of debris covered a section of Russia's main east-west railway, forcing its closure, the Russian media reported.

Television footages showed firefighters walking around the smoldering, shattered remains of the plane. One of the only recognisable pieces of the aircraft was a white fuselage panel showing the logo of Aeroflot, Russia's national carrier.

Investigators have found two recording boxes from the crash site, which they hoped would reveal why the 16-year-old Boeing crashed. There was no suggestion of an attack or sabotage.

"There were 88 people on board, 82 passengers and six crew," said Emergencies Ministry spokeswoman Irina Andrianova.

"All of them died. There were no casualties on the ground."

Aeroflot said 21 foreign nationals were among those killed — nine from Azerbaijan, five from Ukraine and one person each from France, Switzerland, Latvia, the United States, Germany, Turkey and Italy.

Seven children died in the crash and Russian news agencies said one of the dead was General Gennady Troshev who in 2000 commanded the Russian army against rebels in the north Caucasus region of Chechnya.

Russian aviation had been trying to shake off its patchy safety record and Sunday's accident was the worst crash involving a Russian airliner since at least 170 people died in August 2006 when a TU-154 plane crashed in Ukraine on a flight from the Black Sea resort of Anapa to St Petersburg.

Contact with the airliner was lost when it was at an altitude of 1,100 meters (3,600 ft) while descending to land, said an Aeroflot spokeswoman.

Russian President Dmitry Medvedev was briefed about the crash by Emergencies Minister Sergei Shoigu, news agencies quoted the Kremlin press service as saying.

Aeroflot, a debt-ridden airline in the 1990s when it had a fleet of mainly Soviet-built planes, has transformed itself into an image conscious, profit-making company with global ambitions.

The company immediately said it would pay compensation of 2 million roubles ($77,800) to relatives of the dead and made plans to fly family members from Moscow to Perm.

The last Aeroflot plane crash occurred in March 1994 in Siberia when 70 people were killed. Investigators found that the pilot's teenage son had been allowed to enter the flight cabin and had accidentally switched off the autopilot.

Last month, at least 65 people were killed when a Boeing 737-200 crashed in Kyrgyzstan, a Central Asian country that was once part of the Soviet Union.

Heading: When in doubt, spit it out - Indian Express
Content:
The Bush administration is pushing through a broad array of foreign weapons deals as it seeks to re-arm Iraq and Afghanistan, contain North Korea and Iran, and solidify ties with onetime Russian allies.

From tanks, helicopters and fighter jets to missiles, remotely piloted aircraft, and even warships, the Department of Defence has agreed so far this fiscal year to sell or transfer more than $32 billion in weapons and other military equipment to foreign governments, compared with $12 billion in 2005.

The trend, which started in 2006, is most pronounced in West Asia, but it reaches into northern Africa, Asia, Latin America, Europe and even Canada, through dozens of deals that senior Bush administration officials say they are confident will both tighten military alliances and combat terrorism.

"This is not about being gunrunners," said Bruce S Lemkin, the Air Force deputy undersecretary who is helping to coordinate many of the biggest sales. "This is about building a more secure world."

The surging American arms sales reflect the foreign policy tides, including the wars in Iraq and Afghanistan and the broader campaign against international terrorism, that have dominated the Bush administration. Deliveries on orders now being placed will continue for several years, perhaps turning out to be one of President Bush's most lasting legacies.

The US is far from the only country pushing sophisticated weapons systems — It is facing intense competition from Russia and elsewhere in Europe, including continuing contests for multibillion-dollar deals to sell fighter jets to India and Brazil.

In that booming market, US military contractors are working closely with the Pentagon, which acts as a broker and procures arms for foreign customers through its Foreign Military Sales programme.

Less sophisticated weapons, and services to maintain these weapons systems, are often bought directly by foreign governments. That category of direct commercial sales has seen an enormous surge as well, as measured by export licences issued this fiscal year covering an estimated $96 billion.

About 60 countries get annual military aid from the US, $4.5 billion a year, to help them buy these American weapons. Israel and Egypt receive more than 80 percent of that aid. The US has also recently given Iraq and Afghanistan large amounts of weapons and other equipment and has begun to train fledgling military units at no charge. But most arms exports are paid for by the purchasers without US financing.

The growing tally of international weapon deals, which started to surge in 2006, is now provoking questions among some advocates of arms control and some members of Congress. The US has long been the top arms supplier to the world. Among the recent additions are Argentina, Azerbaijan, Brazil, Georgia, India, Iraq, Morocco and Pakistan, according to sales data provided by the Department of Defence.

Heading: John McCain draws criticism for distortions - Indian Express
Content:
It was a funny thing to be doing in a cocktail dress.

Debra Netschert, a financial analyst, was sitting next to her husband, K C Dustin, an equities salesman, and spitting into a test tube at a party last week in Chelsea to promote a DNA testing company.

As a soundtrack that included Whole Lotta Love blasted, the couple were submitting samples for tests that could reveal disturbing news, like his propensity to develop throat cancer or the chances of her having pregnancy complications.

But Netschert adopted the party mood, focusing, at first, on the less consequential details about her heredity. "I want to figure out why I have freckles," she said.

It was taking a few minutes to fill the tube with the required amount of saliva, so Netschert had a dry-mouthed moment to consider what the couple might do if her husband turned out to be carrying a gene that could doom his offspring.

"Then maybe we'll adopt instead," she said. "Really."

Some people might fear a world where widespread DNA testing would remove the mysteries of their futures or even strip them of privacy. But the testing company 23andMe, which was the host of what it billed as a "spit party" in the middle of New York Fashion Week, filled with celebrities, wants people to think of their genomes as a basis for social networking. As in: You are invited to join the group Slow Caffeine Metabolizers. Co-founded by Anne Wojcicki, the wife of a founder of Google, the company, which has token financial backing from Harvey Weinstein and Wendi Murdoch, hopes to make spitting into a test tube as stylish as ordering a ginger martini.

Typically, customers register and pay online — the price of a test was cut by nearly two-thirds to $399 last week — and are sent a testing kit. A customer spits into a tube, mails it in, and about a month later receives results via a Web account. The information on 89 genetic markers include details of customers' ancestry as well as what current research suggests are proclivities to certain diseases and other genetic traits like one's appetite for sugar and responsiveness to antidepressants.

Wojcicki's own offline networking has built support for her company. She met Ivanka Trump in St Barts, where Wojcicki and her husband, Sergey Brin, were spending the New Year holiday aboard a boat.

Comprehensive DNA tests may one day be a normal part of medical care, but right now 23andMe's efforts to make genetic testing an impulse buy disturbs many researchers.

Wojcicki and Linda Avey, the company's other founder, say their chief goal is to advance science by compiling a database of genetic information that medical researchers can tap. Customers cannot opt out of having their information anonymously shared, but they can refuse to participate in surveys focusing on specific traits.

When customers see their results on the screen, they are instructed about which findings are based on widely accepted science and which are less certain.

Wendi Murdoch said she, her two children with Rupert Murdoch, her husband and his 99-year-old mother had all been tested.

Heading: Once elected, Palin hired friends, lashed foes - Indian Express
Content:
While harsh advertisements and negative attacks are a staple of presidential campaigns, John McCain has drawn an avalanche of criticism this week from Democrats, independent groups and even some Republicans for regularly stretching the truth in attacking Barack Obama's record and positions.

Obama has also been accused of distortions, but this week McCain has found himself under fire for a pair of headline-grabbing attacks. First the McCain campaign twisted Obama's words to suggest that he had compared Sarah Palin, the Republican vice-presidential nominee, to a pig after Obama said, in questioning McCain's claim to be the change agent in the race, "You can put lipstick on a pig; it's still a pig." (McCain once used the same expression to describe Hillary Clinton's health plan.)

Then he falsely claimed that Obama supported "comprehensive sex ed" for kindergartners.

Those attacks followed weeks in which McCain repeatedly, and incorrectly, asserted that Obama would raise taxes on the middle class, even though analysts say he would cut taxes on the middle class more than McCain would, and misrepresented Obama's positions on energy and healthcare.

A McCain advertisement called "Fact Check" was itself found to be "less than honest" by FactCheck.org, a nonpartisan group. The group complained that the McCain campaign had cited its work debunking various Internet rumours about Palin and implied in the advertisement that the rumors had originated with Obama.

"The last month, for sure, I think the predominance of liberty taken with truth and the facts has been more McCain than Obama," said Don Sipple, a Republican advertising strategist.

Indeed, McCain has been increasingly called out by editorial boards, as well as independent analysts like FactCheck.org. The group, which does not judge whether one candidate is more misleading than another, has cried foul on McCain's campaign more than twice as often since the political conventions as it has on Obama's.

Heading: Chechnya war general dead - Indian Express
Content:
Sarah Palin lives by the maxim that all politics is local, not to mention personal. So when there was a vacancy at the top of the state Division of Agriculture, she appointed a high school classmate, Franci Havemeister, to the $95,000-a-year directorship. A former real estate agent, Havemeister cited her childhood love of cows as one of her qualifications for running the roughly $2 million agency.

Havemeister was one of the highschool classmates Palin hired, often at salaries far exceeding their private sector wages.

When Palin had to cut the 2007 state budget, she avoided the legion of frustrated legislators and mayors. Instead, she huddled with her budget director and husband Todd, an oil field worker who is not a state employee, and vetoed millions of dollars of legislative projects. And last May, a Wasilla blogger, Sherry Whitstine, who chronicles the Governor's career with an astringent eye, answered her phone and an assistant to the Governor was on the line, she said.

"You should be ashamed!" Ivy Frye, the assistant, told her. "Stop blogging. Stop blogging right now."

An examination of her swift rise and record as mayor of Wasilla and then Governor finds that her visceral style and penchant for attacking critics — she sometimes calls local opponents "haters" — contrasts with her carefully crafted public image.

Throughout her career, she has pursued vendettas, fired officials who crossed her and sometimes blurred the line between government and personal grievance, according to a review of public records and interviews with 60 Republican and Democratic legislators and local officials.

Still, Palin has many supporters. As mayor she paved roads and built an ice rink, and as Governor she has pushed through higher taxes on the oil companies that dominate one-third of the state's economy. She stirs deep emotions.

In Wasilla, many residents display unflagging affection, cheering "our Sarah" and hissing at her critics.

"She is bright and has unfailing political instincts," said Steve Haycox, a history professor at the University of Alaska. "She taps very directly into anxieties about the economic future."

"But," he added, "her governing style raises a lot of hard questions.

Heading: What the world is reading about... - Indian Express
Content:
A top Russian general was among the 88 passengers killed after the Boeing-737 crashed on Sunday in the Urals city of Perm.

Chechnya war veteran, Colonel-General Gennady Troshev, decorated with the title of Hero of Russia and the Order of Golden Star was among the victims of the crash.

He was on the Chechen militant hitlist. However, investigators have ruled out indications of a terrorist attack at this stage, RIA Novosti said.

Heading: The Politics of Appearance - Indian Express
Content:
British artist Damien Hirst becomes the first artist to sell brand-new work at an auction -and make millions

End of gallery?/ Times Online

Critic Waldemar Januszczak suggests you consider Hirst's latest shark piece, The Kingdom. "The hideously pointy mouth is wide open, as if it is going to eat you, and its evil little piggy eyes search you out with that terrifying one-directional stare." "Imagine that it represents the entire art world and the manner in which it pursues its business. See how predatory it is, how cunning, how fixated on its prey, how implacable and ruthless. Stand in front of this evil killing machine… wiggle your behind at it, stick your tongue out and blow raspberries at it. That, more or less, is what Damien Hirst is doing to the art world by putting 223 new works up for sale at Sotheby's."

Bad Boy Makes Good/Time, Europe

In this cover story, Richard Lacayo recounts how the richest British artist grew up in an impoverished background without ever seeing his biological father. When you ask Hirst about his early influences, it's not an artist he brings up first. It's Charles Saatchi, a former ad tycoon and collector who established a gallery in 1985 to show his own collection. "Britain was always small. Then Saatchi came and put things on a big f---ing American scale. So I just started making work like that. It didn't matter that I didn't know where to put it,'' says Hirst. The royal family of Qatar first briefly made Hirst, 43 the most expensive living artist at auction last year by paying $19.2 million for Lullaby Spring, one of his medicine-cabinet pieces.

Australian critic says Damien Hirst work is overrated/ The Courier-Mail, Australia

Robert Hughes, Australian art critic and a compulsive Hirstologist is unimpressed. Pickling sharks and foals in formaldehyde, he feels is "tacky", "absurd" and "over-rated". Hughes branded the famous artist's works - which includes a diamond encrusted human skull that sold for $108.4 million—as such in a new TV documentary. Quoting from Observer newspaper, this article says Hughes documentary attacks Hirst for "functioning like a commercial brand" and accuses the artist of making the price tag of an artwork more important than its meaning.

A man who is tired of Damien Hirst/The Independent

British media personality Janet Street-Porters rubbishes Hughes,offering a eulogy to countryman Hirst. Porter acknowledges that her views may stem from a package—six large watercolours and a pencil drawing—all signed and dedicated to her by Hirst, but says that, "Hirst, like Warhol and Bacon, is a perfect reflection of our times."

Hirst's auction does not demean the art world/Guardian

Art critic Jonathan Jones. in a review of Hirst's auction says, "Hirst is more interesting than any other artist of his generation. His flaws are part of his bizarre humanity, as an artist. Will that all vanish if this sale is a failure? Er, no. Do artists have the right to sell their own work? Er, yes. So it seems this is not the end of the art world, after all".

Heading: Lord of Swaziland - Indian Express
Content:
Sarah Palin:

The Republican vice-presidential candidate has had more written about her French twist hairstyle and skirts than any of her policies: She is all for oil drilling along the Alaskan coast but… 'did you see her hair'? She is anti-abortion but… her 'rimless glasses are damn expensive'!

Hillary Clinton

When the Democratic presidential hopeful spoke on the Senate floor about the cost of higher education, it set everyone talking—what lay beneath the rose-coloured blazer worn over a black top? "The neckline sat low on her chest and had a subtle V-shape. The cleavage registered after only a quick glance. No scrunch-faced scrutiny was necessary. There wasn't an unseemly amount of cleavage showing, but there it was. Undeniable," said a report in the Washington Post. Clinton's dress sense—or lack of it—was fiercely debated during the Democratic nomination campaign. Why even Versace gave her style tips—swap the pantsuits for skirts.

Segolene Royal

When the French Socialist leader ran for president in 2007, her shoes and style—"incredibly feminine, neat and screams of bourgeois France''—prompted admiring chatter. In 2006, she kicked off a debate on whether it was appropriate for a presidential candidate to wear high heels on a trip to the slums of Chile.

Condoleezza Rice

When the US Secretary of State visited an airfield in Germany in 2005 dressed in military-style jacket and sexy boots, the Post carried a descriptive feature on her "commanding attire". "As Rice walked towards the troops, her coat blew open… to reveal knee-high boots…" Not a word of why she was there or what she said.

Cristina Fernandez de Kirchner

The Argentinean president, who took over from her husband Nestor Kirchner, has stuck to his economic reform policies. But that doesn't make as much news as her dress sense. The Times wrote during her 2007 presidential campaign that Fernandez's "enthusiasm for mascara and designer handbags has played no small part in her seemingly effortless stroll towards victory."

Sonia Gandhi:

It has been her Italian origins rather than clothes that have attracted most comment. Maybe because she has stuck to her mother-in-law's elegant sarees.

Women politicians have always made news for their appearance. Former British PM Margaret Tatcher is said to have ironed her clothes herself. Indira Gandhi's graceful cotton sarees along with that white streak in her hair are still talked about. Eva Peron, Argentina's former first lady, was always applauded for her chic and elegant attire.

Heading: Mannequin Tigers - Indian Express
Content:
Once upon a time, a young and handsome king ruled over a land of mountainous splendor near the southern tip of Africa. He liked to marry, and as the years passed he took 13 wives, each of them a great beauty.

His countrymen wanted His Majesty to be happy, but some also thought so many spouses were an extravagance for a poor, tiny nation. After all, the king, Mswati III, often provided these wives a retinue, a palace and a new BMW. For the 40-40 Celebration—so-named to honour the king's 40th birthday and the nation's 40th year of independence—a 15,000-seat stadium was built and a fleet of top-of-the-line BMW sedans was ordered for the comfort of visiting dignitaries.

Once again, some people wondered how the kingdom, Swaziland, could afford the expense. As the big day neared, protests drew thousands more into the streets of the country's two biggest cities. "The king spends our money and is not answerable to anyone!" complained Mario Masuku, the head of an outlawed political party and a familiar figure of Swazi discontent.

The rowdiest of the demonstrators flung rocks, looted goods from sidewalk vendors and even set off a few small explosions. The angriest of them went so far as to insist that the nation had little to celebrate. Yes, Swazis have enjoyed decades of peace and are proud of their culture. But poverty has entrapped two-thirds of the people, leaving hundreds of thousands malnourished. And these days death casually sweeps away even the strong. The country has one of the worst rates of HIV infection in the world. Life expectancy has fallen from 60 years in 1997 to barely half that now. Nearly a third of all children have lost a parent. "How can the king live in luxury while his people suffer?" asked Siphiwe Hlophe, a human rights activist. "How much money does he need, anyway?"

In the government's latest budget, about $30 million was set aside for "royal emoluments." But surely the king's income exceeds that, people said. The royal family also controls a corporate business empire, investing in sugar cane, commercial property and a newspaper. Forbes.com recently listed Mswati III as the world's 15th wealthiest monarch, estimating his fortune at $200 million.

But is this not the way of the world? The king, after all, is the king. The poor, after all, are the poor. Percy Simelane, the government's spokesman, was quoted by AFP last week as saying: "Poverty has been with us for many years. We cannot then sit by the roadside and weep just because the country is faced with poverty."

Indeed, most of Swaziland's 1.1 million people love their monarch. God gave the country to the king, many of them say, and the king was given to the people by God. Mswati III's father, Sobhuza II, had been especially revered. He was more frugal than his son, transporting the royal family in buses instead of BMWs. But he, too, liked to marry. Some said he had 110 wives.

One of Swaziland's greatest traditions is the annual Reed Dance, when colourfully adorned, bare-breasted young women—all proclaiming purity as virgins—parade before the royal family and others. In recent years, the ritual has acquired additional excitement, for Mswati III sometimes selects his next queen from the throng of virgins.

Heading: Ahmedabad gave Delhi cops many pointers, few specifics - Indian Express
Content:
So much for the Asian century. The Thais are bickering with themselves, and when they're done doing that, they'll bicker with the Cambodians—again. China may be Japan's biggest trading partner, but they hate each other anyway. Malaysia and Indonesia? Two countries divided by the same language.

I've spent a lot of time in Asia over the past decade, as an expat and a traveller. From where I stand, the place is a geopolitical mess. Hogtied by nationalism and narrow self-interest, the countries of the East won't be banding together to replace the West as the seat of global power anytime soon.

Earlier this summer, Thailand and Cambodia moved onto war footing because of a dispute over a mountaintop temple—not exactly a living example of the Beijing Olympics' motto: "One World, One Dream."

Today, the continent battles a kind of split personality. On the one hand, many cultural, economic and political trends suggest that Asian nations are becoming more integrated than ever before. But on the other, a virulent nationalism is spreading in the region, one that feeds on reinterpreted—or even imaginary—history to gin up hatred and push small-minded agendas.

Elites in Asia clearly understand the benefits of integration. In 2004, China replaced the United States as Japan's biggest trading partner. With the expansion of satellite television, Asian airlines and regional hiring by Asian conglomerates, businesspeople watch the same news, cool their heels together in a slew of space-age international airports and mingle at cocktail parties and pan-Asian business summits. Fads that start in Tokyo or Seoul, such as drinking red wine or dying hair blond, sweep through the region.

Despite all that love, most of the region's multilateral institutions do little more than meet for the sake of meeting. In Cambodia and Laos, local officials and fishermen despair that dams built by China on the upper portion of the Mekong River are blocking water flow—and ravaging fishing in the southern stretch of that river that snakes through their countries. "But when we ... try to bring this up at ASEAN meetings," Sokhem Pech, a leading Cambodian Mekong expert, told me, "no one even wants to talk about it."

The problem: nationalism and an obsession with sovereignty are drowning out calls for cooperation. Across the continent, populist politicians have scrubbed school textbooks, whether to minimize Japan's atrocities in South Korea and China during World War II or to erase the memory of the Khmer Rouge in Cambodia. Travelling to Cambodia, I meet teenagers who know practically nothing about what happened in their country in the 1970s. China, too, has whitewashed the memory of the Tiananmen Square crackdown of June 4, 1989. Students at Beijing University shown the iconic 1989 photograph of the man who stopped a tank in its tracks, didn't recognise it.

The Internet has further empowered Asian nationalists, allowing them to air their vitriol unchecked. On Chinese online bulletin boards such as the 'Strong Nation Forum', which is run by the People's Daily, respondents compete for the most aggressive stance and ridicule Chinese leaders for compromising on issues such as relations with neighboring countries or Tibet or Taiwan. In Japan, the blogosphere helped spark sales of the manga comic book Hating the Korean Wave. And in Indonesia, online writers helped fuel anger at neighbouring Malaysia for the use of a supposedly Indonesian jingle in a tourism campaign. Just last week, Vietnam's foreign ministry called in China's ambassador to protest the appearance on Chinese websites of "invasion plans" that purported to detail the occupation of Vietnam by the People's Liberation Army.

Even countries that have little history of animosity toward each other can be swept into a rage by the new nationalists. In 2006, after Singaporean state investment fund Temasek Holdings purchased Thai telecommunications giant Shin Corporation, Thai bloggers and online columnists condemned the deal, arguing that a Singaporean company would have control over sensitive Thai communications infrastructure. Thousands of Thais marched to Singapore's embassy in Bangkok—a move that left urbane Singaporean diplomats a bit flat-footed.

All these problems don't seem to have resonated in the United States, where an entire industry has developed around predictions that the Asian century will replace the American one. And maybe it will—a few centuries from now.

Joshua Kurlantzick is a visiting scholar at the Carnegie Endowment for International Peace and a fellow at the Pacific Council on International Policy.

Heading: Death’s Saturday address: Gali No. 42, Beadonpura, Karol Bagh - Indian Express
Content:
A team of Delhi Police flew down twice to Ahmedabad during August to interrogate at least 12 persons arrested by the Crime Branch in connection with the Ahmedabad blasts. What they got was a jumble of names, aliases of persons still at large, who were part of a larger plan to target other cities, and vague information about a module consisting of persons from Uttar Pradesh that was waiting for the right time to probably target Delhi.

One thing became very clear at that time: Delhi may not immediately be the next target but it was considered priority. One, even with depleted resources and cadre, they could still target Delhi because they had the "capacity" to strike there. Two, the bomb-maker they knew as Tauqeer — his real name is Abdus Subhan Qureshi — was still at large and could assemble bombs as and when they wanted. Third, Delhi would provide them maximum publicity.

When Delhi Police asked what the Indian Mujahideen meant in its email after the Ahmedabad blasts that "the crusade would continue", the accused apparently told interrogators that a plan was in place to target other cities which included Delhi. "For Delhi, they knew of at least two youths recruited from Uttar Pradesh for making the arrangements. But the names they gave didn't mean anything and we knew they were using aliases, so it was difficult to identify them," an officer associated with the investigation told The Indian Express.

A team of investigators of Hyderabad Police too returned from Ahmedabad with the same information. The names and faces "did not fit" and it was difficult to piece together the entire network.

"From what they were saying it was logically clear that Delhi was No.1 target. But so many persons are still large, it is difficult to determine where they are planning to strike next. With their main bomb manufacturer still to be arrested, he could be assembling them as and when required. With their network, planting the bombs is so easy," said Ashish Bhatia, Ahmedabad Joint Commissioner of Police (Crime Branch).

"It is difficult to piece together the entire plan and identify persons because they have cut-offs at every stage which means one group doesn't know the real names of persons in other groups or what their role is. The Delhi blasts are similar to the others and it is amply clear from the material used in the Delhi bombs... the use of cycles and the modus operandi that those who prepared and planted them belong to the same large group that trained together and which is responsible for the blasts in Jaipur, Hyderabad and Ahmedabad," said Bhatia. "It is possible that the persons who we are looking for could be involved in the Delhi blasts," he said.

For Hyderabad police, Delhi is another similar case. "Cycle ball bearings, ammonium nitrate were used in the Delhi bombs, similar to the bombs at Lumbini Park and Gokul Chaat in Hyderabad. Obviously, the same group is involved. We will follow the Delhi investigations for some clues, see if they are linked to Hyderabad," an official said.

Heading: Shortage of anti-gangrene serum multiplies suffering of victims - Indian Express
Content:
If death had an address in Delhi on Saturday, it was Gali Number 42, Beadonpura, Karol Bagh. The narrow street, just across Gaffar Market, recorded the highest number of casualties for any neighbourhood: at least nine dead.

On Sunday, the residents, migrants belonging to Nadibatt Samaj, a Rajasthani tribe, gathered at the crematorium in Sant Nagar for the last rites of their dear ones while many others fought for their lives at Ram Manohar Lohia hospital.

• Four-year-old Arti can't run around as she has injuries in both her legs. She is still looking for her brother Kishan, 2, the youngest victim of the blasts.

"Both the children were with their grandfather Banwari Lal when the bomb went off . Their father Ashok ran to save them and all the three were taken to the hospital... but Kishan died," said his mother Meera. Meera said Kishan would run to the market area often to play there. "He was crying, so his grandfather took him there. But this turned out to be my son's last wish," said Meera.

• Five-year-old Simran is crying for food but there is no one at home to attend to her. Her father Ashok, grandfather Hari Chand and paternal aunt Saroj are dead and her mother, Kamleshwari, is being treated at RML hospital.

Though the hospital had put out a list of the dead, Ashok's teenaged sisters were not aware of it. "The authorities have even abstained from their duty of informing us about our relatives," said Yashoda, Ashok's younger sister.

• Vijay and Aarti are too young to comprehend the high-pitched wailing around them. "The kids could not sleep last night as they were affected by what they saw... they kept telling me about the fire, the dust and the thud," said their maternal grandfather Ram Singh.

They suffered minor injuries and their grandfather Ganga Parsed and his cousins Raju and Billoo are dead. "We ran to every hospital last night but it was only after the hospital started giving the bodies that we realised we had lost them forever," said Ram Singh.

• Ghulab Singh, 74, is still in a daze, for he had never thought he would witness such a horrendous incident. He has injuries on his head and left hand. "Most of those dead grew up before me, took up the trade (the community, which traditionally made leather bags, now makes and sells covers for TV and fridge) and had to maintain their families—usually big because people get married at an early age in our community," Singh said.

Heading: Three days ago, he came to Delhi to escape Kashmir violence - Indian Express
Content:
Injured in the Gaffar Market blast, Promila Gulati's right leg was amputated today at Gangaram Hospital. She considers herself lucky to be alive but her family knows that had the anti-gangrene serum been available, the outcome could well have been different.

As the injured were ferried to hospitals after the blasts, one startling little detail emerged: Delhi has not received a batch of anti-gangrene serum since April. And it is this lack of serum that is hurting at a time like this.

Brothers Anuj (20) and Ankur (25) Kataria are also in desperate need of anti-gangrene serum at the Jessaram Hospital. They were in Gaffar Market when the blasts took place. "These are roadside wounds, more prone to infection which is why both of them require the serum," said Dr M L Monga who operated on the brothers.

Until evening today, the Kataria family was still trying to arrange for the serum. Central government hospitals like AIIMS, Ram Manohar Lohia Hospital and Safdarjung Hospital do not have stocks of the serum. "These are kept in short supply and we usually purchase them from the local market as and when the need arises. Unfortunately, we do not have the medicine right now," said Dr D K Sharma, Medical Superintendent, AIIMS.

Heading: Hunt begins all over again: Same prime suspect, similar bombs, SIMI links - Indian Express
Content:
Mohammad Ashraf is headed back. His dream of finding a home away from the violence of Kashmir lasted just three days. Now bearing one uncle injured in the blast at Gaffar Market, Karol Bagh, and carrying the body of another, the 21-year-old is returning to Anantnag.

However, if his dream lies shattered among the debris of Gaffar Market, what stands strong is a 10-year-old faith born in these very bylanes. The Rs 25,000 required for the rickshawpuller to make his way back home have been put together by the Beadonpura Handloom Traders' Association. His uncles transported goods for handloom traders, and they have been by Ashraf's side since the blast.

It was 10 years ago that Ashraf's maternal uncles Farooq, then 27, and Narim, 35, came to Delhi to earn a living. They became rickshawpullers at Beadonpura. It was only three days ago that Ashraf joined them. Now, Narim is dead and Farooq is in the surgery ward of Ram Manohar Lohia Hospital.

The Kashmiris form a crucial backbone at Gaffar Market, and for the traders of Beadonpura, words like Hindu-Muslim violence or the clashes over Amarnath mean nothing.

"These men have been working with us for 10 years and we had absolute faith in them. We have never thought about their religion," says Praveen Gupta of Mahajan traders. "The fact that we gave these men our goods worth thousands of rupees speaks for itself. They are one of us," says Hemant Punyani of Swastik Emporium.

Gupta and Punyani were with Ashraf all morning at the Lady Hardinge Medical College mortuary, where Narim's body is kept.

"I have never thought about Hindu-Muslim divide," agrees Ashraf. "Coming from Kashmir, I know that terrorists target all humanity," he says, sitting by the bed of Farooq at RML Hospital. With stitches on his head and two deep gashes on his chin and cheek, his uncle nods in agreement.

However, the blasts did snuff out something the Kashmir violence didn't. "We came to Delhi because this place is cosmopolitan, we wanted to get away from the violence," says Ashraf. "But after this blast, everything is like Kashmir: the security, blasts, deaths. We are going back."

Heading: The South-West Monsoon effect - Indian Express
Content:
A day after serial blasts left at least 21 dead and nearly 100 injured, Delhi limped back to normalcy while police, looking for leads, were said to be questioning two persons who had been detained. Police Commissioner Y S Dadwal said they had come across "vital clues" which would help them track down perpetrators of the blasts who police suspect belong to the Indian Mujahideen-SIMI network.

Abdus Subhan Qureshi alias Tauqeer, who remains at large and is wanted by police in Gujarat for his alleged role in the Ahmedabad bombings, is emerging as one of the main suspects in the Delhi blasts too.

Sources said police and Central security agencies were looking for three SIMI sympathisers — Abu Zair, Danish and Aftab — who apparently arranged a safehouse in Delhi for Abu Bashar, arrested from Azamgarh in UP after the Ahmedabad blasts. Bashar, police sources said, stayed in Delhi from July 24 to 26.

Bashar told his interrogators that Zair, 23, was his younger brother who worked as a parking attendant near the Jama Masjid police chowki in the Walled City. Security agencies are not sure whether Zair is involved in SIMI activities but say he can help identify his brother's SIMI associates in Delhi. Investigators believe that the Delhi bombing was a desperate bid by remnants of the SIMI to assert its identity after most who made the organisation's top leadership were rounded up.

Mool Chand, the driver of the auto-rickshaw involved in the Gaffar Market blast that claimed 18 lives, has described the bomber as a 25-year-old, fair-complexioned man who had hired his vehicle from outside Imperial Hotel on Janpath to take him to Patel Nagar. Mool Chand told security agencies that the man told him to take a detour to Ajmal Khan Road, the busiest shopping district in west Delhi, because "he wanted to buy something". Since the police did not allow Mool Chand to park the auto-rickshaw on Ajmal Khan Road, the man got off near the Saraswati Marg-Gurudwara Road intersection at Gaffar Market. The man asked Mool Chand to take care of his bag and got off. Within minutes, the bomb went off.

Sources said an all-out effort was being made to nab remnants of the SIMI top brass. Those who remain at large include Subhan Qureshi alias Tauqeer of Mumbai, Ikram of Madhya Pradesh, Mohammed Ali Musa from MP, Qayamuddin and Akram aka Abu Faisal, a Unani medicine student from Mumbai. These names have been culled from the interrogation reports of Safdar Nagori, Qamaruddin Nagori, Sajid Mansuri, Abu Bashar and Shahbaz — they are all under custody and were part of the critical SIMI meeting at Castle Rock near Hubli in April 2007.

The hunt for Subhan Qureshi alias Tauqeer had taken Gujarat police to Nanded in Maharashtra but Shahbaz told Rajasthan police that Tauqeer could be in Karnataka as the organisation had a sound network there.

One pointer to the desperation in the SIMI ranks following the arrest of its top brass is the fact that the Indian Mujahideen mail was signed by the media centre. According to Shahbaz Hussain, accused in the Jaipur blasts, anyone in the SIMI media centre could sign the mail — from the contents of the mail sent this time, it appears that it was not written by any of its top leaders.

Security agencies suspect not more than five persons were used for the Delhi bombings. The desperation showed in the manner the bombs were placed — in dustbins. The one bomb that turned to be most destructive was the Ghaffar Market device which was apparently ticking as the bomber travelled from Janpath to Ajmal Khan Road.

As in Jaipur and Gujarat, the bomb-makers had used ammonium nitrate, shrapnels, detonators and ball bearings in the Delhi bombs. Gelatin sticks were also used.

"From Greater Kailash, we have taken CCTV footage of three hours before the blasts and it is being scanned," the sources said. Teams from Jaipur and Mumbai police also reached Delhi today to join the probe.

The two teenaged balloon-sellers, who found two bombs which were later defused, have been taken to the Crime Records Bureau and sketches of two suspects are being made with the help of the description the boys provided.

Aussies to review security before tour

• Cricket Australia said it will review the security situation before proceeding with the Test series in India

POTA back if NDA back: Advani

• BJP leader L K Advani said the tough anti-terror law POTA will be restored if the NDA comes to power

Separatists condemn Delhi blasts

• Both factions of the Hurriyat Conference and the JKLF condemned the blasts, calling it a matter of grave concern

Heading: Slowdown hits foreign borrowings - Indian Express
Content:
The rainfall for the country in the last two weeks of July has given hope to the farmers in India. With an estimated 20 per cent below Long Period Average (LPA) of rainfall in the first two weeks of July followed by the precipitation of 33 per cent had worsened the situation for cultivation. The absence of rainfall for 20 days in the month of July, a month for sowing the seeds, had "raised the spectre of drought in the south" according to a CMIE report on the economy. But the latest rainfall in the last week of July through the first week of August has given respite to the farmers on this doubt.

For the week ending 6th of August, 2008 normal to excess rainfall was recorded for the regions of Gujarat, Saurashtra and Kutch, Marathwada, Telengana, Karnataka and south interior Karnataka. These were the regions that bore the brunt of no rainfall for the first three weeks of July.

As a result the live storage in 81 important reservoirs was 55.8 billion cubic meters by 7th August. The gradual increase in the live storage of water may improve the pace of Kharif sowing and generation hydel power in the country.

Content:

Heading: 3G spectrum: DoT snubs finance ministry, retains reserve price - Indian Express
Content:
India's IT sector has come a long way forward and can now boast of a workforce with great process discipline. However, several striking deficiencies still need to be worked on, Nasscom president Som Mittal tells Poorna Bhattacharjee in an exclusive interview. Excerpts:

How has the industry fared in the face of the US recession and surging inflation?

Uncertainties around the globe with problems as acute as banks collapsing have undoubtedly impacted the software industry in India. We are part of a delivery chain for the world and bound to be affected. The combined rate of growth of hardware, software and services has been around 21-24 per cent this year, compared with 29 per cent last year. However, with the world aiming to cut costs, this has in fact led to an increase in outsourcing, much to our benefit. The industry is also diversified and not all sectors have been impacted at the same time. We are also turning towards clients in other countries such as the UK and in Europe. Regarding revenues, we hope to touch $60 billion in software exports and $73-75 billion in total software services and revenues, by 2010.

How would you react to allegations regarding the software industry being too far down the value chain and being "services-centric"?

Business service is hard to define. Advertising, marketing all come under its umbrella and remain crucial links in the production chain. We have come a long way in establishing India as a workforce with great process discipline and technological capabilities. The average age in this industry is 27. So I would say that we have already reversed the value chain, with people without a lot of experience entering and flourishing in the workforce. In 2004, we were responsible for a maximum 18 processes. Now, we have accomplished 43 processes in 2007.

So now that we have established ourselves in services, how far along is the development of software products in India?

A product has to be sold to many, unlike a service that involves a business-to-business agreement. There are 390 companies in the product space right now in India, a huge growth considering there were just 100 last year. We are confident that product business will go up to $9-$15 billion by 2015. Striking deficiencies remain, including problems of early funding and lack of test beds. Microsoft and Intel are now on board to provide test labs.

How is the industry rising to the challenge of penetrating software services within the country?

IT sales were not able to penetrate earlier simply because basic costs were horrible expensive. It is only now that IT cost has come down because of factors such as an enabling telecom policy and lower unit prices, that have helped in getting India connected. Also, there was an influential view within the government and the general public that computerisation would take away jobs. Such views are thankfully obsolete now. The domestic market is growing at a high rate of 25 per cent.

Besides existing hubs such as Bangalore and Hyderabad, what are your suggestions for improving IT infrastructure within India?

Yes, these seven cities are undoubtedly over-burdened, with over 90 per cent of the work happening there. AT Kearney drew up a list of cities that could be potential hubs. Some of the cities we are looking at are Mangalore, Mysore, Hooghly, Coimbatore, Madurai, Trichurapally, Durgapur and Siliguri. The education system also needs to be seriously updated. More than a billion dollars is spent by the top five companies to train people and that needs to change.

Infosys chief Narayana Murthy has been quoted as saying that the software sector need not enjoy tax breaks. What is your official position on this?

He also said that that was his personal view. The industry pays approximately 19 per cent in tax. It is only the very large companies qualifying for SEZs that are getting tax breaks. About 700-800 companies need support. There are no SEZs in Tier II and Tier III cities. Phillippines and Vietnam are competing with us. We have an edge over China which should not be taken away because of policies that are not far-sighted. We need to make it a level playing field for big and small companies.

Heading: MFs sit on Rs 12K-cr cash pile - Indian Express
Content:
The Department of Telecom has ignored Finance Ministry's suggestion to raise the reserve price of spectrum for 3G mobile services to Rs 2,500 crore, saying the auction process would discover the best price.

"DoT has carefully considered the suggestion of the Ministry of Finance to raise the reserve price from Rs 2,200 crore to Rs 2,500 crore but maintained the status quo since the ascending order auction would in any case discover the price in consonance with market conditions, DoT sources said.

The finance ministry held a meeting with the senior officials of the Telecom Commission recently and raising the reserve price was one of the major issues discussed.

According to sources, DoT has already incorporated rest of the amendments suggested by the finance ministry.

The DoT has, however, suitably incorporated the change in the annual spectrum usage charge for 3G services and it would be at the rate of one per cent on the incremental revenue due to 3G mobile services.

On this also, the DoT is planning to have a detailed discussions with all the stakeholders like telecom operators for evolving a formula for fixation of annual spectrum charge. Sources close to the development said that DoT may consider segregation of revenues generated from 2G and 3G services separately to work out the annual spectrum usage charges. Sources said this would be necessary to maintain transparency in disclosing the revenues from their different services for working out annual spectrum usage charge and licence fee.

Heading: Lehman talks resume, Barclays seen frontrunner - Indian Express
Content:
Mutual funds are sitting on a huge cash pile of over Rs 12,000 crore, awaiting right market conditions to deploy the funds. An analysis of the equity and cash allocations of equity diversified funds shows cash piles have increased steadily from 10 per cent in April to over 14 per cent at the end of August.

"Exposure in equities as an asset class to the total market value of the funds has decreased from 86 per cent in July to 85.5 per cent in August, while cash holdings have increased by 48 basis points to 14.53 per cent in August," an HDFC Securities report stated. The allocation to cash in the past four months has increased from 10.70 per cent in April to 11.97 per cent in May and from 13.80 per cent in June to 14.05 per cent in July, the report showed.

Heading: Don’t regret over fiscal deficit: FM - Indian Express
Content:
Regulators and bankers resumed a third day of talks on Sunday in a desperate attempt to reach a deal to sell Lehman Brothers and prevent the struggling investment bank from flooding jittery financial markets with toxic assets at fire sale prices.

Britain's Barclays Plc appeared to be the frontrunner to take over Lehman, excluding the bad mortgage-related assets that have crippled the 158-year-old firm, according to a person briefed on the matter.

Among those arriving at the fortress-like headquarters of the New York Federal Reserve in downtown Manhattan early Sunday were Citigroup CEO Vikram Pandit and Steve Black, who is co-CEO of JPMorgan Chase & Co's investment bank.

Saturday's talks ended without an announcement, but the outcome is likely to include hiving off Lehman's bad assets into a bad bank, in which rivals would acquire stakes, people briefed on the matter said.

If a deal can't be struck, bankruptcy is possible.

A sale would be a huge blow to Lehman chief executive Dick Fuld, who has been adamant that the bank can survive as an independent entity and is blamed by some for being too slow to realize the depth of the crisis faced by the firm. There were conflicting reports on Sunday about what kind of deal might surface or if talks could still fail.

The Wall Street Journal reported in its online edition that Barclays was emerging as a leading contender to buy Lehman but that a deal was still dependent on government support.US Treasury Secretary Henry Paulson is adamant that taxpayer funds not be used again to bail out a financial firm, a source familiar with his thinking said on Friday.

Heading: Dip in seasonally adjusted inflation brings hope - Indian Express
Content: Finance minister P Chidambaram today said there was no point in expressing regret over the Rs 1.50 lakh crore fiscal deficit of a developing country like India under the present circumstances and claimed that the deficit could be wiped out by 2009-2010. Stating that there was no need to panic for the slump in growth, he said it was 'unseen, unexpected and unheard of' in the history of the independent India to achieve a continuous growth of nine per cent for the last four years.

Heading: Apocalypse not right now - Indian Express
Content:
Inflation could well be on its way down as the government today said seasonally adjusted monthly inflation for August fell drastically to 5.5 per cent, the lowest since December 2007.

Even though annual inflation rate, as conventionally measured, fell for the third week in a row, it was quite high at 12.10 per cent for the week ended August 30. However, if seasonal factors are done away with, annual rate of inflation for August fell significantly to 5.5 per cent against the high of 12.7 per cent in July and 29.5 per cent in June, 2008, according to a statement issued by the Finance Ministry today.

"Annualised seasonally adjusted inflation in August 2008 has been the lowest since December 2007," the statement said. Seasonal factors played an important role in build-up of inflation. De-seasonalised index, therefore, was commonly used in assessing price build-up, the statement added. Sources in the finance ministry said this indicated a possible beginning of the fall in inflation. This could be significant since many analysts expect inflation to rise again to 13.5 per cent in November before easing to 9 per cent in March.

Even if annual rate of inflation, as is conventionally measured, is taken into account, inflation for primary food items, which is a main concern for the common man, has declined for the week ended August 30. According to the statement, inflation remained low for some of the important consumer items.

"The inflation for primary food articles at 4.6 per cent on August 30, 2008 was lower compared with the inflation of 7.1 per cent, a year earlier," the statement said.

In manufactured products also, inflation for cement (at 2.0 per cent in the current year compared with 12.9 per cent, a year earlier) and machinery items (at 5.5 per cent in the current year compared with 8.7 per cent, a year earlier) remained lower, according to the statement.

To a question as to why the finance ministry statement released on Thursday said inflation for 30-essential items had increased to 7.52 per cent during the week ended August 30 from 6.9 per cent a week ago, the sources said the rise was mainly caused by sugar inflation, which had declined during the same period a year ago. Sugar falls in the category of manufactured food item and not primary food item.

Heading: The hidden insights of instinct - Indian Express
Content:
Perhaps it's a reflection of the world we live in. A society full of superlatives and superstars, where fantastic visions of the future are just an entertaining, after-dinner, diversion. Whatever the cause, it's ironic that the Large Hadron Collider, possibly humanity's greatest scientific experiment, has attracted far more attention for what it is not, than for all the things that it actually is. Granted, there is a delicious thrill to contemplating the possibility that we've managed to create something planet-destroying, but the LHC unfortunately doesn't make the cut. Of course for those so inclined, since the actual particle collisions only occur in late October, it's perfectly reasonable to continue worrying. If you're going to be honest though, we completed the first tests of life-ending technology as far back as 1945, and since then have gone on to develop that to a point where wiping out everything that moves on this planet is really a solved problem.

Yet while it's not a doomsday machine, there is still much that is colourful, romantic and controversial about the LHC. First of course, is the science behind the project. The LHC will not complete our understanding of our universe — far from it — but it might go a long way towards strengthening or shaking up current theories. It has widely been reported that the 'purpose' of the collider is to detect the theorised (but unobserved) elementary particle known as the Higgs boson, thought to be the key to understanding how particles acquire mass. Yet the project is hardly just a glorified detector. Instead, think of it as an extraordinarily rich source of data, against which we could test not one but many theories that seek to explain why the universe is the way it is (and even whether it could have looked different). Regardless of the precise observations from the collisions, how scientists view the universe is likely to change — possibly in fundamental ways.

Because the LHC is such a groundbreaking creation — expanding the boundaries of phenomena which particle physicists can empirically observe — there is also a lot that rides on its outcomes. You and I may not understand the science, but it isn't hard to empathise with the human drama that underlies the experiment. Take the test for the Higgs boson for instance. Its existence, postulated in 1964 by Peter Higgs, has become an integral part of what is known in physics as the Standard Model. Yet the equally famous Stephen Hawking has often suggested the Higgs boson may not be found — going as far as to suggest he'd bet a 100 dollars it doesn't exist. That playful bet hides what is a deep and public disagreement between two great physicists — one that will very likely be settled by the LHC. And if a hundred dollars doesn't sound like much, consider that a couple-of-million-dollar Nobel prizes might fall one way or the other based on the outcome.

The Higgs-Hawking clash of ideas isn't the only scientific controversy associated with the LHC. Another good example is string theory — the immensely complicated, popular and fashionable theory of the structure of the universe. Much criticised for being effectively untestable and incredibly arcane, the LHC should finally allow empiricists to test a few of the theory's predictions. How things turn out on that front could have major implications for theoretical physics. Remember — even though many scientists might wish it weren't so — which theories get the most attention in physics departments is not just a function of the science but also politics and power. Were the LHC to lead to greater dissatisfaction with String Theory, it might have far reaching effects for the study of physics in universities across the world.

But the science and the human drama isn't the only reason the Large Hadron Collider is interesting. The project has taken over a decade to complete, cost about 10 billion dollars, involves over 8000 scientists from across the world and is the result of a collaborative effort by 85 countries.
