Those are astonishing figures and given how rarely that kind of multinational, long-term effort is successful, makes it worth studying just as an instance of how to make a global endeavour work. It might also be worth questioning, as David King, former Chief Scientific Officer for the UK once pointed out, exactly how we should allocate resources and time to problems that require concerted, long-term, global action. The sort of initiative that made the LHC possible is the kind of effort we might need to develop cleaner energy systems, fight poverty or AIDS, eradicate illiteracy, tackle climate change. It's worth asking then -- how do we make sure we can work in unison in other areas, the same way we have managed to do on this project. How do we decide how much money to put into different areas? And is there something the scientific establishment can teach us about working across borders to complete a task that is of human, and not just national, import?

The writer is doing a PhD in energy and environment policy at Stanford University

Heading: Left in the lurch - Indian Express
Content:
Conservative commentator Peggy Noonan made two mistakes when she was caught on MSNBC riffing on John McCain's choice of Sarah Palin: "The most qualified? No! I think they went for this, excuse me, bull—-t about narratives." Noonan's first mistake was not realising her mic was on. Her second had nothing to do with taste and everything to do with a misimpression of what resonates with voters. In fact, it was the man who has the most to lose from Palin's appeal who got it right. Palin, said Barack Obama, "is a great story."

Note the use of "is" rather than "has." A candidate's personal story, whether captured in snapshots (Jack Kennedy, PT boat captain; Teddy Roosevelt, Rough Rider) or in a biography spanning decades (Bill Clinton, The Man From Hope,), and whether fully accurate or not, comes to define him or her. Narratives have been used to attract voters at least since Lincoln's campaign managers cast him as the rugged rail-splitter from the country's frontier, not the prosperous railroad lawyer and sophisticated writer he was, notes historian Michael Beschloss: voters are drawn to someone they can relate to, and the way to make that happen is by offering them stories. (The human brain is wired so that we can follow a chain of events that have people doing things in chronological order more easily than we can follow abstractions.) But the power of the narrative has grown as party identification has weakened — putting more voters in play — and as the culture has changed. Television has made voters expect to, and think they can, "see into people's souls to take their measure," says Beschloss. To do that, "they need clues," and there are few clues so potent as the challenges a person has faced and how he or she has met them. "The feeling that we need to know who these people are has become so enormous that a good part of Sarah Palin's appeal is her life history, the choices she made, things that let voters form a bond with her," says Beschloss. "It was almost as important in the selection of Joe Biden, with his story of pulling himself up by the bootstraps from a tough childhood in Scranton, Pennsylvania."

The outsized power of the personal narrative today compared with even a generation ago (in 1980, Ronald Reagan ran not on personal narrative, but on hope and the promise of change) reflects something that has become almost a cliché in political analysis — namely, that emotions, more than a dispassionate and rational analysis of candidates' records and positions, determine many voters' choice on election day. The emotion can be hope or fear, pride or disgust. And don't be too quick to pat yourself on the back for thinking you cast your vote based on a logical parsing of a candidate's positions. For all but the most wonkish wonks, what matters is how the prospect of pulling out of Iraq or expanding oil drilling or any other policy makes you feel, and not a pro-and-con analysis of its pluses and minuses, which few people can figure out. (Would it be better to set up universal health insurance through a mandatory opt-in or opt-out? Exactly.)

All of this has been true for decades. What's new is that the circumstances of this election have conspired to push people away from the reason- and knowledge-based system of decision-making and more down the competing emotion-based one. The latter is more ancient and has, throughout the course of human evolution, "assured our survival and brought us to where we are," says neuroscientist Antonio Damasio of the University of Southern California, a pioneer in the study of human emotions and decision-making. In addition, brain circuitry is such that emotion can override reason much more easily than vice-versa. But none of this means that we are always slaves to our passions. Which pathway dominates depends on circumstances, and one of the most salient circumstances of this campaign is the sheer amount of information voters are bombarded with, says Damasio. You can barely pass a screen (TV or computer) or overhear a radio without being pummeled with the latest brouhaha over lipstick-wearing pigs or which candidate was cosier with lobbyists for the failed mortgage giants. When FDR was making radio addresses, "people had the time needed for reflection, to mix emotion with facts and reason," says Damasio. "But now, with 24-hour cable news and the Web, you have a climate in which you don't have time to reflect. The amount and speed of information, combined with less time to analyse every new development, pushes us toward the emotion-based decision pathway." And not even emotions such as hope. Voters are being driven "by pure like and dislike, comfort or discomfort with a personality," says Damasio. "And voters judge that by a candidate's narrative."

That is especially true when it comes to moral choices. There's nothing we're more interested in than ourselves and our own life story, and someone else's can seem like a dress rehearsal: what if I have to face that? what would I do, and how might it come out? (This is also the appeal of novels, of course.) When those questions involve ethics, the narrative can shed light on a candidate's values. And to most voters, there is no more telling indication of where leaders will take the country and what decisions they will make than their core values as revealed in their life stories. Sit back and get ready for seven more weeks of story-telling.

Heading: On Mumbai - Indian Express
Content:
Europe's left is in trouble. In the 1990s the third way - the centre-left of Tony Blair, Gerhard Schröder and Lionel Jospin — governed almost everywhere. Now, it is out of office or struggling almost everywhere. Britain's Gordon Brown has a mountain to climb in the polls. The German Social Democrats hang on as junior coalition partners. Only the government of José Luis Rodríguez Zapatero, re-elected in Spain, bucks the trend in Western Europe. Indeed, for a generation of social democrats heavily influenced by Bill Clinton's New Democrats in the United States, an era has drawn to a close.

If the many policy lessons they promoted about governance and how to prosper in an era of globalisation remain relevant, they are now failing as politics. "We know what we must do to govern, but we do not know how to be elected, having done it," one senior European ex-minister says of the fragmenting electoral base for social democracy.

Now, across Europe, the populists on the right and the left are challenging the shrinking centre. Those who need to construct broad governing coalitions struggle to match the emotional appeal to grievances, particularly among white working-class voters. In Germany, Die Linke (The Left) combines the charismatic oppositionist appeal of ex-minister Oskar Lafontaine with remnants of the former East German Communists — and polls at 15 per cent by voicing the fears and anger of the working class. Other voters stay at home, especially in Britain. The growing salience of issues of identity and immigration divide the liberal-intellectual and working-class base.

Yet Europe's left has important reasons to be confident too. First, Europe's centre-right has prospered by aping the centre-left. European conservatism often now means adapting to a broadly social democratic status quo, and seeking modest reforms within it. With the exception of Silvio Berlusconi, most party leaders of Europe's centre-right show no interest in fighting culture wars against liberalism, and most have political beliefs closer to the US Democrats than Republicans. Angela Merkel leads a grand coalition alongside Social Democratic ministers. Sweden's Fredrik Reinfeldt defeated Sweden's dominant Social Democrats with his "New Moderate" strategy, and he has been an important model for David Cameron, whose strategy has been to "decontaminate" the brand of the British Conservatives by distancing himself from its Thatcherite legacy.

Though Cameron is not typical of Europe's right — he has fallen out with Merkel by pledging to remove his Euro-sceptic party from the international alliance of the mainstream centre-right — he has gone the furthest, rhetorically, in stealing the centre-left's Social Democratic clothes. His claim that his party should be seen as the "true progressives" on the issues of social inequality, the environment and global poverty is based on the knowledge that "the state has failed" to tackle these urgent issues. What, if anything, exhorting greater social responsibility would mean in government is far from clear, but the political positioning exercise has been effective.

Second, the agenda of European politics is primarily a social democratic one. There is a broad consensus on the importance of a coordinated response to climate change, on renewing transatlantic cooperation through multilateralism, and on the need to rebuild support for global openness by ensuring that the gains are spread more evenly, paying more attention to losers as well as winners. Attacks on the state have less resonance in an economic downturn; public pressure is on governments to act.

Third, within the left, the centrists are winning the battle of ideas. The 1968ers have provided neither new ideas nor new leaders. But the next generation of moderates must prove they are not clones who will become a conservative force by simply rerunning the politics of the last decade. Their slogan "Proud, But Not Satisfied" seeks to combine governing credibility and idealism — that they knew why their parties needed to modernise but can remember, too, what they are for. If the Third Way seemed deliberately opaque, this generation is more confident in articulating the ends of reform: a "fairness" mission to extend life chances and equal opportunities.

And there is much interest in doing politics differently, adapting the lessons of the Barack Obama campaign in the United States and grass-roots movements like MoveOn.org to European conditions. British Foreign Secretary David Miliband talks of fusing social-democratic, liberal and environmental traditions to create new progressive movements. Three million voters took part in an open primary in Italy — a major innovation in centre-left politics — to elect Walter Veltroni as leader of the new Italian Democratic Party. Sweden's Mona Sahlin has returned the centre-left to a sustained poll lead, while the Reinfeldt government has shifted rightward in office and lost popularity.

When they listen to their opponents' ideas, or lack of them, the next generation of social democrats are confident they are winning the battle of ideas. They must now figure out how to win the battle of elections, too.

Heading: Stage set for management festival Chakravyuh, based on Olympics - Indian Express
Content:
Prosecutors in an Italian court Thursday asked the key middleman in the IAF's VVIP chopper deal whether the initials 'AP' in an alleged "budget sheet" for bribes to politicians referred to Ahmed Patel, the political secretary of UPA chairperson Sonia Gandhi.

The middleman, Guido Haschke, who has consistently denied bribing Indian officials or politicians, replied that he did not know who or what 'AP' stood for.

As first reported by The Indian Express, Italian prosecutors had last month produced a handwritten document they alleged was a "budget" drawn up by two middlemen — Haschke and Christian Michel — which purportedly lists initials of Indian politicians and designations of bureaucrats and IAF officers who allegedly had to be "handled" to fix the Rs 3,546 crore deal.

The alleged "budget sheet" detailed how kickbacks of 51 million euros would be divided and under the heading "POL" — Haschke has claimed this referred to Indian politicians — there is a reference to "AP" against which "3 million euro" has been listed.

Another amount of 15/16 million euros was listed against "FAM" which is said to be "Family". Haschke has claimed the note was dictated to him by British consultant Michel during one of their meetings in 2008.

On Thursday, Italian prosecutor Eugenio Fusco asked Haschke during a court hearing in Busto Arsizio near Milan whether "AP" in the note was a reference to Ahmed Patel.

In his reply, the middlemen said he did not know what AP meant when he wrote it down. Haschke also denied any bribes were paid for the contract and said that the "budget sheet" was just an imaginary note drawn up and was never acted upon.

He also said the budget sheet was merely bragging by Michel about his Indian contacts and that Haschke tried to disassociate himself from the Briton.

Strongly denying any wrongdoing in the deal, Haschke also claimed to Indian interrogators in the court that no bribes were paid for the contract and that the money he received from AgustaWestland - in excess of 24 million euros - is justified as fees for engineering consultations.

Italian prosecutors also produced another note in court Thursday - a March 2008 fax by Michel to Peter Hulett, said to be the then head of region, govt sales at AgustaWestland's India office. The fax said that among the politicians who would use the choppers once acquired by India would be UPA chairperson Sonia Gandhi and her senior advisors, including Ahmed Patel.

However, Sonia is not entitled to use government helicopters. She can use VIP aircraft only when she flies with the PM, President or ministers who are officially entitled to the aircraft. This fax by the British middleman has also been shared by the Italian side with the CBI team that is in Busto Arsizio for the hearing.

Michel has been elusive and no investigative agency has been able to reach him.

Haschke, who is facing a case in Italy for being part of a conspiracy to bribe Indian officials to ensure the AW 101 chopper was picked by the IAF, faced several questions from the Indian side and denied any irregularity.

But the Indian side did not ask Haschke to explain what AP, FAM or any of the other acronyms in the note - "DS", "JS AIR", "AFA", "DG Acquisition", CVC" etc - referred to, source said.

The middleman, who was quizzed about his association with former Air Chief S P Tyagi - named as an accused in the CBI case in the deal - denied that any money had been paid to the retired Indian officer. Haschke, sources said, admitted that he was in regular touch with three cousins of Tyagi who have also been named in the case.

In response to a question from the Indian side, Haschke said he was not aware if any money was paid to S P Tyagi.

The UPA government had come under pressure in connection with the alleged kickbacks last month after The Indian Express report on the budget sheet of the middlemen. The opposition BJP had demanded the government reveal what or who "AP" and "FAM" stand for. The party also said that it wants a detailed discussion in Parliament on "alleged payments to persons close to the ruling establishment" in connection with the controversial chopper deal and has accused the government of "running away from discussions".

The discussion did not take place as the Parliament session was abruptly called off midway.

Heading: Road caves in at Jacob Circle; 3 killed - Indian Express
Content:
Lala Lajpatrai Institute of Management, Haji Ali, will organise its annual management festival 'Chakravyuh' on September 27 and 28. According to organisers, in its fourth year, 'Chakravyuh' will host competitions in topics related to marketing, finance, human resource and fine arts. A variety of events like mock stock, business plan, ad mad show, brand housie, HR Guru, solo and group dances and fashion show will also be part of the festival. The theme for the fest this year is 'The Olympic Way' that is inspired by the India's recent success at the Beijing Olympics 2008.

Professor HJ Bhasin said, "What we are looking to do at this institute by conducting events like 'Chakravyuh' and various other seminars, is to give students of our institute as well as other institutes, a chance to put their theoretical knowledge into practical use. Also, through the cultural events we try to give the students a well deserved diversion from the rigors of their intensive academics."

Dr VB Angadi, director of LLIM said, "Our objective is to provide a common platform to students from management institutes across the city and help them develop their managerial and creative skills".

Participation is open to students of other management institutes across the city and state. According to the organisers, this year 'Chakravyuh' promises to attract participation of students from over 60 management institutes. Manan Kashyap, head, media relations, said, "The Olympic theme is very special to us because of India's spectacular performance in Beijing Olympics. We have based all our case studies and competitions on Olympics."

Heading: Elderly woman and grandson murdered - Indian Express
Content:
th such incident in a year; experts fear creaky British-era underground utilities will lead to more accidents

Five months after a cavity appeared at a road in Tardeo, another road at Jacob Circle near Mahalaxmi caved in this afternoon, claiming three lives, including that of a 15-year-old, and injuring two others. A leakage in the main sewerage lines led to the weakening of the road surface, which subsequently caved in when a truck full of bamboo passed on it.

Civic officials said this is the fifth such incident in the last one year. As the city grapples with its dilapidated British era underground utilities, road experts say incidents of caving-in will be more common in the coming months.

The incident occurred at around 1 pm when the road failed to bear the load of the truck and suddenly caved in, causing an 8-foot deep cavity on the side-strip covered with paver blocks.

"It happened all of a sudden. The truck came and the road just caved in. Before anyone could offer help, the damage was done. The incident claimed the lives of pedestrians standing nearby," said fruit vendor Suresh Singh, an eyewitness.

The victims have been identified as Jinal Ganesh Sawla, 38, Jiabunnisa Kasambhai Kamdar, 35, and an unidentified 15-year-old. One of the injured, Ashwini Gaikwad, was taken to Nair Hospital. "He is in critical condition and under medical care. He will do better," said Nair Hospital Deputy Dean M H Shah.

Sawla was at Saat Rasta preparing for the home-coming of a relative from the USA. "The Brihanmumbai Municipal Corporation (BMC) is to be blamed for this incident and it reflects their negligence while citizens pay the price. The civic body should seriously question their contractors and investigate the shoddy road repair work," said Sawla's brother-in-law Rajesh.

Senior BMC officials said, "It is wrong to say that the road caved in due to paver blocks. There are three layers of cement concrete above which the paver blocks were laid," said Additional Municipal Commissioner R A Rajeev. He claimed that the reason for the cavity was leakages in the sewer pipelines.

"These pipelines in the island city are old and were laid during British times. Leakage in the sewer pipelines resulted in the washing out of the sandy soil, weakening the ground base," he said. The road is expected to be repaired by Tuesday.

Hydraullic Engineer M M Kamble said that there are leakages in water pipelines too. "There are two 24-inch and 12-inch diameter pipelines, which pass beneath the road. However, it is not known if the cave-in is due to leakages or whether the pipelines busted after the road caved in," he said.

The civic administration has now given orders for inspection of old and dilapidated utilities underground.

Road expert Sudhir Badami said that the city can expect more such incidents in future. "Like the dilapidated buildings which cave in during the monsoon, the roads will also begin to cave in, primarily due to leakages in the old pipelines," he said. "If there is even a small leakage, the water needs to flow out and this pressure results in soil erosion, making the foundation weak and resulting in the caving in of the road."

In April, a spot right outside Harkisondas Hospital along Dr Raja Ram Mohun Roy Road caved in due to leakages of stormwater in the drain line.

Shortage of leak detection staff
The BMC Water Department is struggling with a shortage of staff in the leak detection squad which detects leakages of water pipelines beneath road surface. There are around 500 employees across 24 wards who are responsible for detecting leakages. "There is a need to revamp the whole squad and we need around 1,000 more employees," said Kamble.

"There is also a proposal to purchase state-of-the-art machinery to detect and fix leakages in the city's water pipelines. Its demo is awaited."

Heading: Not quite all green but a start, at least - Indian Express
Content:
In a gruesome double murder, a 74-year-old woman Ushaben Parikh and her 12-year-grandson Harsh were killed after a robbery in their flat in Shobhna building at Tilak road, a stones throw away from Santacruz station. According to the Santacruz police, the culprit fled with Rs 12 lakh worth of jewellery and Rs 4 lakh cash.

The murder is reported to have taken place between 1:30 pm and 2:30 pm this afternoon when Ushaben's daughter-in-law Rajul Parekh had gone to Harsh's school, Khar Education Trust, to collect the homework for the day since he was ill. She returned to find her mother-in-law's body tied up in the dining room.

When she searched for her son, she found his body in an empty water drum. She immediately informed the Santacruz police, who rushed to the spot. A sniffer dog was also present with the police team.

According to the investigators, the Parikhs own Shobna Building and the flat where the murder occurred was on the second floor, where Ushaben lived with her elder son Udayan and his family. Her younger son lives in the floor below.

"The murderer had killed both the woman and her grandson by strangulation and smothering after tying them up," Senior Police Inspector Dilip Gaikwad of Santacruz police station informed. "The culprit seemed to have known exactly where the valuables were kept and we have reason to believe that their domestic servant, Ajay, who has been absconding since the incident is behind the robbery and murders," he added.

"Ajay, a Nepali who had taken up a job of domestic help with the Parekh family five days earlier — after being referred by the watchman of the building Shankar — first tied up Ushaben's hands and legs and smothered her with a pillow when Harsh's mother Rajul had gone to Khar Education Trust School to check out on what her son had missed in school. At that time, Harsh had been playing on his computer and was probably not aware that his grandmother was being murdered. Soon after killing the old woman, Ajay went up to Harsh and tied his hands and legs, too, and then smothered him inside a water drum near the bathroom," said Gaikwad.

Police suspect that Ajay was not alone but had an accomplice. "So far, nobody from the building or the locality has reported seeing Ajay leaving the building. We have picked up his brother from Vile Parle and are trying to find out Ajay's whereabouts. Neither had the family registered Ajay with the police station nor had they acquired a photograph of his. We will try to get his picture from his brother or will have to make a sketch," Gaikwad said.

The bodies were sent to Cooper Hospital for autopsy. Crime branch sleuths are conducting a parallel enquiry in the case.

Heading: Residents opting for individual redevelopment may get 300 sq ft area - Indian Express
Content:
She may not have found great support from her own party or from the big mandals, but Mayor Dr Shubha Raul says her initiative for an eco-friendly Ganpati fest has been an encouraging start

When I first mooted the idea of an eco-friendly Ganeshutsav last year, not many supported it. In fact, this year there was a controversy over my statements appealing to Ganesh mandals to reduce the height of idols and install idols made of natural soil shadu instead of plaster of Paris. However, all that aside, I am happy to see such a strong, positive response from devotees, who chose to immerse idols in artificial lakes instead of the sea.

More than 6,000 idols have been immersed in artificial lakes, including 600 at the Mayor's bungalow. People who came for immersion to the bungalow congratulated me and asked why such a substitute was not introduced earlier, as they too felt unhappy about seeing the sea polluted. We are also recycling the remains of the PoP idols into bricks or tiles; some of the material is stopped from going into the sea.

Annually more than 1.5 lakh idols are immersed in the sea and the figure is only increasing. We cannot stop people from installing an idol, but we can definitely try to keep the environment safe.

I am not sad that my suggestions were met with opposition from mandals, some groups and political parties. In fact I would like to look at the positive side of how so many households supported the idea. It is difficult to change the mindset of people. They fear something will go wrong if they make changes to the festival and with the lord's arrangement, but it is not so.

I can understand that old mandals in the city are hesitant to reduce the height of their traditionally tall idols. But new mandals should have no such problems. I was happy when Khetwadi Ganesh mandal reduced their idol height and a mandal in Ville-Parle set up an idol made of papier mache.

I strongly advocate the cause of idols of small height. I have pasted posters at my office, urging people to install small idols. If we take steps now for our environment, only then will future generations be able to enjoy festivals .

From next year, the management of artificial lakes and eco-friendly festivals will be more organised. We have the numbers of people who used artificial lakes and will convince them to use shadu idols from next year. We are appealing to idol makers to use natural soil instead of PoP and give their numbers to devotees. An analysis will tell us which areas have more household idols, so that artificial lakes can be set up there.

Heading: Kidney racket kingpin, brother granted bail - Indian Express
Content:
Residents who go in for the individual redevelopment of their old buildings may now be able to get larger houses of 300 sq ft carpet area like those opting for cluster redevelopment. In the older system, they were eligible for just 225 sq ft houses under individual redevelopment.

Chief Minister Vilasrao Deshmukh on Monday instructed officials to submit a proposal in this regard, and also asked for a committee under the Maharashtra Housing & Area Development Authority (MHADA) vice-chairman, which would consist of technical officers from the BMC and MHADA, to identify the viable cluster that could be taken up for redevelopment. He also asked for correction of anomalies between the provisions of the 33(7) rule in the development control regulations, which deals with individual redevelopment of buildings and the draft 33 (9) rule for cluster redevelopment.

Senior officials present at the meeting said the CM had also called for uniformity between the two provisions as while 33 (7) dealt with cessed buildings built before 1940, the 33 (9) was concerned with buildings before 1969.

They added that while the 33 (9) regulation provided for 300 sq ft houses to the original tenants who opted for cluster redevelopment, the area was just 225 sq ft for those who went in for individual redevelopment.

"The CM has called for these anomalies to be done away with and to ensure that the provisions are identical," said the official. Accordingly, the change in the law would be brought before the Cabinet for its approval. The individual redevelopment would also necessitate contribution to an infrastructure fund on the lines of provisions in the cluster redevelopment issue.

"In the current scenario, the (redevelopment under) 33 (7) is very attractive as the FSI (floor space index) cap is gone," said the official, while pointing to a recent apex court order in this regard. He added that individual redevelopment would however exert pressure on the island city's already creaking infrastructure. On the other hand, the cluster redevelopment would ensure planned development with adequate focus on infrastructure facilities in the areas being rebuilt.

Deshmukh also called for amenities like schools, open spaces and medical facilities to be provided in the clusters for the benefit of citizens who opted for cluster redevelopment.

Mumbai has around 16,289 old and dilapidated buildings and around 3,356 such buildings have already been felled.

Heading: ‘To do really well, films should focus on small towns and their concerns’ - Indian Express
Content:
The Bandra magistrate court on Monday granted bail to the alleged kingpin of the kidney transplant racket, Dr Amit Kumar Raut, and his brother Dr Jeevan Kumar Raut in a case registered with the Mumbai Police. The police had failed to file a chargesheet in the case within the stipulated time of 90 days. The court released the brothers on bail of Rs 15,000 each.

The court also sent a show cause notice to the Mahim police seeking explanation as to why they failed to file the chargesheet within 90 days of the arrest. The police have been asked to file their reply on September 23. "The police were prompt in filing a case, but could not build a case against both the accused. Amit Kumar and Jeevan, who were arrested by the Mahim police on June 17 this year, have been granted bail in this particular case. However, they have another seven cases pending against them and hence will not be released in those cases," said advocate Ratnakar Singh, appearing for both the accused.

Heading: School students join BMC in cleaning up city beaches - Indian Express
Content:
Lyricist Javed Akhtar and other film luminaries discuss Bollywood's current and future prospects at Screen magazine's 57th anniversary

Weekly film magazine Screen celebrated its 57th anniversary on September 15 by organising a panel discussion — Screen Big Picture Panel Discussion— on the theme New, Improved Bollywood: Can we take on the World? at the JW Marriot in Juhu.

The panelists included film world luminaries like writer-lyricist Javed Akhtar and actors Anupam Kher and Farooque Sheikh. The young turks of Bollywood were represented by actor-director Farhan Akhtar, actor Shiney Ahuja and adman and lyricist Prasoon Joshi. While the technical side of the industry was represented by Pankaj Khandpur, Saurabh Varma represented the marketing side.

The panelists unanimously maintained that the current period is a very good time for Hindi cinema. Farhan Akhtar said, "There is space for all kinds of cinema now and a filmmaker can choose to be individualistic." Ahuja agreed and added, "There is more scope for an actor to perform. They can be more candid as even filmmakers are willing to experiment." To this, Farooque Sheikh added that even in the days when parallel cinema flourished alongside mainstream movies, an actor had fewer chances to exhibit his or her talent.

But Kher brought out the difference between the old and new Bollywood in his own way. "It took me two years to get on the pages of Screen," he said adding, "but now I see even newcomers are featured on the front pages." Javed Akhtar agreed that this is a better time for Indian cinema than the'80s, which he described as "the dark age of Indian movies". However, he warned, "To do really well, films have to keep in mind the smaller towns and their concerns. We have now begun making different films for the rich and the poor."

The panel discussion swung between clear optimism for the future of the industry and wariness about being too self-congratulatory. The main concern expressed by the panelists and the audience was that while most films are excellent with regard to technique, many are failing to connect with the audience, or worse, connecting with only urban audiences and are refusing to address small town India.

The discussion's theme was aptly addressed by Prasoon Joshi when he questioned the parameters required to judge Indian cinema. "Are we aiming for an Oscar?" he asked. "If we judge ourselves by our own standards and milieu, we're doing a very good job and Indian cinema can only move forward," he concluded.

Heading: Festive spirits of people remain high, traffic normal - Indian Express
Content:
A day after the city celebrated Anant chaturdashi, the last day of the ten-day long Ganapati festival, various groups from city schools and colleges geared up to clean the beaches. Seven schools that form a part of the Children's Movement for Civic Awareness (CMCA) conducted a beach clean up drive in the early hours of Monday.

Around 700 students from Villa Theresa School, Little flower of Jesus, Green Lawn School, Kamla High School, St. Elias High School, Janaki Devi High School, and SS Sahani High School visited the Girguam Chowpatty, Juhu beach and Versova beach at 8.30 am to kick start the drive. CMCA joined hands with the Brihanmumbai Municipal Corporation (BMC) to clean up the beaches.

"We have been conducting this drive for the past four years; it is our way of sensitizing children towards environment concerns. Unless they see for themselves the large scale of environmental degradation, they will never learn the importance of having a clean environment," said Mumbai coordinator of CMCA, Vinodini Lulla.

According to Lulla, the students after working for two hours collected approximately 40 kilos of garbage from the three immersion points. "BMC workers manned the area and helped the kids in collecting the garbage from far flung areas. We always blame the civic body for not doing their work. But now after cleaning the beach for ourselves, we have understood the gravity of the situation," said Lulla.

A similar drive was conducted near Tulip Star hotel in Juhu by the students of Rotract club of NM College. "We visited the beach at 7.30 am and re-immersed the remains into the sea. The idea was to clean the beach, as after every visarjan the remains of the previous day become an eye-sore to the people," said Rakhee Jain, director of the rotract club, NM College.

Immersion figures
* Total immersion on Sunday: 41,479
* Total immersion this year: 1.76 lakhs
* Nirmalya collected: 2300 tonnes.

After more than 41,000 Ganpati idols were immersed in the city beaches, the Brihanmumbai Municipal Corporation set-on the task to empty the nirmalaya kalash and convert the flower-offerings in fertilizer.

A total of 2,300 tonnes of floral offerings was collected from 150 urns which were specially set-up for the disposal at 84 immersion points in the city. The floral offerings will be now made into fertilizer and utilised in civic gardens and even distributed to interested citizens at ward level.

Heading: Ham operators chip in to ensure a smooth visrajan at Chowpatty - Indian Express
Content:
Bomb blasts in the capital just before the conclusion of the ten-day Ganesh festival in Mumbai did not dampen the spirits of the people and the movement of traffic during visarjan was normal on Sunday. Deputy Commissioner of Police (Traffic), Harish Baijal, said that due to detailed and precise planning of the department they were able to maintain a smooth flow of traffic.

"There is no relation between the bomb blasts and traffic and moreover we are not in charge of the security arrangements. The traffic department's priority is to ensure a smooth movement of traffic and enable citizens to reach any part of the city by ensuring that no area is inaccessible just because its choc-a-bloc with mandals. That was accomplished," said Baijal who was overseeing his fourth Ganesh visarjan in Mumbai.

While Sunday morning saw relatively less crowd at the Girgaum Chowpati due to rains, the traffic police had expected the crowds to increase in the afternoon.

Baijal, who promptly arrived at the Girgaum Chowpati on Sunday to survey the visarjan arrangements amidst heavy rains, admitted that he was skeptic about the rains. "Rainy mornings are usually a dampener for the Ganpati devotees as they prefer to wait till the rains subside and then they proceed with the visarjan process. However, by afternoon all mandals and individuals rushed for immersion which will inevitably lead to traffic congestion," said Baijal.

After surveying the beach, overseeing the removal of a tempo stuck in the mud, Baijal consulted his officials and strictly prohibited television crews to enter the beach. Horse-drawn carriages meant for light vehicles were also diverted.

While there was minimal crowd on the roads leading to Shivaji Park and Juhu Chowpati areas at around 3 pm, within a couple of hours the arterial roads leading to the immersion points were packed with several small trucks and tempos. However, police personnel stationed at all crucial points ensured that the flow of traffic was normal.

"During the peak hours between 6 to 11 pm all the main arterial roads like Gorai Road, Linking Road, VM Road and Shivaji Park were solely marked for the mandals to pass," said Baijal.

Towards 6 pm the Babulnath Road leading to Girgaum Chowpati was infested with devotees which caused the traffic to come to a standstill but did not witness any traffic jams. Lalbaugcha Raja was delayed by a couple of hours as Baijal explained that traffic moved at a 'snail's pace' at the Don Taki area. "The area's Muslims garland the Lalbaugcha Raja and the whole process delays the movement. It is not possible for us to rush as there is a fear of confrontation," he said.

"Traffic management is all about an alert eye for detail and keen observation. "This visarjan traffic personnel ensured that no vehicles were improperly parked, vehicles blocking the road were immediately cleared and the pedestrian-mandal movement was co-ordinated," he said.

Through the day, not once did Baijal's driver honk. The DCP and his driver both wore seatbelts. And, though Baijal was in a mad rush through the day, his driver had clear instructions that no traffic signal was to be broken.

Measures on visarjan day
* No drunken driving cases or any major traffic offence was registered on Sunday. Around 1,600 traffic personnel, 300 of them of the officer cadre were at work on Sunday till the last idol was immersed.
* Around 45-50 traffic patrol vans, 300 walkies, 81 CCTVs and 31 Variable Messaging Systems displaying awareness messages were all a part of the planning for visarjan.

Heading: Take a Metro ride and shop for grocery too - Indian Express
Content:
This year during Ganesh visarjan, the Mumbai Police and Brihanmumbai Municipal Corporation (BMC) officials, were ably aided by members of the Mumbai Amateur Radio Operators (MARS) who were on duty at Girgaum Chowpatty on Sunday evening.

Forty-five members of the group, who peppered around the busiest immersion point in Mumbai were doing their bit to ensure that anyone with a 'Lost and Found complaint' could reach the police control room.

The Ham operators decided to use the 145.300 frequency for Lost and Found cases. Children and elders could approach MARS members for help, in case they needed to reach the main control room.

Explaining the working of the system Manohar Bhatija, one of the members present at the beach said, "The report will be sent to the main tower, after which the police will deploy some people to check out the problem." He added, "We are also tied to an ambulance in case there is an emergency." For the past eight years, MARS has been contributing a fair deal for Mumbai's busiest immersion spot. "If a member finds a case, then it is passed on to the police control, after which we help search for the person in question, since often the police don't have time to do it," said Ulhas Paralkar, another member of MARS, adding that there were over 124 cases on the immersion day last year where MARS helped out.

This time, the system included announcements in different languages, including Hindi, Marathi, English and Gujarati. "Ham communications work when other aspects like mobiles and other forms of communications fail," added Paralkar. Each of the operator is identified by a number, which is unique to them."

This is the only hobby that requires a government permit," said Paralkar.

Heading: Report says maternal mortality rate on rise, but civic body claims it’s a system error - Indian Express
Content:
MMRDA plans to lease station space for commercial use to make second Metro route financially viable

Once Metro rail starts in the city, Mumbaiites could get off a metro train and pick up some groceries on their way home. THE Mumbai Metropolitan Region Development Authority (MMRDA), the nodal agency for the Mumbai Metro project, has decided to exploit the station space on the Charkop-Bandra-Mankhurd corridor for commercial use. The authority is contemplating of using this model on the other proposed metro rail corridors as well.

According to Ratnakar Gaikwad, Metropolitan Commissioner, the MMRDA has decided to commercially exploit space over 27 stations on that route. "We are proposing to utilise the first floor of the station. Around 4,000 sq ft would be set apart at each station, which is substantial space to house offices, shops, etc, when we invite financial bids for the corridor," Gaikwad told Newsline. Apart from 4,000 sq ft, the MMRDA had been allowing around 1,000 sq ft which would be use to house coffee shops, small eateries, etc.

The MMRDA is also thinking of utilising this commercial usage of station area as a mean to make the metro corridors more "financially viable". With the commercial exploitation, the MMRDA expects to bring down the viability gap funding (VGF) by nearly half the amount. "We estimate the VGF to come down from Rs 2,400 crore to around Rs 1,400 crore with the commercial usage," Gaikwad said.

The second metro corridor, which is in the tendering stages, is expected to reduce the travelling time, and the running time from Charkop to Mankhurd is likely to be around 45 minutes.

Meanwhile, the MMRDA wants utilise station spaces in the other proposed metro corridors also in a similiar fashion. "We want to commercially exploit as much space possible so as to make the metro corridor self-financed," Gaikwad said. He added such exploitation of space has been done in countries across the world and is found to be highly successful. Delhi Metro Rail Corporation (DMRC), which is the principal consultant for the Mumbai metro rail project, too has used space by leasing it. "We'll explore the possibility to go even further up on other metro routes. This would not only facilitate commuters but will make corridor financially viable," said Gaikwad.

When asked how the nodal agency plans to utilise space for the third metro corridor —Bandra-Mahim, which is an underground route, Gaikwad responded by saying, "Across the globe underground shopping has not been very successful, but we are still exploring the options."

Heading: UDRI meeting disrupted by protesters over language issue - Indian Express
Content:
Civic officials on Monday informed that data published in the recently released Enviroment Status Report by the Brihanmumbai Municipal Corporation (BMC) on moratlity rates in the city may be incorrect as there could be a serious lapse in the recording system after the civic body's adoption of the SAP Enterprise Resource Planning System.

According to the report, maternal mortality rate shot up sharply from 82 deaths per 1000 live births in 2006 to 244 deaths per 1000 live births in 2008. However, doctors of the BMC's Public Health department it was the Enterprise Resource Planning (ERP) system error and maternal deaths in fact reduced drastically. The data released from the BMC's Women and Child Welfare department showed a steep decline in last two years - 61 deaths per 1000 live births in 2007 and 49 deaths per 1000 live births this year, they said.

According to the Environment Status Report, maternal mortality rate in 2006 was recorded 82 deaths per 1000 live births and in 2007 it shot up to 114 deaths per 1000 live births.

"It's an SAP error. Maternal mortality has reduced drastically," said Dr Jairaj Thanekar, executive health officer, Public Health department. When contacted, SAP Project Manager Suresh Mhatre said, "There could be two reasons. Officials of the Public Health department are forced to fill up questions that were not filled up earlier or else it is data entry error. We checked the system and it is absolutely fine."

"We have informed the Public Health department's IT nodal officer about the issue. He will in turn talk to officials at all the wards and they will manually cross check all 244 cases with our records. It will be easy to check all the records as we have data of all hospitals where these cases were attended. Time, date, doctor in-charge and other details are also available with us," said Mhatre.

"Maternal mortality rate defiantly reduced after interventions initiated in December 2007. The BMC started Janani Suraksha Yojana, a scheme that helps encourage institutional delivery and in turn reduce maternal mortality. Till date, as many as 2469 women are benefited under the scheme. They received Rs 600 each with two days rest at the hospitals," said Dr Asha Advani, special officer, Women and Child Welfare department.

A Public Health department official told Newsline that this is not the first time, the officers of the SAP have reported maternal deaths wrorngly. "Earlier, deaths of a 92-year-old woman and a 1-year-old were reported as maternal deaths," he said.

Heading: College students in city to be educated about WiFi threat - Indian Express
Content:
A public meeting on the implications of the recent DCR 33/7 Supreme Court judgment on Mumbai was abruptly cut short after some political workers disrupted the proceedings over the issue of language.

The meeting organised by the Urban Design Research Institute (UDRI) on Monday was chaired by eminent panelists such as former Supreme Court judge Justice BN Srikrishna, former High Court Judge Hosbet Suresh, lawyer Gautam Patel, architects Charles Correa and Shirish Patel, environmentalist Debi Goenka, former MHADA Vice President Chandrashekar Prabhu, former Municipal Commissioner DM Sukhtankar and former MMRDA Chief Planner VK Phatak.

While the panelists were being introduced by heritage activist Cyrus Guzder, a few people in the audience stood up to protest the proceedings that was being carried out in English. Before two of the speakers finished their talks on the SC judgment, the scene turned ugly as the ' trouble-makers' started screaming. While some of the protesters demanded that the proceedings should be carried out in Marathi, others wanted the proceedings in Hindi. The meeting had to adjourned after Justice Srikrishna's attempt to placate the protesters.

Parvati Gorivale, Shiv Sena corporator from Parel who had attended the meet along with party workers, was one of the many protesters.

When Newsline contacted her, she said, "The meeting was meant to be for the 'aam' public, hence it should have been in Marathi." When asked about her views on the subject of redevelopment of old cessed buildings under DCR 33/7, she said, "Marathi-speaking people should also get homes in these redeveloped buildings."

Interestingly, Gorivale's colleague Vaishali Chaudhary immediately came to her rescue and said, "For more clarifications on today's protest, you can speak to builder Rajesh Jain." When Newsline contacted Rajesh Jain, he said, "I represent the Property Redevelopers Association. I was present at the meet as I was interested in the discussion. They should not have disrupted the meet over the issue of language."

When asked why Chaudhary, who was one of the prime protesters, gave his reference, Jain said, "I don't know why they had asked you to contact me. She is an employee of mine."

Heading: Neeraj Grover case: Defence argues murder was not pre-planned - Indian Express
Content:
In the wake of lurking threats surrounding the misuse of insecure WiFi networks, the Maharashtra Police along with the Federation of Indian Chambers of Commerce and Industry (FICCI) and Indu Shahani, sheriff of Mumbai have launched a movement on "Creating a secured WiFi network" for college students in Mumbai. A training session to be held on Tuesday will acquaint students of HR College on ways to secure WiFi. They in turn will go to over 40 other colleges in South Mumbai to train other studentsas well as some corporate houses.

"At the first level, we will teach students to detect WiFi networks that are not secure. Once detected, we will teach them how to secure them", said Vijay Mukhi who chairs the IT committee at FICCI "After the Ken Haywood and Khalsa College incidents, there is increased awareness about the threat of insecure WiFi networks, but people have still not realized the importance of securing it", he added.

Professor Heena Thakkar of HR College said, "I believe students can easily understand and grasp new technologies. They are also most susceptible to such threats because their internet usage is massive. We want students to realise that WiFi can be secured easily given the right kind of software and guidance."

The 'awareness drive' has already been conducted in a few colleges in the city.  Mukhi said that students were concerned and eager to learn more about securing WiFi.

Professor Rajesh Bansode, of the department of Information Technology (IT), Thakur College of Engineering and Technology, Kandivali said, "From third year itself IT students start learning about wireless technologies and using routers. We have organised guest lectures with Ankit Fadia, (a computer security and digital intelligence consultant) in the past to acquaint students with computer security aspects."

Professor SB Patil, dean, Computer Science department at the University of Mumbai added, "It is essential for students to know about wireless routers etc. In our curriculum we are yet to introduce WiFi." He added that WiFi should be restricted to 50 meters in educational institutes as it is easier to keep watch.

Heading: Kingfisher Red flight fails to take off at Kolhapur airport due to technical snag - Indian Express
Content:
Responding to the prosecution's argument in the Neeraj Grover murder case, defence lawyer Harshad Ponda on Monday challenged the conspiracy theory claimed by the prosecution. Ponda told the court that the testimonies given by accused Maria Susairaj's neighbours and Emile Jerome's friends in Cochin proved that Grover's death happened in a fit of rage and was not preplanned.

The prosecution had earlier in its argument told the court that Susairaj and Jerome had planned the murder and then went ahead executing it.

But Ponda, giving instances of the airline ticket and Jerome's correspondence with his colleague Vasant Kumar back in Cochin, argued before the court that "had they conspired to kill Neeraj, there were slim chances of them discussing it with any one and the killing should have been executed secretly".

According to the phone records, Jerome had called Susairaj at 11 pm on May 6, the day of the murder. Ponda told the court had Jerome wanted to kill Grover, he would have planned it earlier would have booked the tickets in advance and not late night at 11.30 pm.

Defence also argued that Susairaj was "very close" to Neeraj and had introduced him to her neighbours. She never intended to kill him, but it was their closeness that Jerome did not approve off.

Susairaj had filed an application seeking bail before the sessions court and contended that as the chargesheet in the case was filed last week, her custody was therefore not required anymore. Ponda on earlier dates had argued that Susairaj could, at the most, be charged with destruction of evidence in the case, but not murder.

Additional sessions judge ST Mahajan has now adjourned the case till September 16.

Heading: Lawyer moves HC against K L Prasad’s statements - Indian Express
Content:
A Mumbai-bound Kingfisher Red flight failed to take off from the Kohlapur Airport after developing technical complications as soon as the pilot switched on the flight's first engine. Maharashtra Non-Conventional Energy Minister, Vinay Kore was among the ten passengers who were on board.

"The flight, Mumbai-Kolhapur-Mumbai, Kingfisher Red flight number IT 4114, took off from Mumbai's Chhatrapati Shivaji International Airport at 12:20 this afternoon and reached Kolhapur by 1:15. The incident took place at 1:25 when the pilot switched the plane's first engine. Incidentally, the pilot had switched the plane's second engine first," said a spokesperson from Kingfisher Red.

B.T.Paymal, personal assistant to the minister said that the passengers were deplaned after there was trouble with one of the engines and the minister left for Mumbai via road as the flight was cancelled for inspection

"Guests were immediately deplaned and asked whether they wanted to leave by ground transport or wait for the next day's flight," added the spokesperson for the airlines.

Heading: Notice to Suniel Shetty on Salt Water Grill PIL - Indian Express
Content:
A lawyer has moved the Bombay High court against remarks made by Joint Commissioner of Police (Law and Order) K L Prasad, while reacting to the threats by Maharashtra Navnirman (MNS) party chief Raj Thackeray of banning all films and promotion campaigns of the Bachchan family.

According to the petition filed by lawyer Vijay Pandurang Patil, which is not yet admitted by the High Court, Prasad made lawless statements on television, which is a serious misconduct by a senior police officer in force and in independent India as the subject is of public importance.

The petitioner also states that Prasad's statement covered by the media has lowered the dignity of the country.

Accordingly, the petition prays for disciplinary action against Prasad for his misconduct and also suspension of Prasad from service or his transfer till the petition is disposed off by the court.

The petition is to come up for hearing in due course.

Heading: 66 infant deaths in city due to malnutrition : Report - Indian Express
Content:
The Bombay High Court on Monday issued notices to Bollywood actor Suniel Shetty and others, while hearing a public interest litigation opposing the sea-side restaurant 'Salt Water Grill' owned by Shetty, alleging that the restaurant was built in violation of Costal Regulation Zone (CRZ) norms.

The notices were issued to Shetty, who is a partner in the H2O, and directors of sports complex Rajiv Somani and Manoj Agarwal, asking them to file their reply to the public interest litigation (PIL) challenging the construction of the restaurant in the sensitive Coastal Regulation Zone (CRZ). They have to file their reply by October 1.

Amit Maru, a city-based social activist, has filed the PIL alleging that the restaurant has violated several regulations by erecting a permanent structure on the beach. YP Singh, Maru's counsel, said that the government had issued a circular in May 2000 allowing establishment of sports complex at Chowpatty. However, the Government Resolution (GR) expressly mentioned that there would be no construction there, as the land falls in CRZ I area, said Singh.

Earlier Maharashtra Tourism Development Corporation (MTDC) was to develop the sports complex there. However, the MTDC gave permission to operate water sports facilities to M/s. Dhrushti Adventure Sports Pvt. Ltd. However, in the guise of water sports they constructed a huge restaurant by the name of Salt Water Grill on the said land, alleges the PIL. The PIL seeks demolition of the restaurant as no such construction is allowed in CRZ area. Despite making several representations to the BMC, no action was taken against the restaurant, Maru then filed the PIL.

Heading: Draw We Have Coming to Dover - Indian Express
Content:
Last year, after malnourishment surfaced in adivasi padas in Aarey Colony, ICDS along with tribal department started anganwadis and mini anganwadis

It took a week and one death of a six-month-old for the Integrated Child Development Service (ICDS) of Woman and Child Development Department to wake up to the fact that there could be malnourished children in the tribal belt of Kandivali's national park area. ICDS will soon survey 13 to 14 padas in that area to start mini anganwadis.

Suffering from fever she had boils in side her mouth and all over her neck and succumbed to death on September 13. Following the death, Deputy Commissioner visited the site a week later after specific instructions from the Woman and Child Development Secretary Dr Vijay Satbir Singh and ICDS Commissioner Rakesh Kumar.

After the visit on Monday, Manjusha Molvane Deputy Commissioner, ICDS, said, "We are starting a survey of the 13-14 padas in this area to get an account of the number of under-six year children and lactating mothers. Based on the survey, we can start 2-3 mini-anganwadis. Right now, there is a balwadi in the area, but we will start setting up anganwadis. There are no ICDS centres near their houses as it is in a tribal area, currently only one balwadi exists." According to the monthly progress report posted on the website of ICDS, this year alone (from January to June) deaths due to malnutrition in Mumbai in the age group of zero to one is 66 and one to six is 29.

When asked about the cause of death of six-month-old Aarti Kaule in the adivasi belt of Akrachibhatti near Kandivili on September 13, Deputy Commissioner said, "The mother is 25-year-old and is undernourished and has had six deliveries. Four children, including Aarti are already dead. This child was not enrolled with us, and no government services reach them. Therefore there has been no monitoring. I do not agree with this because there are no deaths due to malnourishment. Malnourishment leads to other complications like infections and other diseases," she said, adding, "The problem is the same as last year, neither the BMC and ICDS have any programmes here.It is our fault that after last year incidents in Aarey Colony, we did not provide the same facilities here. But we will start now."

For the other two children suffering from malnutrition, ICDS is now checking how the medical team can be sent to them. "Maybe through NGOs who work with malnourished children," she said.

Last year, after malnourishment surfaced in adivasi padas in Aarey Colony, ICDS along with tribal department started anganwadis and mini anganwadis.

Heading: Cube Root - Indian Express
Content: Last year, when Daljit Nagra brought out his slim volume Look We Have Coming to Dover!, rapping in verse about his mother with "mustard-oiled trail of hair, brocaded pink sandals and the smell of curry" and Everyimmigrant in the UK, he was feted as the brave new voice. Now the publishing house Westland has floated a contest called "Djinn and Tonic" in collaboration with the British Council, inviting artists, designers and illustrators to send in their creations based on the debut collection of the British poet of Indian origin. At the end, a limited-edition 2009 calendar with Nagra's poetry and a dozen winning images would be published. "Nagra's poetry is very visual. It fitted the format of the contest perfectly. Since verse does not sell like fiction does, this will give a boost to poetry," says Priyanka Chowdhury, head (publicity), Westland. The contest is open till September 30.

Heading: Top Gear - Indian Express
Content:
Veteran Pakistani artist Jamil Naqsh's penchant for Eastern calligraphy has been replaced with Cubist contours. At his first solo exhibition in India, he pays tribute to Pablo Picasso through quintessential nudes and horses. The London-based artist spoke to VANDANA KALRA about the Spanish master, association with India and art in Pakistan. Excerpts:

In the 1990s, you paid homage to Italian sculptor Marino Marini and in this solo the focus is on Pablo Picasso. How have these artists influenced your work?
Marini is one of my favourite artists, therefore working on a show that paid homage to him was enjoyable. His Horse and Rider series prompted me to juxtapose the female form with horse. For Picasso, I did a lot research on his life and works. Surface and lines were not important for him; he was interested in colour and form. I particularly admire his La Toilette, Les Demoiselles d'Avignon, Guernica, Peace and War. My exhibition comprises drawings over the past 10 years while the paintings are from 2006-7.

Several of your contemporaries have had solo exhibitions in India. Why did your show take this long?
My work has been featured at group shows in Delhi and Mumbai since 2005, but I waited for the solo. I won't be present at the exhibition as I don't like travelling, but I might come to India for a retrospective with Nitanjali Art Gallery in September next year.

You were born at Kairana, Uttar Pradesh, and part of your childhood was spent in India. Do you have any early memories of India?
India is my birthplace. My father sent us to Lahore during Partition but he stayed back. I was eight then. Then I visited India in 1952 and travelled through Chittagong, Calcutta and Colombo. I was only 13 so I have little memory of those journeys, but I do remember the tall temples of Madurai.

What prompted you to shift base to London in 1993?
I wasn't keeping too well in the early 1990s and London suited me. Finally, I shifted here with Najmi Sura, my companion and muse whom I have known since childhood.

Nudes made an appearance in your art in 1962. There have been cases in India where artists have being accused of obscenity. What were the reactions you received? Does the tense political situation in Pakistan affect artists in the country?
We painters really don't care about what is happening politically. I have always received admiration from my art lovers. Pakistani art is now getting its due internationally, and several Indian and international galleries and auction houses are showcasing art from Pakistan. I'm the highest paid artist in Pakistan, but compared with Indian masters there is a long way to go.

The exhibition at Alliance Francaise is on till September 20

Heading: Home Run - Indian Express
Content:
Will the India Couture Week, opening today, be a sartorial coup?

If you go by couturiers like Pallavi Jaikishen, Tarun Tahiliani, JJ Valaya, Anamika Khanna and Rohit Bal waxing eloquent about how India invented luxury before the French invented parfum, then the Couture Week, starting today, is an indigenous extravaganza. And they have a point. With a healthy economy and a gargantuan marriage market, couture is probably the most sought-after in India.

For one week the luxurious Grand Hyatt, Mumbai, will be the hub of all that glitters on Bollywood beauties, svelte models, Botoxed socialites and brides-to-be. The HDIL India Couture Week will not just showcase wedding fashion, but as designers claim, it will move beyond the lehnga-choli culture into chic, ethnic-rich wear, married with stylish hairdos, make-up trends and fine accessories as well. Hmm.

Anamika Khanna says, "There will be varied styles. I will begin with international silhouettes and move on to Indian wear." Ashish Soni is quick to add, "Lehngas and saris are not my style," but then sherwanis definitely are. While his women's wear is going to be in the form of slim pantsuits or slim skirt-suits, his men's wear primarily comprises a modern interpretation of the classical sherwani by incorporating avant-garde embroidery techniques.

Unlike the regular fashion weeks, the India Couture Week is not going to be a business-driven event but more a celebration of the cultural heritage and other ostentations. "The emphasis will be more on individual clients rather than on large buyers. And everybody has a clientele. So neither the crowd nor the designs will be repeated," says Jaikishan. Suneet Varma, who will showcase just two lehngas and 18 gowns in his couture line, says there is nothing wrong in showing an all-Indian line. "Couture means made-to-order. It doesn't matter if it is Indian or western," he says.

Of course, there'll be glamour. The buzz is Karisma Kapoor and Sonam Kapoor will be sashaying down the ramp for Manav Gangwani and Anamika Khanna respectively. Ritu Kumar will have Miss Indias walking her runway at the opening show tonight, and so will Valaya.

Of course, there'll be more. Luxury is infectious.

Heading: The agony of waiting - Indian Express
Content:
Three Delhi designers make their way through one of the biggest fairs in Europe — not with pret but with home products

Until now, the Indian designers who trotted in the global mart were sartorial specialists, but apparently it is not just Manish Arora who shows in Paris. Three young Delhi-based designers showcased at Paris's Maison & Objet, one of the biggest home fairs in Europe, last week. And the trio displayed everything from bowls to throne-shaped chairs, all of them blending ancient styles and modern designing trends.

Kapil Mathur and his associate Shilpa Budhiraja, both 29 and newcomers to the market, created copper accessories in geometrical shapes. Since he launched his company Aline Design Industry last year, Mathur has been mostly selling his products to Indian shops, but Maison & Objet changed it, with international clients getting in touch with the duo. Mathur says Indian designs are suddenly capturing attention in the global bazaar. "Before 2000, what was going out of here was just an imitation of old Indian designs," says Mathur. "Now designers are giving a modern Indian edge to them."

Gunjan Gupta of the brand Wrap is one of these designers. A graduate of the London-based design and art school, Central College of St Martins, she has used old throne-decoration techniques to create silver-wrapped chairs that look radically modern. Gupta says this mix of styles has helped her get international clients, such as Sephora and Swarovski. "People are interested in Indian designs," she says, "but India has yet to make a mark."

True. It is difficult for India to compete with avant-garde designs from France and Italy. Phillipe Chomat, organiser of Maison & Objet, agrees: "Nowadays, there is no outstanding Indian designer at the international level." Thankfully, he adds: "But the Indian designers we showcased are to become famous."

Heading: Sonia meet off, Modi to rally against terror in city - Indian Express
Content:
'He was a good father, a good husband, a good citizen'

On Saturday afternoon, Chandra Bhan, 50, a driver with the MCD, left home in Karol Bagh with a promise to wife Laxmi: he would be back for dinner. By evening, Laxmi and son Chandra Prakash were waiting patiently at the police post in RML Hospital — a moment caught by Newsline on camera.

Minutes before that, she had learnt about the blasts on television and rang up his cellphone. There was someone else on the other end. "I knew right away that everything was over," Laxmi, waiting for Bhan's body at RML Hospital, said.

A policeman had answered Laxmi's call, Bhan's nephew Uday said. "He had said my uncle was among those injured in the blast at Gaffar Market, so we rushed to RML. But doctors here said he was dead on arrival," Uday said.

Uday said his uncle was the family's sole breadwinner. "But how am I going to explain this to his six-year-old son?"

Laxmi said young Chandra Prakash has not slept since Saturday. "He still insists on waiting till his father returned home. How am I going to explain to him what happened that evening?

"Sab barbaad ho gaya hai. How will his death change anything for terrorists? He was a good father, a good husband and a good citizen. Is this how we have been paid for being good citizens of this country?"

She does not know what lies in future but what she knows for certain is the fact that she cannot go back to the same house. The house where the family lived as one till Saturday. "His clothes, his things are all in that house," she said, amid sobs, "I will move out as soon as I can."

Heading: Two days on, CCTVs in markets still out of action - Indian Express
Content:
Kicking off the politicking over Saturday's bomb blasts, the Delhi BJP declared on Monday that Gujarat Chief Minister Narender Modi would hold an anti-terrorism rally in Ajmal Khan Park in Karol Bagh on Friday. Congress President Sonia Gandhi has, meanwhile, cancelled her rally scheduled for Wednesday.

The Delhi unit, like the BJP at the national level, is planning to use the security situation in the Capital in the upcoming Assembly elections. BJP prime ministerial candidate L K Advani will also be present. "The September 13 bomb blasts were a government-assisted act of terrorism. It could not have succeeded if the government had heeded the Gujarat chief minister's repeated warnings," Harshvardhan, Delhi BJP president, said. He was, however, quick to point out that they do not want to politicise the blasts.

The Delhi Congress has gone into a huddle since the bomb blasts and put a stop to all preparations for Sonia Gandhi's rally. She was scheduled to distribute provisional certificates to 11 RWAs and to congratulate the Delhi government for beginning the regularisation process for 40 lakh residents living in unauthorised colonies. "When the city is mourning, we did not want to celebrate. So we have postponed the rally. A fresh date will be announced later on," Delhi Congress President J P Aggarwal said. This decision was taken late on Saturday night, during a meeting between Chief Minister Sheila Dikshit and Sonia Gandhi.

The Sonia Gandhi rally was being seen by many as the beginning of campaigning for the Assembly elections. The BJP had earlier held a rally, attended by senior BJP leaders, on August 31.

Heading: L-G says make more citizens part of police eyes and ears scheme - Indian Express
Content:
Two days after serial bomb blasts shocked the Capital, the state of regular surveillance through Close Circuit Television (CCTV) cameras in the city's major markets remains a matter of concern.

While senior officers of the Delhi Police could not be contacted, shop owners in major markets say the cameras were installed only a few months ago. And almost all of them need 24-hour monitoring, as the "recording system" is still not in place at some police stations. Others either have very few cameras or many have stopped working due to neglect by the police.

Greater Kailash-I
Cameras at the GK-I M Block market were not able to capture images of the people who planted the two bombs, allegedly because the recording system is still not in place. Two days after the incident, one of the four cameras installed is not functioning. "It had developed some problem and we tried to repair it; it will take some time," a policeman posted at the market said on condition of anonymity. The camera is presently attached to a pole with the help of tape even though it is not functional. "The police hardly check the cameras and they have proved ineffectual even in solving cases of robbery in shops," a worker at the Prince Pan Shop, where the blast took place on Saturday, said.

Karol Bagh
The blast at Gaffar Market claimed close to 20 lives and many people are still critically injured. Here, there is just one camera installed at the crossing close to the site of the blast. S P Ratawal, MLA from Karol Bagh, said: "The camera at the crossing was facing the other way and there is no way it could have recorded images of the people who placed the bomb."

It is also possible that the camera was not working at all," he said.

There are at least 10 cameras installed in and around the market. Most of them were installed many years ago and had been checked close to a month ago. "The traders' associations had together paid more than Rs 1 crore for the cameras and monitoring system, while the Delhi Police had chipped in with about Rs 20 lakh," Ratawal said. "That cannot be enough," he said.

Sarojini Nagar
At the Sarojini Nagar Market, security was tightened on Monday and police personnel were deployed in the area. There are 27 cameras installed in and around the market and only one of them is not functional. "So few cameras cannot be enough for such a big market," Rajesh Chand, a shopkeeper, said. It was the shopkeepers who had paid for the cameras.

They still talk about the blast that shook the market on October 29, 2005. "We do not want such an incident to happen again," a worker at Shyam Juice Corner, where the bomb had been planted, said. Fifty people died in those blasts. Data from cameras in this market is also not recorded everyday, as there is no recording system in place. "The cameras are, however, monitored round-the-clock," a police officer at the Sarojini Nagar police station said. ACP Kumar Gyanesh could not be contacted for comments.

Lajpat Nagar
There are at least 30 cameras installed in and around the busy Lajpat Nagar Market and "all of them are functional", Dalbir Singh, the beat officer, said. Security arrangements have been tightened at the market, even as the number of people coming to the market has dropped to some extent, shopkeepers said. At least 16 people were killed in the May 23, 1996 blasts that rocked this market. The police station had arranged for CCTV cameras with the help of shopkeepers close to three months ago, Singh said. The recording of camera visuals has also been arranged but "is not totally functional" yet, he said.

Palika Bazaar
The bomb blast in Central Park was not very far from the Palika Bazaar, which was shut down within minutes of the blasts. While the NDMC has been planning to install 32 cameras in the market for the past eight months, the Palika Bazaar Welfare Association has already installed cameras in the market. "The NDMC and Delhi Police have been promising action but we have paid for a camera each at the nine entrances and also for the monitoring system, which is installed at the police station," Vinay Kumar, general secretary of the association, said. The police had not been able to capture images through the cameras installed around the central market, allegedly because they were not functional.

Heading: Class after blasts: more guards, talks on terror in schools - Indian Express
Content:
Urging the Delhi Police to work on the eyes and ears scheme initiated by Police Commissioner Y S Dadwal, Lieutenant Governor Tejendra Khanna has asked all deputy commissioners of police to be more vigilant and to include more and more local people in their security net, and also have a regular interaction with them.

Khanna has asked the police to seek help and cooperation from citizens to avert such incidents in the future.

These directions were given in a meeting held with all DCPs and Dadwal, chaired by the L-G this morning.

While Khanna said the eyes and ears scheme was helpful in diffusing the bomb found near Regal Cinema, he has asked the police commissioner to prepare a detailed master plan on security for the Capital.

Khanna said the damage caused by the blasts in GK Part I was far less than that in CP, because the market association was trained well by the police through drills.

When the second blast took place, people immediately evacuated the area and collected in the park, as per directions given out by the market association office bearers.

Heading: SC rap for Delhi govt’s ‘provisional regularisation’ - Indian Express
Content:
The terror weekend over, schoolchildren across the Capital got back to business on Monday. With a prayer in their heart for the victims, additional security personnel at the gates, and much discussion on braving the chilling times.

St Mary's School, Safdarjung, held prayers for the victims during their morning assembly today. Principal Annie Koshy said all schools should take a long-term perspective of terror. "We can give lessons to students on crisis management on a regular basis," she said. "Our teachers today asked the children to remain calm in the face of this crisis — there is nothing more to be done."

Richa Sakhuja, economics teacher at Vasant Valley School, said security at the gates has been tightened following Saturday's blasts. Tagore International-Vasant Vihar principal Madhulika Sen also said security has been raised, and that the students were told to avoid crowded areas.

Tejinder Khosla, of DPS-Noida, said discussions with students today revolved around topics such as helping people cope with the loss and security methods the children and their family and friends could follow while out in crowded public areas.

Tagore International School in East of Kailash would, meanwhile, hold a special assembly in memory of the blast victims on Tuesday. Principal Suman Nath said, "I may also ask some of the students to make posters to depict the need to reach out and help the victims and also the need to put up a brave face in these terror times." The school, though, has not taken a final decision on that, she added.

Some schools, however, put discussions on the blasts on the backburner, preferring to get on with life. Modern School principal Lata Vaidyanathan said, "We would prefer to carry on with regular schedule to make sure that the children remain free from terror. There is no need to create panic by continually discussing the blasts."

Jyoti Bose, principal of Springdales-Dhaula Kuan, also said the school did not emphasise discussions on the blasts since children anyway get exposed to scenes of terror on television "far too much". She said, "Our teachers talked to students in a general manner, about safety and avoiding crowded areas. But we don't plan to highlight the blasts because children are very sensitive to such things."

Heading: Battle for survival on in Capital’s hospitals - Indian Express
Content:
Taking strong exception to the Delhi government's much-advertised populist measure before the polls of providing "provisional regularisation" to unauthorised colonies in the city, the Supreme Court on Monday sought to know how it has gone ahead with the decision, without the court's nod.

After advocate Jasbir Singh Malik for the Delhi Pradesh Citizen's Council pointed to two specific orders — one passed in 2006 and another in 2008 — preventing the State from going ahead with regularisation unless it provides basic services, the bench headed by Justice Arijit Pasayat ordered the government to file an affidavit as to whether the order has been complied with.
