Each hi tech dairy would provide scientific methods of raring, management, feeding, breeding of milch animals along with the production of clean milk. "The first dairy will come up at Bohatwala village in Jind and the construction is in progress. Around 1000 milch animals are being procured by Baljit Singh, a farmer of the village, for the purpose," he said.

Under the scheme, anyone with more than 20 milch animals can apply for establishing a high-tech dairy. "The short-listed farmers would be first provided 11 days' training and then would be recommended to the various banks for providing loans on subsidised rates. Additionally, the department would be providing a subsidy of Rs 1.5 lakh to all those setting up such dairies," added Dangi.

The milk production from these dairies would then be purchased by the Haryana Dairy Development Corporative Federation at the best possible price. "The system would help generate a lot of employment too, besides augmenting the infrastructure for milk production," he said.

Heading: Wonder Kids - Indian Express
Content:
Time to let go of Friendship bands, Evil Eye bracelets and slip on a wristful of charms, the current style pick

Remember the time you were in school, when your cool quotient was judged by the number of colourful bands on your wrist. Friendship bands were as much a rage then as Lance Armstrong bands are now. While the former spoke of your popularity, the latter impressed with its contribution towards a cause. Then came the Turkish Evil Eye bracelets. Round blue balls with white dots for eyes coupled with some beads spelt their look. And whether they came in shipped from Turkey or the trinket store in the neighbouring sector, we all slipped them on with a vengeance!

So what brings us to talk about what's wrapping your wrist? Well, it's the next cool thing in the ever-changing accessory world and they are truly charming! "Bracelets have been around but the latest to arrive are bracelets with charms," they tell us at Trenz, the jewellery store in Sector 37 that has on its shelves bracelets with lots of trinkets hanging from them. Stars, moon, pearls, crystals, beads, marbles...there's enough jingle-jangling it's way in here.

Traditionally though, charm bracelets meant an inter-locked chain in either silver or gold with trinkets or small decoratives hanging from it. It is believed that in ancient Egypt charms were used for identification and as symbols of faith and luck but its Queen Victoria who actually made them fashionable and charming! "I like the chunkier versions that come with lots of attachments," mentioned model and emcee Divya Jaitely who was in town to host a show. If you are looking to flaunt one of your own, we spotted really nice ones at Dewsons in Sector 11, Ebony in Sector 9, Tit-Bits in Sector 19, Trenz in Sector 37 and the jewellery kiosk at DT Mall. As far as prices go, you don't have to have deep pockets. Rs 55 to Rs 250 should get you a natty one!.

Heading: Watch Out! - Indian Express
Content:
A world beyond mere love stories and entertainment, that's what Anita Shabdeesh creates through theatre

The arc lights of the stage have a charm but eventually it's the movies that most want to settle in. And if you are a woman the popular conceptions like glamour, entertainment and a lot more would force a bend in your path, again towards the silver screen. "That's precisely why we don't have many young girls taking to theatre. Even if they do, cinema remains the goal," Anita Shabdeesh has seen this happen but refused to be a part of it. Theatre is where she finds her ultimate satisfaction. The Mohali-based theatre actor-director presented Pali Bhupinder's 'Agali Dastak Hon Ton Pehlan' at the Punjab Kala Bhawan on Tuesday evening. With a mother as the protagonist, the play highlighted how women are the eventual victims of wars and riots.

"More girls should come forward to make theatre a commitment. Their lack is a terrible void in theatre in our region," Anita highlights, aware that money would any day prove more attractive than 'tapassya'. She, however, was lucky enough to have had the support of her family and later her husband Shabdeesh. "My father is a poet. Growing in a literary atmosphere it was natural for me to step onto the stage. Shabdeesh is a writer-poet so that works for all of us!" smiles Anita. As an actress she believes that there is no meaning in doing mere love stories and entertainment. "If I have to work regularly it makes more sense to utilize that time and effort to create awareness. We have enough of the rest already," Anita's group Suchetak Rangmanch has been working on those lines since '98. One common thread that one sees in her plays is the importance of female characters. Anita did venture into comedy with 'Kuchh Taan Karo Yaaron' last year but that too had a definite purpose. "I wanted to highlight that mere talks are leading us to nowhere. We must take definite steps to change things about and around us. And as portrayed in 'Agali Dastak Hon ton Pehlan', to change things we need to be born again!" she signs off.

Heading: RAIL TRAIL: Patiala State Mono Rail Tramways - Indian Express
Content: This comes as a mother of all surprises. Either the European sensibilities have changed or it's their way of thanking the Indian industry, especially Yash Chopra for promoting the place as a huge tourist attraction. We don't deny that fact that the film was a complete entertainer, but when 'Bachna Ae Haseeno' gets nominated for the Art Cinema Award at Filmfest Hamburg, you do rack your brains to find out why. The report states that this "Yash Raj Films production starring Ranbir Kapoor, Bipasha Basu, Deepika Padukone and Minissha Lamba, swayed critics and audiences in India and abroad with its fresh treatment, vibrant performances and sunny locales". Close on heels of its release in Germany, the film has appealed to 'critical' sensibilities in Europe and has also been selected for the official programme, and is part of Agenda 08. FYI: The Art Cinema Award was established in 1969 by the Confédération Internationale des Cinémas d'Art et d'Essai (C.I.C.A.E.) (International Confederation of Art House Cinemas). In Germany, the award is given at the Berlinale and at Filmfest Hamburg. Here's the catch: the confederation's extensive network will support the distribution of the winning film throughout Europe. Also, Filmförderung Hamburg Schleswig-Holstein is contributing 5,000 euros to the award in support of PR measures by the German distributor. As for the  international jury, it consists of directors Daniel Lavaud (France), Dietmar Zingl (Austria) and Erdmann Lange (Germany). Let's see how well these guys know bollywood. Watch out!

Heading: Viva Italia - Indian Express
Content:
The Patiala State Monorail Tramway engine is an unusual locomotive that runs on a single rail. Under this arrangement, nearly 98 per cent of the weight of the engine is placed on a single rail. The rest is supported by an additional wheel on an outrigger running on the road surface, on the side of the track. The idea was to run this locomotive with mules but it was finally run by steam power. Mr Bowles, an engineer with a British firm, worked on this type of monorail system and was successful. The then maharaja of Patiala, H.H. Maharaja Bhupinder Singh, was greatly impressed by his engineering skills and took him in his service. Thus, the first monorail was built between Sirhind and Alampur and later Morinda in undivided Punjab. The monorail system, however, failed as it came a few years too late. It could only solve the problem of finding a replacement for bullock carts, a problem solved in a different way by the advent of the Railway system.

Four such 0-3-0 locomotives were supplied by Orenstein and Koppel of Berlin in 1907. One monorail still survives on the plinth of the Diesel Component Works in Patiala and the other, still in working order, can be seen at the National Rail Museum in New Delhi.

This over 100-year-old engine is perhaps the only working steam monorail in the world. You can still ride it every Sunday afternoon at the National Rail Museum.

The Railways and the 1964 Olympic Gold
The date: November 23, 1964. It was the 41st minute of the hockey finals at the 15th Olympic Games in Tokyo, the first on Asian soil. Appropriately, two Asian giants, India and Pakistan, were playing the match. All ears were glued to the radio (those were the days before the advent of TV) and time stopped in India, as it did for every Indian at the stadium in Tokyo.

The ever-dependable Mohinder Lal, India's right half-back, walked slowly to the penalty spot that the umpire had pointed to in front of the Pakistani goal. Calm and composed, he took position and pushed the ball. It flew into the top of the net past the hapless Pakistani goalkeeper. India went ahead 1-0 and maintained that lead till the end of the match, regaining the Olympic hockey gold they had lost in 1960.

Mohinder Lal was a member of the Indian Railways and part of a great Railway heritage in Indian hockey. The penalty stroke that he converted was set up by another Railway man, Prithipal Singh, the penalty corner expert of the team, whose rasping shot had been stopped by a Pakistani defender with his leg. The 1964 team included another Railway man, mercurial centre forward Harbinder Singh, who also had a great tournament.
— J L singh, retired railway official

Heading: Fashion weak - Indian Express
Content:
A travelling Italian exhibition maps the history of art and design from post World War II to the present

For post-World War II Italy, the word design acquired a new dimension—the allusion of which ranged from functionality and clarity to lucidity. And how the pursuit of lucidity became a way of life for Italians and also gave rise to Italian pop art of the 60s, the Architettura Radicale experiments and the movement of the 80s is currently on display at an exhibition "Italian Genius Now" with 90 works of 53 creative minds at Travancore Palace at Kasturba Gandhi Marg. The venue was transformed to accommodate household objects such as lamps, designer furniture, a typewriter and even the iconic GS 150 Vespa designed by Corradino D'Ascanio in 1955 that put Italy on the world map.

Organized by Italian Cultural Institute and ICCR and promoted by Italian Ministry of Foreign Affairs, the itinerant exhibition opened on Monday evening with the new Ambassador Roberto Toscano hosting the ceremony. "The exhibition is not just about the most famous, but about people who did something inventive, radical and changed the design scene," says Sergio Fintoni, who has been the Director of Ent Art Polimoda, an Italian fashion school for several years.

No wonder, that the iconic Vespa shares space with

Salvatore Ferragamo sandals ranging from 1955-56 worn by legendary figures like Sophia Loren. "Ferragamo invented the ciabattino (cobbler) mule shoes, an example of exquisite craftsmanship combined with aesthetics," exults Fintoni. The exhibition is curated by Marco Bazzini of the Centre For Contemporary Art "Luigi Pecci".

Expounding on the history of Italy's radical design movement, Fintoni said, "It was the American buyers who renewed confidence in post WW-II Italian industry by investing money. In those days, labour was very cheap. Today's renowned designers, Gucci, Valentino and Emilio Pucci (now part of Louis Vuitton group) emerged from "those days". The Vespa, Fintoni explains stands for a bee and made a waspish noise. "It was designed for comfort but made a racket," smiles Fintoni.

This exhibition has works from the 40s to the radical architectural designs from the 70s of Isabella Gherardi and Stefano Giovannoni, the Italian designer who gave a playful touch to household items such as a tooth-pick box. "The idea was to make furniture or an object look ironical and funny," says Fintoni.

New York based Gaetono Pesce, the architect-artist-designer made a remarkable chair titled Nobody's Perfect (made in 2002) in orange, green and yellow in Polyurethane based with resin and nylon pins. It stands as a symbol of the merging between practical design and art. The show has been exhibited in Seoul, Taipei and Tokyo.

The exhibition is on display till September 28

Heading: This be the BeatThis be the Beat - Indian Express
Content:
It was a tepid opening for the HDIL India Couture Week

When the red carpet turns into a wet carpet, part of the venue's tent collapses, and it takes about an hour to get your car to hop across to the adjacent hotel for the after-party—the first day of India Couture Week wasn't exactly the lap de luxe.

If the elements can be forgiven, so be it. But a very senior designer's poorly put out collection was the real dampener. Ritu Kumar, the mistress of ready-to-wear and queen of prints, the designer every burgeoning fashionista dreams of getting married in, showcased a retrospective of all that Indian fashion used to be.

With a Rajasthan fort as backdrop (originality anyone?), Kumar presented a line of lehngas with churi sleeved cholis, chogas, long tunics, kutchi gathered coats worn over divided loose pants, ghararas, khara dupattas with intricate embellishments, interspersed with a line of antique textiles like kalamkari and jaamdaani. What were lovely embroideries and techniques, the treatment left us with a feeling of déjà vu.

The showstopper for the evening was Priyanka Chopra, delicious in a burgundy lehenga and an emerald choli, earned the hoots of Karan Johar and Varun Bahl on the front row, while Shabana Azmi and Javed Akhtar saved their nods for Neha Dhupia and Raima and Riya Sen. The Comeback Clique of Anna Bredmeyer, Sonalika Oberoi and Shyamoli Verma (she really needed a drink to calm her nerves) were still delightful to watch.

Among other guests, Madhu Sapre looked like a tropical tease in all black, Suchitra Pillai dressed like an astronaut and Rozza Catalano beamed in red.Kumar got a standing ovation, but as one Delhi designer told us later: "Out of respect for her age." The after-party was where the young and hip headed. Shah Rukh and Gauri Khan came with Raveena and Anil Thadani, Anil Kapoor, Fardeen Khan, Laila Khan Rajpal, Sohail Khan, Malaika Arora and Ritesh Deshmukh proved there's no shine like the afterglow of Bollywood.

Heading: Weather gods spoil the endgame - Indian Express
Content:
British Asian beatboxer Jason Singh returns to Rajasthan to look for that perfect beat

British Asian beatboxer Jason Singh's first performance in India was not at a fancy auditorium and that suited him just fine. "In 2006, I was a tourist travelling around Jaipur. I started beatboxing alongside some folk musicians at the City Palace, we were having a casual jam. It was amazing because people's reactions were of shock and amazement that there were all these sounds coming out of my mouth," says Singh, who subsequently performed professionally at the Rajasthan International Folk Festival in Jodhpur. For the uninitiated, beatboxing is the art of producing drum beats, rhythm, and musical sounds using one's mouth, lips, tongue and voice. Next month, Singh is one of the international artists performing at the annual festival in Jodhpur that counts Rolling Stone's Mick Jagger among it's official patrons.

But since his debut performance, Singh is neck-deep in collaborations with Rajasthani folk musicians and is manning an acoustic folk outfit called the Jodhpur Express. "It is a developmental music project which aims to preserve, nurture and share, to a national and international audience the folk music of Rajasthan. The name is inspired from one of the tracks we produced called Jaipur Express, because it moved like a huge train making its way across the deserts of Rajasthan. It consisted of folk musicians Munshi Khan on vocals and harmonium, Dawoo Khan on Khartals, Kuttla Khan on Morchang, Manzoor Khan on Dholak and myself on Beatbox," says Singh.

The project was initiated in November 2007 as a recording session at Morchang Studios in Jaipur. Supported by the Jaipur Virasat Foundation and the British Council, the idea behind the Jodhpur Express project is about creating music acoustically only. Singh asserts, the music has the quality and potential to go mainstream. He feels it would be a hit in international festivals and club venues, not just in concert halls. Singh self-confessedly enjoys collaborations as it enables him to express myself. "I can create a dialogue with another human being regardless of their race, political views, language or religion by using the universal language of music and feel totally natural," says Singh who will land in India in early October with British singer-songwriter/guitarist Bex Mather. Together, they will work together with a specially picked group of Rajasthani folk musicians. "We will have just two weeks to meet, collaborate and create a performance which will become the basis of the Jodhpur Express album and tour," says Singh. Book your tickets to the festival now for an evening of vocal and percussive jugalbundis, soaring vocals, beatboxing and percussion battles.

Heading: Backward journey: Randhawa eyeing home advantage - Indian Express
Content:
Despite being out of contention, the St John's Secondary School, Shillong and Scottish Universities Mission Institution, Darjeeling, had a lot to play for in their under-17 pre-quarter-final league match of the Subroto Cup at the Ambedkar Stadium on Wednesday.

The Darjeeling team, first in four decades from the West Bengal hill station to make the main round of the tournament, wanted to end their historic appearance on a high. The Meghalaya team also had a reason to believe they could've signed off with a win under conditions that were identical to those back home.

If only the weather gods had relented. The match that started late due to rain didn't even last the first half after a fresh spell of showers. Meghalaya were leading 1-0 when the match was stopped.

The enthusiasm in qualifying after 41 years was evident in Shailendtra Tamang's restless to-and-fro walks inside the tunnel leading to the ground. "Former India captain Prem Dorji was also from our institution. He also played for Mohunbagan and East Bengal," he said.

This year, SUMI have squandered an opportunity to add to that history but coach Ganesh Dahal attributed it to the unfamiliar playing conditions.

"The environment was completely new for the boys. They just didn't get time to acclimatise. The grounds in Kalimpong are sandy. So the basic techniques need to be adjusted. And today, conditions got even tougher with the slippery surface," said Dahal.

Meghalaya coach Bobby Lnongbet and his wards, though, were home amid the slipperiness, mud and small pools in front of the goal posts and Dennis Mawphniiang didn't take long to put his team ahead.

Bobby in fact wished that conditions were like this when his team played and lost to Mizoram and Chandigarh in their previous matches. "Had it been raining during the matches against Mizoram and Chandigarh, who knows we might have won," said Bobby.

Other results: Pre-quarterfinal league: Sub-juniors (u-14): Army Boys (Lucknow) defeated The Air Force School, Subroto Park, New Delhi 6-0 with goals from Robert Metie (3), Lenin Angom (1), Roel Lepcha (1) and Bijay Subba (1). Govt. Kolasib High School (Mizoram) defeated SAI (Haryana) 2-0 with goals from Lallawmkima and Lalrosanga.

Heading: In-form Simi takes lead - Indian Express
Content:
Being a regular on the European Tour has its advantages. Among other things, that elusive trip to a Manchester United game may not be too far for Jyoti Randhawa. "There is little time to travel around golf, but now that I've become good friends with Ian Poulter, hopefully he'll give me a ride on his private jet," he laughs, sitting in what he calls his backyard, his neighbourhood DLF golf course in Gurgaon.

But the English golfer wasn't the only friend Randhawa found himself on the journey through Europe, a severe case of 'British bug' has left the 36-year-old's season's showings rather itchy.

In his last 10 tournments on the tour, Randhawa missed cut in six. The highest finish in the other four was a tied 43rd in the BMW International in Germany. Not really the state of mind you would want to bring into the high-pressure tournaments at home.

"I've been laid low with this virus that seems to come back every time I'm in Britain. It's really been a hard past few months, as each time I seemed to get my touch back, the virus returned," he says. "In fact I haven't yet completely recovered."

Back in India to defend two titles, the DLF Masters starting Thursday and the Indian Open in early October, Randhawa feels it's the right time to get back into rhythm.

Better under pressure
"It's a good thing I tend to play better under pressure," he laughs. "With so many people expecting you to do well, following you around the course, I just feel like giving my best. But it's important also to keep the negatives of a pressure situation blocked."

He gave ample proof of the fact that he's not completely out of touch at the BMW PGA Championship, ironically in Surrey, England, during one of the healthy patches. Randhawa finished in fifth spot, above names like Retief Goosen, Angel Cabrera and Paul Casey.

"That is a big positive I can take away from the season till now. Whenver I'm facing tough times, I like to look back on happy memories, try to recall what I did right."

There is the small matter of the World Cup in November, where he plays with Jeev Milkha Singh in one of the few tournaments where golfers get to wear their nation's colours. "We have a really good team. Jeev has been in great touch, and I feel it's time I got consistent," Randhawa says.

But before that is of course the Indian Open, where Randhwa will try what has never been done in the tournament's history: win it for the fourth time in a row.

"I have many happy memories on that course, and I'm sure there'll be a lot of pressure too, so it's a perfect situation for me," he smiles.

Bigger purse and some big names
Gurgaon: The second edition of the DLF Masters features top names from the PGTI field and an increased prize money of Rs. 80 lakh.

Jyoti Randhawa, the defending champion is back, and joining him will be his European Tour mate Shiv Kapur, Asian Tour stars Gaurav Ghei and Digvijay Singh, domestic tour bigwigs Ashok Kumar, Rahul Ganapathy and Mukesh Kumar, and youngsters Gaganjeet Bhullar and Himmat Singh Rai.

The tournament also features a new format, with the pro-am being spread over a two-day team event. An amateur wll be attached to two professionals each in the three-balls for the weekend action, with the team score counting towards the team championship prize. Two best scores will count out of the three on a hole-by-hole basis.

Heading: Lohan keeps lead despite bad finish - Indian Express

Heading: Disaster management cell a disaster - Indian Express
Content:
Abhinav Lohan's bright day ended somewhat palely. Two-under and looking at stretching his overnight lead to dominating proportions, Lohan finished with two bogeys in his last three holes to finish the second round at the LG Golden Greens Amateur even par. He still keeps a big lead, though cut to four shots now.

He stays at five-under par at the halfway stage, with Rudresh Sharma in second after a one-under on Wednesday.

Starting from the 10th tee, Lohan played solidly to be two-under after 15 holes before two consecutive bogeys on the seventh and the eighth holes undoing all the good work.

On the seventh, Lohan's second shot went past the green and a poor chip resulted in a bogey. With a big lead from the first round, that one bogey wasn't disastrous, but another dropped shot right after spoilt his chance of carding two consecutive under-par rounds.

Speaking about that eighth hole bogey, Lohan said: "My tee shot found the bunker and I thought I would be able to make the up and down but my ball was plugged in the bunker, making it nearly impossible to control the shot out of the sand."

Following his even par 72 in the first round, Rudresh's one-under 71 was just in time to propel him up the leaderboard.

A double bogey on the 13th hole looked like spoiling his card but he made up for it with an eagle on the fifth. He seemed pretty chuffed after his round, but did add a note of caution: "I want to keep my head down and play well in the next two rounds. I might have a chance on the final day."

In-form local boy Rashid Khan could only manage two-over, and will start the third round in the penultimate group. Despite an improved performance by the players, the cut fell at fifteen-over par because of the big numbers the players carded on the first day. Tour veteran Simarjeet Singh was one of the big names to miss out.

Heading: Who goofed up? IB, city police pass the buck - Indian Express
Content:
Meant as a one-stop shop to coordinate relief work in emergency, it gets household queries; got none on blasts evening

On June 24, Chief Minister Sheila Dikshit inaugurated the Capital's first Disaster Management Call Centre helpline: 1077. A novel idea that came into being after several hiccups, the call centre was meant as a one-stop centre for all disaster management operations.

On Saturday evening, when five bombs ripped the Capital in three areas leaving 28 dead and nearly 130 injured, there were no calls to the specialised cell.

In fact, ever since inception instead of handling disaster, 1077 is fielding domestic and civic problems. Here's one query: "How can we provide help to physically challenged persons?" A senior government official admitted as much: "Most residents take it as a helpline to lodge civic-related complaints to the government."

Developed on lines of other international helplines, the call centre is supposed to inform and coordinate with all other agencies and stakeholders the moment it receives a call about a mishap. An 'incident command system' is also in place, on paper at least.

All that came to nothing, though, on Saturday.

"We cannot take action on our own or based on media reports — the situation could get more slipshod in that case," said Goutam Banerjee, Head (Projects), Vcon Services, the private firm that has received outsourced work of the call centre. "We can get into action only after we receive calls informing us about the situation.

"Even on Saturday, initial media reports said it was only a cylinder blast."

Delhi government officials, meanwhile, are on the backfoot. Vinay Kumar, convener of the Disaster Management Authority of Delhi, "I rang up 1077 soon after the blast. The call centre immediately alerted the administrative staff, hospitals and blood banks. We did not inform the police and fire service (because) they were already at the site."

How the centre works
The call centre is meant to come into action after mishaps such as building collapse, earthquake, fire, flood, landslide, railway or road accident, and terrorist attacks among others. There is an action plan to tackle each such emergency.

According to protocol, each call is recorded in the call logger and the record — right down to minute details — is to be maintained forever. Among these are facts like caller's name, location of incident, and type of incident. As part of the system as soon as the mishap location is mentioned, phone numbers of the concerned police station and administrative officers would flash on screen. While the call centre agents alert fire department, hospitals and police officers, text messages are simultaneously sent out to other stakeholders.

A list of officers under emergency support function is maintained at the call centre. This list includes key officers of MTNL, Delhi Fire Service, Delhi Police, Home Guard, Home Department of Delhi Government, Delhi Health Service, CAT, Indian Red Cross Society, Delhi Jal Board, Irrigation and Flood Control, Delhi Development Authority, MCD, PWD, NDMC, CPWD, NCC, and scouts.

The call centre is supposed to coordinate with each agency to closely monitor rescue work. All this, though, was missing when Delhi bled on Saturday evening.
